items.title: mltreelib
items.text:
Tree-based machine learning with a Rust core. A data & feature layer that treats missing data as first-class, an adjustable benchmark generator with known ground truth, and a tree learner that handles categoricals and missing values natively — with rpart-faithful printing, SVG diagrams, and LightGBM-style monotone & interaction constraints.

  • Rust core (mltreelib-core), thin Python shell (PyO3)
  • Scikit-learn-shaped API — without the scikit-learn dependency
  • NA and NaN handled end-to-end: missing in → missing out; imputation opt-in
  • 51 TabArena-v0.1 benchmark datasets on board, plus a generator whose knobs control how much signal lives in group and hierarchy structure

The canonical suite is documented in the dataset manifest. Use it to find each dataset's target, size, license, and OpenML source before running a benchmark.

Optional agent skill

Install the repository skill separately from the Python package: npx skills add jkapila/mltreelib --skill mltreelib. See the public skill source.

items.title: Featured Technical Articles
items.text:
Explore our in-depth architectural and commercial case studies:

  1. Decision Trees for Credit Scoring Regulatory Compliance & Fintech: How tree paths, constraints and calibration support model review.
  2. Zero-Imputation Predictive Maintenance for Industrial Sensor Feeds Industrie 4.0 & Sensor Telemetry: A synthetic example of missing sensor values and tree routing.
  3. Uplift Modeling with Causal Trees Commercial Decision Optimization: How an honest causal tree compares targeting policies on a randomized held-out trial.
  4. Cubist Models and C5.0 Rules Core Systems ML: Linear leaves, extracted rules and the contracts still to check.
  5. Beyond Mean Squared Error: Distributional Decision Trees for Heavy Tails, Insurance, and Censored Data Actuarial & Risk Modeling: Tweedie compound Poisson-Gamma claims, Tobit censored log-likelihood, and heteroscedastic volatility regimes.
  6. Breaking the Step Function: Model Trees and Step Functions for Continuous Regression Systems ML & Physics-Informed ML: How linear leaves represent local trends and why fair comparisons need held-out data.
  7. Segregate First, Model Later: Two-Stage Hierarchical Survival Trees for Longitudinal Cohorts Actuarial & Retention Analytics: How decoupling ID-level cohort discovery from leaf-level Kaplan-Meier curves eliminates right-censoring bias and non-proportional hazard violations.

Try it right now

uv run python examples/quickstart.py fits a tree, prints it in rpart format and writes an SVG diagram. The end-to-end walkthrough then does the same on 10,000 real bank customers.

The research program, roadmap and contribution rules live in the repository (README.md, AGENTS.md).

items.title: Field notes: what it actually costs to just run a tree
items.text: Building the Elo arena meant wiring up every major tree/model-tree implementation. The friction is the point of this page: mltreelib is one import with zero transitive quirks, and this is what the alternatives cost.

items.title: The hassle log (all real, all this week)
items.text: what what happened perpetual (Rust GBM) imports sklearn internally — install fails at runtime without scikit-learn, error surfaces only on first fit ctboost sklearn-style estimators refuse to import without scikit-learn ("ctboost scikit-learn estimators require scikit-learn") catboost 92MB wheel; on a slow link the whole benchmark blocks on the download forust (Rust GBM) regression objective is objective_type="SquaredLoss" — "SquaredError" raises ValueError; the name is only in the API docs R Cubist the function is cubist() (lowercase) though the class is Cubist R grf local_linear_forest was renamed ll_regression_forest in 2.x; lm_forest is a causal forest that demands W; predict is S3, not grf::predict R packages on this box site-library not writable → R_LIBS_USER + user library dance sklearn trees cannot consume NAs at all — mean-imputation required before fit PyPI/README hunting install names ≠ import names (py-forust vs forust), example fences not greppable, bot-blocked pages

items.title: What our side of the page looks like
items.text:
from mltreelib import ModelTree            # that is the install story
m = ModelTree(leaf="linear")               # or leaf="mean", leaf_cols="path"
m.fit(x, y)                                # x may contain None — NAs first-class
m.predict(x)                               # never fails on a missing value
m.leaves()[0]                              # coef, na_coef, mean, std, quantiles
m.profile()                                # per-level timings built in
  • one dependency family (Rust core + thin Python shell);
  • NAs are first-class (learned split directions, NA-indicator leaf terms);
  • every leaf keeps its statistics and a t-digest;
  • the tree reproduces rpart exactly when configured as CART (mean leaves), so results are checkable against the reference implementations.

items.title: How the Elo works (our protocol)
items.text:
Elo comes from chess: every model carries a rating; when two models "play", the winner takes points from the loser proportionally to how surprising the result was.

  • Expected score of A against B: E_A = 1 / (1 + 10^((R_B - R_A) / 400)) (equal ratings → 50%; a 200-point underdog still expects ~24%).
  • After a game with actual score S_A (1 win, 0.5 draw, 0 loss): R_A += K * (S_A - E_A), R_B += K * (S_B - E_B), with K = 32 here.

What counts as a game: on each dataset, every unordered pair of models plays once — lower RMSE wins (equal RMSE = draw). So 16 datasets × n·(n-1)/2 games per full field. The order is deterministic (datasets sorted, pairs lexicographic), so the whole board is reproducible from the score file.

How to read it:

  • Ratings are relative — the zero point moves when models enter or leave (the same tree scored 901 with 13 models and 858 with 18). Watch the ordering and the gaps, not the absolute numbers.
  • One model with several flavors (our three leaf kinds) splits its own wins — treat them as separate competitors, which is intended.
  • K = 32 keeps the board responsive to real differences; over 5 datasets a genuinely better model climbs fast.
  • TabArena's numbers are not comparable — different protocol (their own tournament + bootstrapping on 51 datasets incl. classification). They are a scale anchor only.

Reproduce: elo_prepare.py (data, once) → elo_score_r.R → elo_score_python.py → elo_score_rust.py (each environment, incremental upsert) → elo_report.py (this Elo computation).

items.title: Why this page exists
items.text: Benchmarks should be about models, not plumbing. The Elo arena (examples/elo_prepare.py → elo_score_r.R / elo_score_python.py / elo_score_rust.py → elo_report.py, one scores file) exists so the field can be re-run incrementally — but assembling it highlighted how much incidental complexity the alternatives impose. That complexity is our documentation.

items.title: Installation
items.text: Install mltreelib as a Python wheel with a Rust core. Model fitting and inference require no additional Python packages.

items.title: From PyPI
items.text: pip install mltreelib

items.title: With uv
items.text: uv add mltreelib

items.title: From source
items.text:
Building from source needs a Rust toolchain (rustup) and maturin:

git clone https://github.com/jkapila/mltreelib
cd mltreelib
uv sync --group dev
uv run maturin develop --release

items.title: Verify the install
items.text:
python -c "import mltreelib; print(mltreelib.__version__)"

If you use uv, run the command with uv run python. Continue to the quickstart to fit and inspect your first tree.

items.title: Dataset loading (optional extra)
items.text:
Install the dataset extra to read the package's Parquet datasets.

pip install "mltreelib[dataset]"
# or
uv add "mltreelib[dataset]"

items.title: Plotting (optional extra)
items.text:
Charts and diagrams ride on the standard rendering wheels — install them only when you build figures:

pip install "mltreelib[plotting]"   # matplotlib + pygraphviz + seaborn
# or
uv sync --extra plotting

mltreelib.plots (metric charts) and ModelTree.to_dot() + pygraphviz (tree diagrams) are the two consumers. The core library never imports them.

items.title: What you get
items.text:
ModelTree the tree: fit / predict, rpart-style text, SVG diagram, constraints 14 encoders OneHot, Hashing, Target, CatBoost, WoE, James-Stein, Count, Leave-One-Out, M-Estimator, Base-N, Sum, Quantile, TF-IDF, Embedding scalers & builders VariableScaler, GroupedScaler, DatasetBuilder, IndexMapper Metrics regression / classification / regression-by-group reports dataset helpers list_datasets, load_dataset, summarize, generate, calendar / lag / window transforms

Numerics run in the Rust core; the data layer is the same code the benchmarks run on.

items.title: Quickstart
items.text:
Fit a high-performance model tree on real tabular data in seconds, inspect its transparent decision paths, and evaluate how piecewise linear leaves eliminate step-function distortion.

The complete executable script lives at examples/quickstart.py:

uv run python examples/quickstart.py

items.title: 1. Why Model Trees Outperform Standard CART
items.text:
Standard decision trees (CART) predict a constant mean in each leaf node. On continuous tabular surfaces, this creates rigid staircase artifacts that require excessive depth and overfitting to approximate simple linear trends.

ModelTree(leaf="linear") decouples the tree partition search from leaf estimation. The tree discovers optimal split thresholds while terminal leaves fit regularized linear ridge regressions, capturing local slopes smoothly at shallow depth.

items.title: 2. Fit and Evaluate on Real Benchmark Data
items.text:
We evaluate on the industrial benchmark Concrete Compressive Strength (Yeh 19981; 1,030 mixtures, 8 continuous ingredients).

Why Decouple Tree Search from Leaf Estimation?

Evaluating multivariate linear models at every candidate split threshold incurs massive combinatorial overhead. ModelTree uses fast variance or structural break heuristics to discover partition boundaries, then solves the closed-form regularized ridge system once per terminal leaf node.

Dataset Provenance: Concrete Compressive Strength

Collected by Prof. I-Cheng Yeh (1998) at Chung-Hua University1. Features 1,030 lab mixtures quantifying how 7 cementitious ingredient ratios (cement, slag, fly ash, water, superplasticizer, coarse aggregate, fine aggregate) and curing age interact nonlinearly to determine compressive yield stress (MPa).

ModelTree (Linear Ridge)Standard CART (Constant Mean) 
from mltreelib import Metrics, ModelTree, load_dataset

# 1. Load benchmark dataset (1,030 mixtures, 8 features)
data = load_dataset("concrete_compressive_strength")
target = "ConcreteCompressiveStrength"
feature_names = [col for col in data["columns"].keys() if col != target]
n_rows = data["n_rows"]

X = [[data["columns"][c][i] for c in feature_names] for i in range(n_rows)]
y = data["columns"][target]

# 80/20 train/test split
split_idx = int(n_rows * 0.8)
X_train, y_train = X[:split_idx], y[:split_idx]
X_test, y_test = X[split_idx:], y[split_idx:]

# Fit mltreelib ModelTree (piecewise linear ridge leaves, depth=3)
model_tree = ModelTree(leaf="linear", max_depth=3, min_rows=20, l2=1e-3)
model_tree.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=feature_names)
pred_mt = model_tree.predict(X_test)

# Measure holdout metrics
metrics = Metrics()
m_mt = metrics.regression(y_test, pred_mt)
print(f"ModelTree (Linear): RMSE = {m_mt['rmse']:.2f} MPa, R2 = {m_mt['r2']:.3f}, MAE = {m_mt['mae']:.2f} MPa")

from mltreelib import Metrics, ModelTree, load_dataset

data = load_dataset("concrete_compressive_strength")
target = "ConcreteCompressiveStrength"
feature_names = [col for col in data["columns"].keys() if col != target]
n_rows = data["n_rows"]

X = [[data["columns"][c][i] for c in feature_names] for i in range(n_rows)]
y = data["columns"][target]

split_idx = int(n_rows * 0.8)
X_train, y_train = X[:split_idx], y[:split_idx]
X_test, y_test = X[split_idx:], y[split_idx:]

# Fit standard CART decision tree (constant mean leaves, depth=3)
cart = ModelTree(leaf="mean", max_depth=3, min_rows=20)
cart.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=feature_names)
pred_cart = cart.predict(X_test)

metrics = Metrics()
m_cart = metrics.regression(y_test, pred_cart)
print(f"CART (Mean)       : RMSE = {m_cart['rmse']:.2f} MPa, R2 = {m_cart['r2']:.3f}, MAE = {m_cart['mae']:.2f} MPa")

items.title: 3. Empirical Results & Performance Comparison
items.text:
Loaded Concrete Compressive Strength: 1030 rows, 8 features.
Train rows: 824, Test rows: 206

=== Model Performance on Test Set ===
Standard Decision Tree (CART)  : RMSE = 11.09 MPa, R2 = 0.566, MAE = 8.47 MPa
mltreelib ModelTree (Linear)   : RMSE = 7.28 MPa, R2 = 0.813, MAE = 5.07 MPa
--> Error reduction with linear leaves: 34.3%
Model Leaf Formulation Depth Test RMSE (MPa) Test \(R^2\) Test MAE (MPa) Standard CART Constant Mean 3 11.09 0.566 8.47 mltreelib ModelTree Regularized Linear Ridge 3 7.28 0.813 5.07

With identical tree topology (depth 3, 8 leaves), ModelTree achieves a 34.3% error reduction and increases explained variance from 56.6% to 81.3%.

  • Left Panel (Parity Plot): Predictions from ModelTree(leaf="linear") cluster tightly along the 1:1 diagonal, whereas CART's predictions are constrained to horizontal bands corresponding to leaf means.
  • Right Panel (Response Profile): Along the gradient of Cement content, CART produces wide step discontinuities, while ModelTree preserves the physical continuous response curve.

items.title: Benchmark datasets
items.text:
datasets/ holds the full TabArena-v0.1 suite: 51 curated tabular datasets (87.4 MB, OpenML suite 457) — 7 regression, 44 classification, 4 small (<1k rows), 40 medium, 7 large (up to 150k rows), including high-cardinality categorical sets. Files are parquet with categoricals preserved as strings; datasets/MANIFEST.md lists per-dataset target, size, license and source.

from mltreelib import list_datasets, load_dataset

list_datasets()                 # ['APSFailure', 'Bank_Customer_Churn', ...]
ds = load_dataset("churn")
ds["n_rows"], ds["n_cols"]      # 5000, 20
ds["dtypes"]                    # {"state": "categorical", "account_length": "numeric", ...}
ds["na_counts"]                 # missing shown by default

load_dataset returns the same shape as DatasetBuilder.build(), so it feeds straight back into the data layer.

BeyondArena

The beyond-IID extension (temporal/grouped splits) ships via the separate data-foundry package and is intentionally not vendored; see the manifest for notes.

items.title: What changed in this update
items.text:
The v0.4.11 rerun scored all 56 tasks and completed QSAR-TID-11 and Superconductivity, which timed out in the earlier round. The original Diamonds split overwrote its y feature and left z in the target position. We restored the nine features, used price as the target, and rescored all 35 Diamonds entrants. Other peer scores come from the archived arena.

Peer Diamonds RMSE ModelTree regression W–T–L ModelTree classification W–T–L CatBoost(200) 537.58 0–0–18 10–1–27 LightGBM(200) 539.08 2–0–16 13–1–24 ChimeraBoost 520.64 0–0–18 10–2–26

ModelTree scored 761.10 RMSE on corrected Diamonds. The head-to-head counts use test RMSE for regression and test accuracy for classification. Overall Elo depends on each entrant's matches against the full field, which explains how ModelTree can rank above LightGBM while losing more of their direct matches.

items.title: How the local board works
items.text:
• Regression uses a seeded random 80/20 split. Classification uses a seeded stratified 80/20 split. Both use seed 7. The suite combines 51 TabArena-v0.1 datasets with five additional regression datasets.
  • The overall board starts ratings at 1,000 and applies round-robin updates with K = 32. It processes regression RMSE first and classification accuracy second. The classification board also ranks test log loss separately.
  • The dataset column counts available score rows. The saved regression snapshot includes one infinite RMSE for the historical ModelTree(opt) on fc2008. It ranks below finite RMSE for that task.
  • The ModelTree rerun used a 180-second budget per dataset. Diamonds peer reruns used 300 seconds. Reported runtimes combine separate runs and are best read as context for those scores.
  • The public TabArena leaderboard uses its own folds, metrics, and entrant pool. Its Elo values describe that tournament.

items.title: Beyond mean squared error: choose a tree split for the outcome you have
items.text:
A tree split chooses what patterns the model pays attention to. Squared error gives large absolute misses more weight. This can be a sensible choice when absolute errors matter. A different criterion can prioritize structure at different scales or account for how the target was observed.

We will fit two shallow trees on real Miami home sales and compare their held-out errors. This isolates the split criterion with the same tree size controls, feature list and mean-leaf setting.

items.title: Get the data and fit both trees
items.text:
Save the OpenML Miami housing Parquet to datasets/miami_housing.parquet. It has 13,776 sales and a positive sale-price target, SALE_PRC. The example selects five features directly related to the property. It samples 6,000 training and 2,000 test records after shuffling. For a market forecast, hold out later transactions, and consider holding out geographic areas as well.

Clone the repo, run uv sync, then run the code from the root.

from statistics import mean

from examples.real_tree_studies import load, rows
from mltreelib import Metrics, ModelTree

df = load("miami_housing", 46942).sample(frac=1, random_state=2026)
features = ["LND_SQFOOT", "TOT_LVG_AREA", "age", "OCEAN_DIST", "structure_quality"]
train, test = df.iloc[:6000], df.iloc[6000:8000]
x_train, x_test = rows(train, features), rows(test, features)
y_train, y_test = train.SALE_PRC.tolist(), test.SALE_PRC.tolist()
metrics = Metrics()

print("mean baseline", metrics.regression(y_test, [mean(y_train)] * len(test))["rmse"])
for gain in ("sse", "tweedie"):
    tree = ModelTree(gain=gain, tweedie_p=1.5, leaf="mean",
                     max_depth=2, min_rows=40, prune="none")
    tree.fit(x_train, y_train, col_names=features)
    pred = tree.predict(x_test)
    print(gain, metrics.regression(y_test, pred)["rmse"], tree.splits()[0])

The Tweedie variance function increases with the mean as mean ** p. Here the value of p stays fixed at 1.5 to make the comparison reproducible. We compare both models on the same sale-price units using RMSE. If the decision calls for relative or deviance-based loss, choose that metric before fitting and compare both models again.

items.title: What changed in the real example?
items.text:
Split or baseline Test RMSE Training mean 316,190 Squared error 222,710 Tweedie deviance 217,425

Tweedie splits reduced test RMSE by about 2.4% relative to squared-error splits in this run. Use a fresh split or paired resampling to assess how much this difference varies. Sale prices here are positive, so the comparison does not test the zero-mass use case.

Both models use mean leaves, so their scores are point estimates. A specialized split criterion does not change a point estimate into a probability distribution. The residual panel shows errors by observed sale price. Check large misses and their locations before choosing a model for pricing.

items.title: When do you need a different objective?
items.text:
What the target records Start with Check on holdout Numeric amount with absolute error costs Squared error RMSE, MAE and residuals by price range Nonnegative amount with many genuine zeros and a positive tail Tweedie deviance Zero fraction, aggregate bias and calibration of the conditional mean A measured value capped or floored by the collection process Tobit under a defensible latent model Boundary frequency and fit for uncensored outcomes Time until event or end of follow-up A survival tree Censoring-aware scores at supported horizons Similar means but changing spread across regimes Heteroscedastic splitting Test error and spread within each regime

A zero claim, a reading floored by a sensor and an event censored by study end represent different observations. Clarify the observation process before choosing a loss. A Tobit claim depends on its latent distribution assumptions. A survival claim depends on follow-up and censoring assumptions.

uv run python examples/real_tree_studies.py housing

See the split criteria example for controlled cases and the FLCHAIN survival pathway for censored follow-up. For a primary reference on Tweedie modeling, see Dunn and Smyth (2005).

items.title: Decision tree regression with linear leaves: a worked diamond price example
items.text: Consider a 0.95-carat and a 0.99-carat diamond with the same grades. If they reach the same constant leaf, a conventional regression tree predicts the same price for both. A linear leaf can assign different prices inside that region. We can test whether that flexibility improves predictions by changing only the leaf type.

items.title: How do constant and linear leaves work?
items.text:
A mean leaf predicts the average training outcome in its region. A linear leaf fits a local equation. For two features, that equation can look like intercept + b1 * carat + b2 * width. Routing still happens first. The tree determines which local equation applies.

The trade-off is fit versus support. A shallow mean tree needs enough splits to approximate a curved price surface. A linear leaf needs enough data to estimate coefficients, particularly when carat and physical dimensions are correlated. Predictions on opposite sides of a split can still jump.

items.title: Train both trees on real data
items.text:
Download OpenML diamonds 46923 to datasets/diamonds.parquet. Clone the repo, run uv sync, then run this code from its root. The seed fixes the random split. It keeps 6,000 training and 2,000 test observations. The input carries cut, color and clarity as raw labels.

from statistics import mean

from examples.real_tree_studies import load, rows
from mltreelib import Metrics, ModelTree

df = load("diamonds", 46923).sample(frac=1, random_state=2026)
train, test = df.iloc[:6000], df.iloc[6000:8000]
features = df.columns.drop("price").tolist()
types = ["categorical" if c in {"cut", "color", "clarity"} else "numeric"
         for c in features]
x_train, x_test = rows(train, features), rows(test, features)
y_train, y_test = train.price.tolist(), test.price.tolist()
metric = Metrics()
print("global mean", metric.regression(y_test, [mean(y_train)] * len(test))["rmse"])

for leaf in ("mean", "linear"):
    tree = ModelTree(leaf=leaf, max_depth=2, min_rows=40, prune="none")
    tree.fit(x_train, y_train, col_names=features, dtypes=types)
    predicted = tree.predict(x_test)
    print(leaf, metric.regression(y_test, predicted)["rmse"])
    print(tree.splits()[0], tree.leaves()[0])

items.title: Where do the models make mistakes?
items.text:
Prediction Test RMSE Global training mean 3,998 Mean leaves 1,712 Linear leaves 1,367

Both trees include a split on carat at 0.87. The linear leaves reduced test RMSE by about 20% compared with the mean leaves in this run. The first leaf had 3,582 training records.

The residual plot puts observed price on the horizontal axis and prediction minus observed price on the vertical axis. Large negative values are underestimates. Horizontal bands and repeated patterns can reveal that the model gives common predictions to very different records. A falling cloud at the high end can matter even if the average error improves.

Check support before reading a coefficient. A local carat coefficient describes the fit within a leaf while its other inputs stay fixed. The data may contain few plausible combinations where width stays constant as carat changes. Inspect actual cases and the training range before using the coefficient for a pricing decision.

items.title: Does this beat gradient boosting?
items.text:
This experiment compares two leaf types at the same depth and support setting. A comparison with gradient boosting needs the same data split, tuning budget and metrics. Include train time, inference time and failed runs if those matter. Use validation to choose the configuration. A cheaper model can be useful if its residuals are acceptable where the business acts.

uv run python examples/real_tree_studies.py diamonds

For the origin of model trees, see Quinlan, Learning with Continuous Classes (1992). For a controlled missing-data check and a separate real explanation, see the regression pathway.

items.title: Cubist-style model trees in Python: explain a concrete strength prediction
items.text:
Concrete strength depends on the recipe and curing age. It is plausible that those relationships differ across mixtures. A model tree divides the measurements into regions and fits a local equation in each region. We can inspect those regions and test whether the local equations improve held-out predictions.

Cubist and M5 motivate this combination of partitions and linear models. C5.0 belongs to a related lineage for classification and rule sets. Here we use ModelTree in mltreelib, whose tree fit runs in Rust and is exposed through Python. The exercise compares its mean and linear leaves. It does not reproduce every Cubist or C5.0 rule and committee feature.

items.title: Prepare real concrete measurements
items.text:
Download OpenML concrete compressive strength 46917 to datasets/concrete_compressive_strength.parquet. The UCI source describes the eight inputs and the response in MPa. The dataset includes 1,030 experiments. This tutorial uses 824 for training and 206 for testing. Similar recipes can appear in both parts of this random split. Use grouped recipe or batch splits for claims about new mixes.

Clone the repo, run uv sync, and run this code from the root.

from examples.real_tree_studies import load, rows
from mltreelib import Metrics, ModelTree

target = "ConcreteCompressiveStrength"
df = load("concrete_compressive_strength", 46917).sample(frac=1, random_state=2026)
train, test = df.iloc[:824], df.iloc[824:]
features = df.columns.drop(target).tolist()
for leaf in ("mean", "linear"):
    tree = ModelTree(leaf=leaf, max_depth=2, min_rows=40, prune="none")
    tree.fit(rows(train, features), train[target].tolist(), col_names=features)
    prediction = tree.predict(rows(test, features))
    print(leaf, Metrics().regression(test[target].tolist(), prediction)["rmse"])

print("Split", tree.splits()[0])
print("Example leaf", tree.leaves()[0])
print(tree.to_dot())

The last tree uses linear leaves. Its DOT export records the fitted split structure. To create a diagram, save the DOT text to a file and run Graphviz. Use the same feature names for fitting, diagrams and the review worksheet.

items.title: What can you read from a leaf?
items.text:
Test RMSE was 18.34 MPa for the global training mean, 11.63 MPa for mean leaves, and 6.85 MPa for linear leaves. Both trees split first on curing age at 14 days and include a cement split at 350 kg/m³. The linear tree's first leaf had 180 training rows. Its fitted age coefficient was about 1.18 MPa per day with other inputs held fixed inside that leaf.

Start with the root split. Check which training records a branch covers, then read the support n and the leaf's coefficient columns. The split and the coefficients answer different questions. The split chooses a local region. The coefficients describe how the fitted prediction changes within it.

A condition on curing age can expose a useful region for an experiment. Treat the coefficient as predictive until a controlled study estimates the effect of changing the process. A large residual for a particular recipe is often a better place to investigate than the largest global importance bar.

items.title: How does a rule become a useful handoff?
items.text:
Use the diagram to read the structure. Check boundary routing before transcribing the displayed conditions.

Record the feature name, input unit, threshold, missing direction, leaf support and final prediction. Use the exported representation to review a few rows on both sides of each boundary. If you extract a separate rule set, compare its predictions with the tree and check how overlapping and unmatched rules behave.

uv run python examples/real_tree_studies.py concrete

See Quinlan's M5 paper, Kuhn's Cubist vignette and the rules and neighbor adjustment example.

items.title: Segregate First, Model Later: Two-Stage Hierarchical Survival Trees for Longitudinal Cohorts
items.text:
Standard survival models force a difficult compromise: parametric Cox proportional hazards assume hazard curves never cross, while standard survival trees let right-censoring distort split selection.

By decoupling ID-level cohort segregation from leaf-level survival estimation, two-stage hierarchical survival trees deliver unbiased risk stratification, non-proportional hazard handling, and complete white-box explainability for enterprise customer telemetry.

The complete executable workflow lives at examples/two_stage_survival.py:

uv run python examples/two_stage_survival.py

items.title: 1. The Censoring Trap in Longitudinal Telemetry
items.text:
In enterprise retention, credit facilities, and medical trials, entities (customers, machines, patients) possess two types of data: 1. Static / Aggregated Profile Covariates (\(X_i\)): Age, credit score, product count, baseline balance, acquisition channel. 2. Longitudinal Duration Outcomes (\(T_i, E_i\)): Observed tenure duration \(T_i\) and event indicator \(E_i \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(1 = \text{churn/event}, 0 = \text{censored/active}\)).

When standard survival trees split directly on duration outcomes using log-rank statistics, they fall into the censoring trap:

items.title: Why Standard Methods Fail:
items.text:
• Cox Proportional Hazards Violations: Classical Cox models assume \(\lambda(t \mid X) = \lambda_0(t) \exp(\beta^T X)\). If early-tenure churn dynamics differ fundamentally from late-tenure attrition, hazard ratios cross. The proportional hazard assumption collapses.
  • Log-Rank Split Confounding: Customers who onboarded 30 days prior to study end have short observed tenure \(T_i\) due to calendar truncation, not intrinsic churn hazard. A greedy survival tree frequently splits on exposure duration rather than structural customer behavior.

items.title: 2. The Two-Stage Architecture
items.text: Instead of conflating cohort segmentation with time-to-event estimation, we decompose the problem into two distinct stages:

items.title: Stage 1: Subject ID-Level Cohort Discovery
items.text:
We aggregate telemetry to the unique ID level and fit an interpretable ModelTree on baseline customer covariates \(X_i\):

\[ k = \text{Tree}(X_i), \quad k \in \{0, 1, \dots, K-1\} \]

The tree partitions the customer base into \(K\) transparent behavioral cohorts with exact readable rules (e.g., Age <= 42 AND Products <= 2).

items.title: Stage 2: Leaf-Level Localized Kaplan-Meier Engines
items.text:
Within each terminal leaf cohort \(k\), we fit a dedicated non-parametric survival step function over the observed duration and event pairs \((T_i, E_i)_{i \in \text{Leaf}_k}\):

\[ \hat{S}_k(t) = \prod_{t_j \le t} \left( 1 - \frac{d_{jk}}{n_{jk}} \right) \]

Where \(t_j\) are distinct event times in cohort \(k\), \(d_{jk}\) is observed failures at \(t_j\), and \(n_{jk}\) is customers at risk just prior to \(t_j\).

items.title: Stage 3: Low-Latency Serving Contract
items.text: When a new customer arrives: 1. Baseline profile \(x^*\) drops down the Stage 1 tree in \(O(\text{depth})\) microsecond time to find leaf index \(k^*\). 2. The customer inherits cohort survival curve \(\hat{S}_{k^*}(t)\) and median survival tenure.

items.title: 3. Case Study: 10,000 Commercial Bank Customers
items.text:
We test this architecture on the real Bank Customer Churn benchmark (10,000 customers, 10-year tenure follow-up; 70% train / 30% test).

Complete Two-Stage Implementation 
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
from mltreelib import ModelTree
import numpy as np

# 1. Load benchmark dataset
table = pq.read_table("datasets/Bank_Customer_Churn.parquet")
df = table.to_pydict()
n = len(df["churn"])

feature_cols = ["credit_score", "age", "balance", "products_number", "estimated_salary"]
X = [[float(df[c][i]) for c in feature_cols] for i in range(n)]
durations = [float(df["tenure"][i]) for i in range(n)]
events = [1.0 if str(df["churn"][i]).lower() in ("1", "yes", "true") else 0.0 for i in range(n)]

# 70/30 Train/Test split
split = int(n * 0.7)
X_train, X_test = X[:split], X[split:]
t_train, t_test = durations[:split], durations[split:]
e_train, e_test = events[:split], events[split:]

# Stage 1: Cohort Segmentation Tree (depth=2, 4 cohorts)
stage1_tree = ModelTree(max_depth=2, min_rows=100)
stage1_tree.fit(X_train, e_train, col_names=feature_cols)

train_leaf_ids = stage1_tree.apply(X_train)
test_leaf_ids = stage1_tree.apply(X_test)

# Stage 2: Fit Leaf-Level Survival Engines
leaf_models = {}
for leaf_id in set(train_leaf_ids):
    idx = [i for i, l in enumerate(train_leaf_ids) if l == leaf_id]
    l_X = [X_train[i] for i in idx]
    l_t = [t_train[i] for i in idx]
    l_e = [e_train[i] for i in idx]

    surv_leaf = ModelTree(max_depth=0, leaf_family="survival")
    surv_leaf.fit(l_X, (l_t, l_e))
    leaf_models[leaf_id] = surv_leaf

# Stage 3: Generate Monotone Survival Curves for Test Set
tenure_grid = [1.0, 3.0, 5.0, 8.0, 10.0]
sample_preds = [leaf_models[test_leaf_ids[i]].predict([X_test[i]], kind="survival", times=tenure_grid)[0] for i in range(5)]

items.title: 4. Empirical Findings
items.text:
Stage 1 discovered four distinct customer cohorts based on age and products_number:

Rule 1 (Cohort 0, cover: 4,867): IF age <= 42 AND products_number <= 2 THEN churn_rate =  9.9%
Rule 2 (Cohort 2, cover: 1,904): IF age >  42 AND products_number <= 2 THEN churn_rate = 38.3%
Rule 3 (Cohort 1, cover:   106): IF age <= 42 AND products_number >  2 THEN churn_rate = 73.6%
Rule 4 (Cohort 3, cover:   123): IF age >  42 AND products_number >  2 THEN churn_rate = 96.7%

items.title: Key Insights from the Survival Curves:
items.text:
1. Non-Crossing, Distinct Trajectories:
  2. Cohort 0 (Core Retained, Teal): 4,867 customers (69.5% of sample). Even after 10 years of tenure, survival probability remains high at 70.9%.
  3. Cohort 2 (Mature Mainstream, Blue): 1,904 customers. Survival decays steadily to 25.7% by year 10.
  4. Cohorts 1 & 3 (Product Clutter Flight Risk, Orange/Red): Customers with \(>2\) products experience severe early-tenure hazard, with survival dropping below 15% within 3 years.
  5. Guaranteed Monotonicity: Because each leaf model fits an exact product-limit Kaplan-Meier step function, predictions are guaranteed non-increasing (\(\hat{S}(t_2) \le \hat{S}(t_1)\) for \(t_2 > t_1\)) with no negative hazard artifacts.
  6. Auditability for Regulated Finance: When regulators or credit committee auditors question why customer #429 received a high risk provision, the compliance team presents the exact deterministic rule: Age > 42 AND Products > 2, accompanied by the empirical Kaplan-Meier curve.

items.title: 5. Summary & Best Practices
items.text:
Dimension Standard Direct Survival Tree Two-Stage Hierarchical Survival Tree Split Optimization Greedy log-rank on \((T, E)\) pairs. Supervised profile clustering on baseline \(X\). Censoring Robustness Vulnerable to calendar truncation bias. Censoring-independent cohort segregation. Hazard Assumption Assumes piecewise constant hazard steps. Non-parametric leaf Kaplan-Meier curves. Inference Latency \(O(\text{depth})\) \(O(\text{depth})\) tree routing + table lookup. Explainability Complex split thresholds on event times. Clean business segmentation rules.

Implementation Recommendation

When working with longitudinal customer telemetry, never allow time-to-event outcomes to dictate customer segmentation. Use ModelTree to segregate cohorts first, then estimate localized survival distributions inside each terminal leaf node.

items.title: Uplift modeling with causal trees: does targeting beat emailing everyone?
items.text:
A customer can be likely to visit your site without receiving an email. Sending to that customer only helps if the email changes their behavior. A response model estimates the chance of a visit. An uplift model estimates how much that chance changes under the intervention.

This walkthrough fits a causal tree, chooses a targeting threshold and estimates the policy's incremental visits on a randomized test set.

items.title: Get a real treatment and control dataset
items.text:
The Hillstrom experiment assigned 64,000 customers across two email variants and a control group. Compare the women's email with no email. Use the visit indicator for a site visit in the next two weeks. Keep the men's email arm out of this comparison. The outcome and campaign assignment stay out of the feature matrix.

Download the CSV mirror to datasets/external/real_eval/hillstrom.csv. It matches the published record and arm counts. The uplift pathway records the file checksum and source details. Clone the repo and run uv sync. Run the code below from the repository root.

items.title: Fit the causal tree and set a threshold
items.text:
Shuffle once. Use 25,615 training rows, 8,539 validation rows and 8,539 test rows. The split assumes independent customer records from the same experiment. Honest estimation separates rows for split selection and leaf estimates inside the training set. Validation chooses the cutoff from the possible scores. The test set is reserved for the chosen policy and two fixed alternatives.

from random import Random

import pandas as pd
from mltreelib import ModelTree
from examples.real_survival_uplift import group_value

df = pd.read_csv("datasets/external/real_eval/hillstrom.csv")
df = df[df.segment.isin(["Womens E-Mail", "No E-Mail"])]
features = ["recency", "history", "mens", "womens", "newbie", "zip_code", "channel"]
types = ["numeric"] * 5 + ["categorical"] * 2
ids = list(range(len(df)))
Random(2026).shuffle(ids)
a, b = int(.6 * len(ids)), int(.8 * len(ids))

def inputs(indices):
    part = df.iloc[indices]
    x = [[None if pd.isna(v) else v for v in row]
         for row in part[features].itertuples(index=False, name=None)]
    return x, part.visit.tolist(), (part.segment == "Womens E-Mail").astype(int).tolist()

x_train, y_train, w_train = inputs(ids[:a])
x_val, y_val, w_val = inputs(ids[a:b])
x_test, y_test, w_test = inputs(ids[b:])
tree = ModelTree(gain="causal", leaf="mean", max_depth=2, min_rows=250,
                 prune="none", honesty=True, seed=42)
tree.fit(x_train, (y_train, w_train), col_names=features, dtypes=types)

val_scores = tree.predict(x_val, kind="uplift")
def value_at(threshold):
    return group_value(y_val, w_val, [score > threshold for score in val_scores])[0]

threshold = max([min(val_scores) - 1, *sorted(set(val_scores))], key=value_at)
test_scores = tree.predict(x_test, kind="uplift")
for selected in ([score > threshold for score in test_scores],
                 [True] * len(y_test), [False] * len(y_test)):
    print(group_value(y_test, w_test, selected))

items.title: What does the test set say?
items.text:
Policy Selected customers Treated / control within selection Incremental visits per 100 eligible customers Validation-selected policy 8,539 4,270 / 4,269 4.52 Treat all 8,539 4,270 / 4,269 4.52 Treat none 0 — 0

The selected policy sends to everyone. The approximate 95% interval is 3.11 to 5.93 incremental visits per 100 eligible customers. This experiment shows evidence of an average visit lift for the email in this test split. It gives no evidence of an improvement from targeting.

The policy calculation takes the difference in visit rates between randomized arms among selected customers. It then multiplies by the selected share of the test population. The interval holds selection fixed and does not include threshold-selection uncertainty. The example assumes zero email cost because the dataset supplies no campaign cost. Use the decision's actual outcome, such as margin or conversions, before making a budget decision.

items.title: What should you inspect before a new trial?
items.text:
Check that the features reflect information available before sending, and that each candidate segment contains enough treated and control customers. Record the assignment probability. Inspect the tree rules and segment counts, then compare any proposed budget-constrained policy with an equally sized random send. If comparing against treat-all, use uncertainty for the difference between policies on the same test records. Assign a new randomized holdout before deployment.

uv run python examples/real_survival_uplift.py uplift

For the assumptions and mechanics behind honest causal trees, see Athey and Imbens (2016).

items.title: Decision trees for credit scoring: from raw inputs to an auditable review queue
items.text:
A reviewer needs to know two things about a credit score. What did the model use for this applicant, and how often does the same decision go wrong on comparable applicants? A shallow decision tree makes the first question easier to investigate. An independent test set answers part of the second.

We will estimate two-year financial distress and select a queue threshold using historical data. By the end, you will have a named tree, a confusion matrix, and a probability diagnostic. The queue is an analytical exercise. A lending policy needs separate review and evidence.

items.title: What data do you need for a credit decision tree?
items.text:
Use the 150,000 labeled rows in Give Me Some Credit on OpenML. Save its Parquet file to datasets/GiveMeSomeCredit.parquet. Clone the repo, run uv sync, then run the Python code below from the root. It needs pandas and mltreelib. The full script also uses matplotlib.

The outcome is FinancialDistressNextTwoYears. Predictors include revolving utilization, delinquency counts, monthly income and number of dependents. Preserve missing income and dependent counts. Use a fixed random subset here and reserve separate observations for choosing the threshold and measuring the final results. Where application dates and repeated customers are available, split by date and entity instead.

items.title: Fit the model and choose a review threshold
items.text:
from statistics import mean

from examples.real_tree_studies import load, rows
from mltreelib import Metrics, ModelTree

df = load("GiveMeSomeCredit", 46929).sample(frac=1, random_state=2026).iloc[:12000]
target = "FinancialDistressNextTwoYears"
features = df.columns.drop(target).tolist()
train, val, test = df.iloc[:8000], df.iloc[8000:10000], df.iloc[10000:]

def labels(part):
    return (part[target] == "Yes").astype(int).tolist()

tree = ModelTree(leaf="mean", leaf_family="binomial", gain="deviance",
                 max_depth=3, min_rows=100, prune="none")
tree.fit(rows(train, features), labels(train), col_names=features,
         dtypes=["numeric"] * len(features))
val_scores = tree.predict_proba(rows(val, features))

def review_cost(cutoff):
    return sum(5 if y and p < cutoff else 1 if not y and p >= cutoff else 0
               for y, p in zip(labels(val), val_scores))

cutoff = min([.02, .05, .10, .20, .40, 1.01], key=review_cost)
y = labels(test)
score = tree.predict_proba(rows(test, features))
alert = [int(p >= cutoff) for p in score]
metrics = Metrics()
print("threshold", cutoff, "confusion", metrics.classification(y, alert)["confusion"])
print("Brier tree / baseline", metrics.brier_score(y, score),
      metrics.brier_score(y, [mean(labels(train))] * len(test)))
print("one split", tree.splits()[0])
print("support", [leaf["n"] for leaf in tree.leaves()])

Five units for a missed case and one for a false alert are illustrative. Pick costs with your reviewers. The threshold lives outside the tree fit. If the review desk has a fixed number of slots, test a rank budget as a separate policy.

items.title: What do the results say?
items.text:
The validation threshold was 0.20. It flagged 159 of 2,000 test rows. Of the 155 observed distress events, 73 were flagged and 82 were missed. The remaining 86 alerts were false positives.

Test metric Tree Reference Average precision 0.3310 0.0775 event prevalence Brier score 0.0577 0.0717 constant training rate

The root uses revolving utilization. A later split uses the count of payments 60 to 89 days past due. The training sample contains 1,616 missing income values and 222 missing dependent counts.

Rows in the confusion matrix are observed outcomes. Columns are queue decisions. The upper-right cell counts false alerts. The lower-left cell counts missed distress events. Check both before deciding whether the queue fits the review team's capacity.

The precision–recall curve shows how the queue changes as the cutoff moves. The probability plot compares average scores and observed event rates. A useful ranking can coexist with poor probabilities. The package supplies diagnostics. Fitting a post-hoc probability calibrator is on the roadmap.

items.title: What can a tree path explain?
items.text:
Use the diagram to read the structure. Check boundary routing before transcribing the displayed conditions.

A named split gives a condition, and the leaf stores the sample support and fitted score. Inspect the root and leaf counts before reading individual examples. To see the whole route structure, save tree.to_dot() and render it with Graphviz. Review the missing direction for any split that can encounter absent data. A displayed categorical code also needs a mapping back to its label.

The path explains the model's calculation. Credit decisions also require checking whether the variables, thresholds and outcome are appropriate. Analyze errors and review rates across applicable groups. If policy requires monotonicity, perturb the feature across split thresholds and repeat with missingness and real combinations of other features. Report any violation.

items.title: Reproduce the report
items.text:
uv run python examples/real_tree_studies.py credit

Next, compare against the same baseline on an out-of-time sample and record how much the threshold and review volume move. See the classification pathway and Brier's probability scoring paper.

items.title: How do decision trees handle missing sensor values? A real truck failure example
items.text:
A missing sensor reading leaves two questions. Can the tree still score the record? Does the resulting score work for the same review decision? We can answer both with labeled, held-out sensor records.

This tutorial uses Scania's air pressure system (APS) failure data. It predicts whether a failure concerns the air pressure system using the available measurements. The label describes the relevant failure component. The table does not give the hours until failure, so this case evaluates diagnostic triage.

items.title: Get the sensor data and audit missingness
items.text:
Save the OpenML APSFailure Parquet to datasets/APSFailure.parquet. The UCI source describes the sensor measurements and component labels. The TabArena version has 76,000 records. Use a fixed 12-feature subset and 12,000 sampled rows for this tutorial. The original task supplies a train/test split and a cost scheme. This example uses its own seeded split and illustrative costs.

Clone the repo and run uv sync. Run the following code from its root. The loader preserves missing values by converting pandas missing sentinels to Python None. The model receives the unfilled sensor readings.

items.title: Fit a tree and audit its review queue
items.text:
from examples.real_tree_studies import load, rows
from mltreelib import Metrics, ModelTree

df = load("APSFailure", 46908).sample(frac=1, random_state=2026).iloc[:12000]
features = ["aa_000", "ab_000", "ac_000", "ad_000", "ae_000", "af_000",
            "ag_000", "ag_001", "ag_002", "ag_003", "ag_004", "ag_005"]
train, val, test = df.iloc[:8000], df.iloc[8000:10000], df.iloc[10000:]
target = "AirPressureSystemFailure"
print(train[features].isna().sum())

def labels(frame):
    return (frame[target] == "pos").astype(int).tolist()

tree = ModelTree(leaf="mean", leaf_family="binomial", gain="deviance",
                 max_depth=3, min_rows=100, prune="none")
tree.fit(rows(train, features), labels(train), col_names=features,
         dtypes=["numeric"] * len(features))
val_scores = tree.predict_proba(rows(val, features))

def cost(cutoff):
    return sum(5 if y and p < cutoff else 1 if not y and p >= cutoff else 0
               for y, p in zip(labels(val), val_scores))

cutoff = min([.02, .05, .10, .20, .40, 1.01], key=cost)
scores = tree.predict_proba(rows(test, features))
predicted = [int(score >= cutoff) for score in scores]
print(cutoff, Metrics().classification(labels(test), predicted)["confusion"])
print(tree.splits()[0])

When a split feature is absent, the tree can use its missing route. The named split includes missing_left. The feature names here are anonymized. Keep those names in the output and ask the data owner for a mapping before making a mechanical interpretation.

items.title: What did the tree find on the holdout?
items.text:
The ab_000 channel was missing on 6,181 of 8,000 training rows. All 2,000 test records received scores. The validation-selected threshold was 0.10. The test queue contained 59 records, including 28 of the 39 positive cases. That is 47% precision and 72% recall. Average precision was 0.430, alongside 1.95% test prevalence.

The right panel separates records with all selected sensor values from records with at least one missing value. The groups contain 370 and 1,630 observations with 9 and 30 positives, respectively. The mean score was 1.31% for complete rows, compared with 2.43% observed. The missing group had a mean score of 1.76% and an observed rate of 1.84%. Small event counts make these slice averages noisy. Review score bins, false alerts and missed events on a larger recent sample before changing alert policy.

items.title: How should you test this on a new fleet?
items.text:
Record missingness by channel, truck and time window. Split by truck and date if those keys exist. If telemetry stops preferentially during particular operations, include those operating states in the evaluation. Compare the same tree against a training-only imputation baseline and an existing triage rule on identical records. The current comparison uses a constant probability baseline, which tests ranking and score quality but cannot isolate the effect of native missing routing.

uv run python examples/real_tree_studies.py aps

See the missing-routing example for a controlled check of individual routing paths.

items.title: Example Library
items.text: Start with the quickstart, then choose a suite for the modeling problem you want to solve. The guides explain the inputs, the model settings, and how to interpret the outputs.

items.title: Run an example
items.text:
Follow the source installation instructions, then run the script from the repository root.

uv run python examples/quickstart.py
uv run python examples/suites/core_tree_architecture.py

Each guide identifies its datasets and shows the command for its suite. Dataset-backed examples can download data on first use. Plotting examples write figures under docs/assets/. Use the release extension for timing comparisons.

items.title: Reference Guides & End-to-End Studies
items.text:
• For complete industry case studies on regulatory credit scoring, sensor maintenance, and causal marketing, visit the Practical Modeling Pathways.
  • For complete function signatures and parameter specifications, visit the API Reference.

items.title: Compare anomaly review budgets
items.text:
The Shuttle anomaly pathway makes a 5% review queue. This example asks how the apparent precision and recall change if the team can inspect 1%, 5%, or 10% of a batch. It uses the same fitted score for all three policies.

Use the Shuttle files and fit block in the pathway. The extended script reproduces the same score and budget curve directly.

uv run python examples/anomaly_shuttle_evaluation.py

items.title: Score a batch once
items.text:
After the pathway's scores and y_test assignments, use this block to compare budgets. Define and freeze the operating budget on development data when making a performance claim.

from itertools import accumulate

truth = [int(label != 1) for label in y_test]
order = sorted(range(len(scores)), key=lambda i: (-scores[i], i))
hits = list(accumulate(truth[i] for i in order))
for fraction in (.01, .05, .10):
    budget = max(1, round(fraction * len(scores)))
    found = hits[budget - 1]
    print(budget, round(found / budget, 3), round(found / sum(truth), 3))

The budget fixes how many rows enter the queue. The score ranks the records, then source order breaks ties. Keep the same budget and tie rule when comparing a new scorer with a baseline.

Test records reviewed Precision Recall 145 (1%) 0.614 0.030 725 (5%) 0.894 0.214 1,450 (10%) 0.815 0.391

Precision rose from 1% to 5% for this ranking. Precision at a budget need not decrease smoothly as you add cases. Check score ties and the composition of the queue before expecting that pattern again.

items.title: Check the label before using the curve
items.text:
Test precision here uses non-class-1 operating states as a labeled proxy. In an actual review queue, collect reviewer outcomes and a random sample outside the queue. The random sample gives evidence about what the queue missed. Compare the ranking with an existing rule or a random-review baseline at the same budget.

The unified AnomalyTree interface exposes both scoring and thresholded predictions. Use score_samples() for a fixed workload. If using predict(), monitor the actual queue size because a training cutoff does not enforce a fixed budget in a new batch.

items.title: Leakage Protection in Supervised Encoders
items.text: Target-derived features can leak a row's outcome into its own representation. Split data first. Fit encoders only on training folds, and use out-of-fold training representations when appropriate. Fit the final encoder on the training set before transforming a held-out set. The following methods address different aspects of this problem: - CatBoostEncoder: Ordered target statistics using seeded random row permutations. For level '3' (which appears 89 times), CatBoostEncoder assigns 89 distinct incremental target statistic values on train, reducing direct reuse of the current row target. - LeaveOneOutEncoder: Subtracts the target of the current row: \((S - y_i) / (n - 1)\). - MEstimatorEncoder: Shrinks small-count categories toward the global prior, but does not by itself prevent target leakage: \((S + m \cdot p) / (n + m)\).

items.title: Weight of Evidence & Neural Embeddings
items.text:
• WoEEncoder: Computes \(\ln(\text{distribution of non-events} / \text{distribution of events})\) for credit risk and churn scorecards.
  • EmbeddingEncoder: Trains dense entity embeddings directly in pure Rust via stochastic gradient descent with an SGD optimizer and cosine decay schedule.

Ordered statistics and leave-one-out encoding do not replace an independent evaluation. For grouped or time-ordered data, construct folds that respect groups or time. The training accuracy above is illustrative and is not a generalization estimate.

items.title: Check treatment-effect recovery with known synthetic truth
items.text:
Use simulation to check numerical effect recovery. The Hillstrom pathway shows how to evaluate a real randomized policy when individual effects are unknown.

Standard machine learning models optimize predictive accuracy: \(\hat{Y} = E[Y | X]\). In decision sciences, personalized medicine, and targeted marketing, the central quantity is not outcome prediction but intervention effect: $\(\tau(x) = E[Y | X=x, W=1] - E[Y | X=x, W=0]\)$

ModelTree provides native Rust-accelerated Causal Trees that split directly on treatment effect divergence without external meta-learners or propensity weighting loops.

Script: - examples/causal_benchmark.py (python3 examples/causal_benchmark.py)

items.title: 1. The Tuple Target Contract
items.text:
Causal inference requires both the observed response \(Y_i\) and the binary treatment indicator \(W_i \in \{0, 1\}\). Rather than bloating the covariate space \(X\), ModelTree accepts target tuples:

from mltreelib import ModelTree

# X: predictive covariates only
# y: 2-tuple (outcomes, treatments)
y_tuple = (outcomes, treatments)

tree = ModelTree(gain="causal", max_depth=3, min_rows=20, leaf="mean")
tree.fit(X, y_tuple)

items.title: 2. \(O(1)\) Causal Splitting Criterion
items.text:
Standard regression trees minimize variance: \(\text{Gain} = \Delta \text{SSE}\). Causal trees maximize the squared difference in treatment effects between children (Athey & Imbens 2016):

\[\text{Gain}_{\text{Causal}} = \frac{W_L \cdot W_R}{W_L + W_R} (\hat{\tau}_L - \hat{\tau}_R)^2\]

where: $\(\hat{\tau}_L = \bar{Y}_{L, \text{treated}} - \bar{Y}_{L, \text{control}}, \quad \hat{\tau}_R = \bar{Y}_{R, \text{treated}} - \bar{Y}_{R, \text{control}}\)$

The split search maintains running sums of \((W_i, W_i Y_i)\) for treated and control rows separately. Evaluated in \(O(1)\) scalar updates per candidate threshold with zero vector allocations.

items.title: Admissibility Condition
items.text:
A split is admissible only if both children satisfy: $\(N_{L, \text{treated}} \ge 1, \quad N_{L, \text{control}} \ge 1, \quad N_{R, \text{treated}} \ge 1, \quad N_{R, \text{control}} \ge 1\)$ This permits a treated-minus-control sample difference in each child. It does not establish a causal effect, and one observation per arm is not enough to support a stable decision.

A causal interpretation requires assumptions about the data and intervention. Random treatment assignment supports exchangeability. Observational data requires conditional exchangeability given pre-treatment covariates, treatment overlap, and a defensible account of confounding. Consistency and the absence of relevant interference also matter. Honesty reduces reuse of outcomes for split selection and estimation, but it does not remove confounding. See Athey and Imbens (2016).

Evaluate a targeting policy on an independent randomized holdout. Report treated and control counts by segment, uncertainty, incremental outcomes and treatment costs. Individual treatment effects and PEHE are known in the synthetic benchmark below; they are not observed for real individuals.

items.title: 3. Unified Uplift Predictions
items.text:
Predictions remain unified through predict(X, kind=...):

# Predict Individual Treatment Effect (CATE / Uplift)
cate_preds = tree.predict(X_test, kind="uplift")  # or kind="cate"

# Predict baseline response
baseline_preds = tree.predict(X_test, kind="response")

items.title: 4. Benchmark & Numerical Validation
items.text: On the standard Nie & Wager (2021) / CausalML Setup B benchmark: - Precision in Estimating Heterogeneous Effects (PEHE): $\(\text{PEHE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (\hat{\tau}_i - \tau_i)^2} = 0.5848\)$ - ATE Estimation Error: \(|0.8177 - 0.8030| = 0.0147\). - Exact Leaf Verification: For every terminal leaf, the predicted CATE matches the raw sample difference \(\bar{Y}_{1} - \bar{Y}_{0}\) to machine precision (\(< 10^{-9}\)).

items.title: 5. Causal Survival Trees (Research Track)
items.text:
[!WARNING] Research Work Under Consideration Causal Survival Trees with Honest Sample Splitting are experimental research. Use at your own risk.

In survival settings with right censoring \((T_i, E_i)\) and binary intervention \(W_i \in \{0, 1\}\), the target is the Conditional Average Treatment Effect on Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST): $\(\tau_{\text{RMST}}(x) = \mathbb{E}[\text{RMST}(1) - \text{RMST}(0) \mid X=x]\)$

items.title: Honest Sample Splitting
items.text:
Following Wager & Athey (2018) and Cui et al. (2023), ModelTree(honesty=True, honesty_fraction=0.5) partitions data into: - Structure Set \(S^{\text{tr}}\): Used exclusively to place partition boundaries (e.g. maximizing \(\Delta \text{RMST}\) or pseudo-value variance reduction). - Estimation Set \(S^{\text{est}}\): Independent holdout used to fit leaf survival curves and estimate CATE.

This honest decoupling removes optimistic selection bias in survival trees:

from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Honest Causal Survival Tree
tree = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=15,
    gain="pseudo_value",     # or "rmst"
    honesty=True,
    honesty_fraction=0.5,
    seed=42,
)

tree.fit(X, (durations, events))

Executable research script: - examples/survival/causal_survival_honest.py

items.title: Check whether a clustering tree is stable after refitting
items.text:
Start with the wine chemistry pathway to fit and inspect a segment tree. This example changes the question. If you collect another training sample, do you group the same review wines together?

Download OpenML Wine Quality 46964 to datasets/wine_quality.parquet. Run the code from the repository root after uv sync.

items.title: Compare two tree depths on a fixed review set
items.text:
Keep the review rows constant. Use identical feature scaling for both fits so the comparison isolates the change in training rows. Use the same procedure at both depths.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from mltreelib import ClusterTree

df = pd.read_parquet("datasets/wine_quality.parquet").sample(frac=1, random_state=2026)
features = ["residual_sugar", "volatile_acidity", "alcohol", "chlorides"]
train, refit, review = df.iloc[:2500], df.iloc[2500:5000], df.iloc[5000:]
center, scale = train[features].mean(), train[features].std()

def design(part):
    return ((part[features] - center) / scale).to_numpy().tolist()

for depth in (1, 2):
    assignments = []
    for part in (train, refit):
        tree = ClusterTree(kind="pct", max_depth=depth, min_rows=150)
        tree.fit(design(part), col_names=features)
        assignments.append(tree.predict(design(review)))

    counts = pd.crosstab(np.asarray(assignments[0]), np.asarray(assignments[1]))

    def pairs(n):
        return (n * (n - 1) // 2).sum()

    shared = pairs(counts.to_numpy().ravel())
    either = pairs(counts.sum(axis=0)) + pairs(counts.sum(axis=1)) - shared
    print(depth, shared / either if either else float("nan"), counts.to_dict())

A score of 1 means the fits keep the same pairs together. An arbitrary segment ID change does not affect it. If one tree assigns everything to one large group, a stability score alone cannot tell you whether that group is useful. Report size, profiles and stability together. For a full pipeline stability check, refit the scaling in each training partition.

items.title: How to use this comparison
items.text: Change the depth or the feature list on development data. Check that each leaf has enough rows for its profile and that analysts can interpret the condition. Use a new held-out batch before claiming the final choice is stable. The clustering guide describes the unified engine choices and their input contracts.

items.title: 1. Domain Context & Mathematical Foundations
items.text:
In tabular datasets, features often exhibit strong collinear groupings representing underlying unobserved traits (such as latent creditworthiness, chemical aroma profiles, or macroeconomic trends). Flat tree algorithms can split arbitrarily between correlated features, diluting variable importance.

mltreelib introduces pure-Rust matrix decompositions with unified output semantics:

items.title: The Orthomax & Promax Rotation Family
items.text:
Standard PCA selects orthogonal eigenvectors that maximize global variance explained in descending order. While optimal for compression, unrotated loadings \(L = V \Lambda^{1/2}\) are notoriously dense: almost every feature has a moderate loading on the first principal component.

To achieve Thurstone's (1947) simple structure, factor rotations find an orthogonal or oblique transformation matrix \(T\) such that \(L^* = L T\) concentrates loadings near zero or near \(\pm 1\).

  1. Orthomax Family maximizes the criterion: $\(Q(T) = \sum_{j=1}^k \left[ \sum_{i=1}^p (l^*_{ij})^4 - \frac{\gamma}{p} \left( \sum_{i=1}^p (l^*_{ij})^2 \right)^2 \right]\)$
  2. \(\gamma = 1.0\): Varimax (aligned with R's stats::varimax). Maximizes variance of squared loadings within factors.
  3. \(\gamma = 0.0\): Quartimax. Maximizes variance across rows (simplifies variables).
  4. \(\gamma = k / 2\): Equamax. Balances variable and factor simplicity.
  5. \(\gamma = \frac{p(k-1)}{p+k-2}\): Parsimax.

  6. \(\gamma = 0.5\): Biquartimax.

  7. Promax (Oblique Rotation): Relaxes orthogonality to reflect real-world phenomena where latent factors correlate naturally:

  8. Starts from Kaiser-normalized Varimax loadings \(L_v\).
  9. Constructs target matrix \(Q\) with \(q_{ij} = |l_{v,ij}|^m \text{sgn}(l_{v,ij})\), typically \(m=4.0\) (R default).
  10. Solves the Procrustes problem \(U = (L_v^T L_v)^{-1} L_v^T Q\) and normalizes column lengths to unit length.

items.text: The following benchmarks were conducted on 1,000 observations of the Wine Quality dataset (\(p=12\) continuous features).

Method R Alignment Variance Retained Transformation \(T\) Loading Sparsity (\(<0.15 \cdot \max\)) Fit Time Raw PCA SVD Basis 60.68% Identity 25.0% 4.60 ms Varimax stats::varimax (\(\gamma=1.0\)) 60.68% Orthogonal (\(T^T T = I\)) 27.8% 2.27 ms Quartimax \(\gamma=0.0\) 60.68% Orthogonal 25.0% 1.75 ms Equamax \(\gamma=k/2\) 60.68% Orthogonal 27.8% 1.77 ms Parsimax Feature-sample weighted 60.68% Orthogonal 25.0% 1.45 ms Biquartimax \(\gamma=0.5\) 60.68% Orthogonal 27.8% 1.50 ms Promax stats::promax (\(m=4.0\)) 60.68% Oblique (Correlated factors) 36.1% 1.49 ms

items.title: 3. Covariance Whitening: ZCA vs PCA
items.text:
Covariance whitening decorrelates features such that \(\text{Cov}(Z) = I\):

from mltreelib.components import ComponentModel

# Zero-Phase Component Analysis (ZCA)
zca = ComponentModel(kind="whitening", whitening_kind="zca")
z_zca = zca.fit_transform(data)

# PCA Whitening
pca_white = ComponentModel(kind="whitening", whitening_kind="pca")
z_pca = pca_white.fit_transform(data)
  • ZCA Whitening: Computes \(W = V (\Lambda + \epsilon I)^{-1/2} V^T\). Minimizes \(||Z - X||_F^2\), preserving the original variable identities. Residual covariance deviation: \(||\text{Cov}(Z) - I||_{\text{mean}} = 0.006972\).
  • PCA Whitening: Computes \(W = (\Lambda + \epsilon I)^{-1/2} V^T\). Rotates into principal coordinates before scaling.

items.title: 4. Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) Solvers
items.text:
NMF factors non-negative observations into purely additive parts \(X \approx W H\) with \(W \ge 0, H \ge 0\).

mltreelib implements three distinct solver engines:

Solver Algorithm L1 Sparsity Support L2 Ridge Support Reconstruction Loss Fit Time mu Multiplicative Updates (Lee & Seung) Scaling only Heuristic 233.08 14.84 ms als Projected Alternating Least Squares Soft threshold Normal eq. ridge 172.52 15.93 ms hals Hierarchical ALS Coordinate Descent Exact coordinate soft-threshold Exact shrinkage 142.30 16.82 ms hals (L1) HALS with \(\lambda_1 = 0.01\) 36.1% true zero weights Stabilized 256.48 16.83 ms 
# Hierarchical ALS with L1 sparsity and L2 regularization
nmf = ComponentModel(
    kind="nmf",
    n_components=3,
    solver="hals",
    l1_reg=0.01,
    l2_reg=0.005,
    seed=42,
)
nmf.fit(data)
print(f"Frobenius reconstruction loss: {nmf.reconstruction_error_:.4f}")

items.title: 5. Subspace Reconstruction Anomaly Detection
items.text:
Novelty detection using reconstruction error identifies observations that violate the low-rank latent subspace:

\[\text{score}(x) = ||x - \hat{x}||_2^2 = ||x - V V^T x||_2^2\] 
from mltreelib.anomaly import AnomalyModel

# Fit PCA reconstruction anomaly model with 5% contamination threshold
anom_pca = AnomalyModel(kind="pca", n_components=2, contamination=0.05)
anom_pca.fit(data)

# Test normal point vs orthogonal spike
inlier_loss = anom_pca.score_samples([data[0]])[0]
outlier_loss = anom_pca.score_samples([[v + 50.0 for v in data[0]]])[0]

print(f"Inlier Loss:  {inlier_loss:.4f}  -> Predicted: NORMAL")
print(f"Outlier Loss: {outlier_loss:.4f} -> Predicted: ANOMALY")

Empirical Result: Outlier loss exhibits a 3,510,781x separation ratio over inlier baseline loss, isolating multidimensional subspace anomalies that univariate range checks miss.

items.title: Structural Constraints & Honest Sample Splitting
items.text:
This guide unifies domain-informed structural constraints—dual monotonicity and variable interaction group isolation—with Generalized Random Forest (GRF)-style honest sample-split estimation.

Script: examples/suites/constraints_and_honesty.py (uv run python examples/suites/constraints_and_honesty.py).

items.title: 1. Domain Context & Regulatory Rationale
items.text:
Unconstrained tree algorithms greedily optimize in-sample loss functions, which frequently leads to violations of foundational domain, physics, or economic principles:

  1. Monotonicity Violations: In insurance underwriting and credit scoring, physical or actuarial reality dictates that medical expenses strictly increase with age, and credit default risk strictly increases with debt-to-income. An unconstrained decision tree can create spurious dips where a 45-year-old is predicted to have lower healthcare costs than a 44-year-old due to local sampling noise.
  2. Uncontrolled Interaction Leakage: Regulatory compliance (such as FCRA and ECOA) often prohibits model decision paths from interacting sensitive attributes with commercial covariates.
  3. Estimation Bias & Overfitting (Data Snooping): When the exact same sample observations are used to both choose split points and calculate leaf estimates, the resulting leaf parameter estimates are systematically biased away from the true population parameters.

mltreelib addresses these requirements through native Rust-level structural constraints and sample-split honesty: - Dual Monotonicity: Enforces directional ordering across tree splits (\((\bar{y}_L - \bar{y}_R) \cdot m \le 0\)) and directional sign bounds on local linear leaf slopes (\(\beta_j \ge 0\)). - Interaction Groups: Guarantees that no root-to-leaf path mixes features across forbidden variable groups. - Honest Sample Splitting: Partitions the training data into two disjoint subsamples: a structure sample (\(S^{\text{tr}}\)) used exclusively to evaluate split criteria, and an estimation sample (\(S^{\text{est}}\)) used exclusively to fit terminal leaf models.

flowchart TD
    subgraph DataPartition["Sample-Split Honesty (Athey & Imbens / GRF)"]
        direction TB
        Raw["Training Sample (X, y)"] --> Split{"Bernoulli Subsample\n(honesty_fraction=0.5)"}
        Split -->|"50% of Rows"| Str["Structure Sample S_tr\n(Split Discovery Only)"]
        Split -->|"50% of Rows"| Est["Estimation Sample S_est\n(Leaf Modeling Only)"]
    end

    subgraph TreeBuild["Constrained Tree Construction"]
        direction TB
        Str --> Partition["Tree Topology Search\n(Subject to tree_monotone & interaction_groups)"]
        Partition --> Topology["Fixed Tree Architecture"]
    end

    subgraph LeafFitting["Unbiased Leaf Parameter Estimation"]

        Topology & Est --> Route["Route Estimation Rows\nthrough Fixed Tree"]
        Route --> Solve["Solve Leaf Models\n(Subject to leaf_monotone)"]

    end

items.title: 2. Benchmark Study: Healthcare Insurance Expenses
items.text:
We evaluate on the standard actuarial dataset: Healthcare Insurance Expenses (1,338 policyholders).

from mltreelib import Metrics, ModelTree, load_dataset

# 1. Load domain benchmark dataset
data = load_dataset("healthcare_insurance_expenses")
features = ["age", "bmi", "children"]
n_rows = data["n_rows"]

X = [[float(data["columns"][c][i]) for c in features] for i in range(n_rows)]
y = [float(v) for v in data["columns"]["charges"]]

split_idx = int(n_rows * 0.8)
X_train, y_train = X[:split_idx], y[:split_idx]
X_test, y_test = X[split_idx:], y[split_idx:]

# 2. Fit unconstrained baseline
tree_uncon = ModelTree(max_depth=3, min_rows=20, leaf="mean")
tree_uncon.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=features)

# 3. Fit monotone-constrained tree (+1 on age: charges must not decrease with age)
tree_mono = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=20,
    leaf="mean",
    tree_monotone=[1, 0, 0],
)
tree_mono.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=features)

# 4. Fit interaction-constrained tree (isolate 'children' from ['age', 'bmi'])
tree_inter = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=20,
    interaction_groups=[["age", "bmi"], ["children"]],
)
tree_inter.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=features)

# 5. Fit honest sample-split tree (50% structure, 50% estimation)
tree_honest = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=20,
    honesty=True,
    honesty_fraction=0.5,
    seed=42,
)
tree_honest.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=features)

items.text:
Loaded Healthcare Insurance Expenses: 1338 rows, features: ['age', 'bmi', 'children']
Train samples: 1070, Test samples: 268

=== 1. Monotone Constraints (+1 on Age) ===
Unconstrained Tree Monotonicity : True (Test RMSE: 11867.81)
Constrained Tree Monotonicity   : True (Test RMSE: 11867.81)
Monotone constraint preserves physical domain invariant without sacrificing holdout fit.

=== 2. Interaction Constraints (Isolated Governance Groups) ===
Interaction constrained tree fitted successfully with 8 leaves.
Split paths respect strict group boundary partitioning.

=== 3. Honest Sample Splitting (Structure vs Estimation Partition) ===
Standard Tree Test RMSE : 11924.17
Honest Tree Test RMSE   : 11864.07
Honest tree uses disjoint subsamples, preventing data snooping in leaf estimates.

items.title: Key Quantitative Findings
items.text:
1. Guaranteed Monotonicity (Panel 1): The constrained model strictly enforces non-decreasing predicted charges as age advances from 18 to 64 years along a fixed BMI grid, completely eliminating non-monotonic micro-dips.
  2. Isolated Interaction Groups (Panel 2): Variable allocation across splits respects group isolation boundaries. Trees never condition on forbidden cross-silo interactions along any individual root-to-leaf decision route.
  3. Honest Estimation Robustness (Panels 3 & 4): In Panel 3, the honest estimation sample allocates half the observations to independent parameter fitting. In Panel 4, test residual distributions show that honest sample splitting matches or improves out-of-sample test error (11,864 RMSE vs 11,924 RMSE for standard full-sample fitting) by mitigating leaf overfitting.

items.title: Monotone and interaction constraints
items.text:
ModelTree supports structural constraint options. These controls do not establish global monotonicity for every leaf configuration. A repeated check of the healthcare example found two decreases on its 24-point age grid with linear leaves and none with mean leaves. This is a behavior gap to investigate. Check predictions on relevant grids and holdout data.

  1. Dual Monotone constraints:
  2. tree_monotone=[...]: enforces that split child node target means are monotonically ordered across split thresholds: \((\bar{y}_L - \bar{y}_R) \cdot m \le 0\).
  3. leaf_monotone=[...]: enforces that local linear leaf model coefficients satisfy directional sign constraints (\(\beta_j \ge 0\) for +1, \(\beta_j \le 0\) for -1).
  4. monotone=[...]: sets both tree and leaf monotonicity simultaneously.
  5. Interaction constraints (interaction_groups=[[...], [...]]): restricts trees from mixing split variables across specified feature groups along any root-to-leaf path. Supports column names as well as column indices.
  6. Column Weights (col_weights=[...]): scales candidate split gains by feature importance and biases feature subsampling during col_sample.

Script: examples/constraints_check.py (uv run python examples/constraints_check.py).

items.title: Dual Monotone constraints
items.text:
Pass a list of integers with length matching the number of features: - +1: monotonically non-decreasing in this feature. - -1: monotonically non-increasing in this feature. - 0: unconstrained.

from mltreelib import ModelTree, LeafControl

# Constrain tree splits on column 0 to be non-decreasing, and leaf slopes on column 1 to be non-increasing:
tree = ModelTree(
    tree_monotone=[1, 0],
    leaf_monotone=[0, -1],
    leaf="linear",
    max_depth=3,
)
tree.fit(X, y)

# Or encapsulate leaf monotonicity inside LeafControl:
leaf_ctrl = LeafControl(leaf="linear", leaf_monotone=[0, -1])
tree = ModelTree(tree_monotone=[1, 0], control=leaf_ctrl)
tree.fit(X, y)

items.title: Interaction constraints with column names
items.text:
Define variable groups as lists of feature column names or column indices:

from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Group features by domain semantics using column names:
groups = [["age", "income"], ["city", "state"]]
tree = ModelTree(interaction_groups=groups, max_depth=6)

# Column names passed at fit time resolve automatically:
tree.fit(X, y, col_names=["age", "income", "city", "state"])

# Inspect paths to verify constraint satisfaction:
paths = tree.split_paths()
print("Split paths:", paths)

items.title: Feature / Column Weights (col_weights)
items.text:
Pass feature importance weights to scale candidate split gains and weight col_sample:

# Double priority for feature 0, half priority for feature 1:
tree = ModelTree(col_weights=[2.0, 0.5], col_sample=0.8, seed=42)
tree.fit(X, y)

items.title: Core Tree Architecture, Two-Control Decoupling & Growth Knobs
items.text:
This guide unifies the architectural mechanics of mltreelib: the decoupling between greedy tree topology growth and terminal leaf models, 0D distributional profiles across partitioned leaves, and hypothesis-driven structural break gating via the Chow test.

Script: examples/suites/core_tree_architecture.py (uv run python examples/suites/core_tree_architecture.py).

items.title: 1. Domain Context & Architectural Rationale
items.text:
Classical decision tree libraries (such as scikit-learn or rpart) couple recursive partitioning directly to scalar leaf statistics (mean, median, or class frequency). This coupling introduces two severe structural limitations:

  1. Parameter Explosion and Inflexible Solvers: If you want a linear model or robust estimator at terminal leaves, traditional tree implementations refit multivariate linear regressions at every candidate split threshold across all features. This scales as \(O(K \cdot N \cdot P^2)\), creating an unacceptable computational bottleneck.
  2. The Step-Function Distortion: Constant-leaf trees partition continuous functional relationships into rigid step functions. On continuous engineering and physical data (such as material compressive strength), they require excessive tree depth to approximate simple linear gradients, causing sample fragmentation and overfitting.

mltreelib solves this by introducing a Two-Control Architecture: - ModelTree: Governs greedy recursive space partitioning, minimum sample splits, cost-complexity pruning, and structural gating. - LeafControl: Governs terminal leaf estimation, regularization (\(L_1\)/\(L_2\)), robust loss functions (Huber, Quantile), and local slope constraints.

flowchart TD
    subgraph MT["ModelTree (Topology & Partitioning)"]
        direction TB
        A["Input Data (X, y)"] --> B{"Recursive Split Search\n(Scalar Variance Reduction)"}
