items.title: 2. Benchmark Study: Yeh (1998) Concrete Compressive Strength
items.text:
We evaluate the architecture on the standard civil engineering benchmark: Yeh (1998) Concrete Compressive Strength (1,030 industrial concrete mixtures, 8 continuous ingredients).

from mltreelib import LeafControl, Metrics, ModelTree, load_dataset

# 1. Load benchmark dataset
data = load_dataset("concrete_compressive_strength")
target = "ConcreteCompressiveStrength"
feature_names = [col for col in data["columns"].keys() if col != target]
n_rows = data["n_rows"]

X = [[data["columns"][c][i] for c in feature_names] for i in range(n_rows)]
y = data["columns"][target]

split_idx = int(n_rows * 0.8)
X_train, y_train = X[:split_idx], y[:split_idx]
X_test, y_test = X[split_idx:], y[split_idx:]

# 2. Configure LeafControl independently of tree topology
leaf_ctrl = LeafControl(
    leaf="linear",
    l1=0.0,
    l2=1e-3,
    leaf_family="gaussian",
)

# 3. Configure ModelTree and inject leaf controls
model = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=25,
    prune="none",
    control=leaf_ctrl,
)
model.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=feature_names)

# 4. Measure holdout performance
preds = model.predict(X_test)
m = Metrics().regression(y_test, preds)
print(f"ModelTree Linear Leaves: RMSE = {m['rmse']:.2f} MPa, R2 = {m['r2']:.3f}, MAE = {m['mae']:.2f} MPa")

items.title: Key Quantitative Findings

1. Immediate Accuracy Lift at Depth 1: A 1-split stump with linear leaves achieves 7.63 MPa RMSE, which is 25% lower error than a depth-4 CART tree (10.16 MPa) and 50% lower error than a depth-1 CART stump (15.24 MPa).
  2. Variance Reduction: At depth 3, ModelTree achieves 7.28 MPa RMSE and \(R^2 = 0.813\), capturing 81.3% of the variance compared to CART's 56.6%.
  3. Parity Alignment: In Panel 4, ModelTree predictions cluster symmetrically along the 1:1 diagonal without the horizontal striations characteristic of step-function leaves.

items.title: 4. 0D Descriptive Leaf Statistics
items.text:
Every terminal leaf in ModelTree computes a comprehensive 0D statistical profile over its assigned partition samples without extra passes. Access these profiles directly via leaf["stats"] or tree.leaf_stats():

leaves = model.leaves()
for idx, leaf in enumerate(leaves[:2]):
    stats = leaf["stats"]
    print(f"Leaf {idx} (support n={leaf['n']}):")
    print(f"  Center : mean={stats['mean']:.2f}, median={stats['median']:.2f}")
    print(f"  Spread : variance={stats['var']:.2f}, MAD={stats['mad']:.2f}, IQR={stats['iqr']:.2f}")
    print(f"  Shape  : skewness={stats['skew']:.2f}, kurtosis={stats['kurtosis']:.2f}")

Leaf 0 (n=143):
  Center : mean=15.44, median=14.37
  Spread : variance=45.41, MAD=4.15, IQR=8.96
  Shape  : skewness=1.10, kurtosis=1.79

Leaf 1 (n=47):
  Center : mean=27.67, median=25.69
  Spread : variance=48.11, MAD=4.43, IQR=10.67
  Shape  : skewness=0.41, kurtosis=-0.51

You can predict these 0D moments row-wise at test time using predict(X, kind="median"|"var"|"stats").

items.title: 5. Chow Structural Break Test Hypothesis Gating
items.text:
Standard trees rely purely on empirical gain thresholds (min_gain) or post-pruning to prevent overfitting. ModelTree implements the econometric Chow structural break test (split_test="chow") as a statistical significance gate:

\[\text{Chow } F = \frac{(\text{RSS}_P - (\text{RSS}_L + \text{RSS}_R)) / k}{(\text{RSS}_L + \text{RSS}_R) / (N - 2k)}\]

If the \(p\)-value exceeds split_alpha (e.g. \(\alpha = 0.01\)), the null hypothesis of structural stability across the candidate split is retained, and subtree branching is automatically terminated:

tree_chow = ModelTree(
    max_depth=5,
    min_rows=25,
    split_test="chow",
    split_alpha=0.01,
    control=leaf_ctrl,
)
tree_chow.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=feature_names)

This prevents the tree from creating spurious subtrees where local regressions show no statistically significant parameter shift.

items.title: Distributional Leaves — GLM, Censored, Survival & Volatility Families
items.text:
Real-world targets often violate Gaussian error assumptions. ModelTree provides native Rust implementations of specialized distributional families: leaf_family="binomial", "probit", "poisson", "gamma", "tweedie", "tobit", "softmax", "survival", and "heteroscedastic".

Run the suite from the repository root. It compares specialized leaves with a Gaussian baseline and prints held-out metrics.

uv run python examples/suites/distributional_leaf_benchmarks.py

Executable Reference Scripts: - examples/leaf_family.py — Link function invariant verifications & 6-family gallery. - examples/stump_distributional_leaves.py — Softmax, Survival, Heteroscedasticity & Microsecond Retraining on clinical and actuarial datasets. - examples/suites/distributional_leaf_benchmarks.py — Real benchmarks on German Credit, US Healthcare, Fair's Affairs, and Mroz Labor Supply.

items.title: Why Distributional Leaves Were Built
items.text:
Standard decision trees and linear models assume constant Gaussian error variances: $\(Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2), \quad \mu = \mathbf{X}\beta\)$

This assumption produces severe modeling failures across empirical domains: 1. Count & Frequency Data: Ordinary regression produces negative event counts. 2. Right-Censored Durations: Dropping or treating censored cases as deaths induces severe survival bias. 3. Severe Multiplicative Cost Skew: High-cost medical and insurance payouts exhibit variance scaling quadratically with the mean (\(\text{Var}(Y) \propto \mu^2\)). 4. Zero-Inflated Continuous Costs: Pure premiums have a point mass at zero with continuous positive claim sizes. 5. Left-Censored Corner Solutions: Censoring at zero induces downward attenuation bias in Ordinary Least Squares.

items.title: 1. Softmax Multi-Class Probability Vectors (\(C \ge 3\))
items.text:
Why Built & Use Case: Multi-tier medical triage, credit rating transition, and multi-option routing. Maps features onto the probability simplex \(\sum_{c=1}^C p_c = 1\). Dataset: Maternal Health Risk in Rural Areas (Ahmed et al., 2020, UCI Repository, 1,014 patients).

from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Fit Softmax tree partitioning on patient physiology
tree = ModelTree(max_depth=1, leaf_family="softmax", min_rows=20)
tree.fit(X, y, col_names=["SystolicBP", "BS", "Age"])

# Predict calibrated probabilities across all classes
pred_probs = tree.predict(X_test, kind="proba")

items.title: 4. Real Benchmark Tour: Probit, Gamma, Tweedie & Tobit
A. Probit Latent Utility (German Credit Risk)
items.text:
• Problem: Binary default scoring \(y \in \{0, 1\}\) with latent normal utility \(y^* \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}\beta, 1)\).
  • Mathematical Link: \(P(Y=1) = \Phi(\mathbf{X}\beta)\) where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function.
  • Interpretation: A positive coefficient increases the z-score index of default. Unlike logit, probit links directly to economic threshold-crossing models under Central Limit Theorem assumptions.

items.title: B. Gamma Continuous Positive Severity (Healthcare Charges)
items.text:
• Problem: Strictly positive charges (\(y > 0\)) with constant coefficient of variation (\(\text{Var}(Y) \propto \mu^2\)).
  • Mathematical Link: \(\ln(\mu) = \mathbf{X}\beta \implies \mu = \exp(\mathbf{X}\beta)\).
  • Interpretation: Coefficients act multiplicatively. For example, a coefficient of \(+0.0294\) for age implies an annual cost multiplier of \(\exp(0.0294) \approx 1.03\times\) (+3% per year of age).

items.title: C. Tweedie Compound Poisson-Gamma (Fair's Affairs)
items.text:
• Problem: Target with a large point mass at zero (75.1% exact zeros) alongside right-skewed continuous positive counts.
  • Mathematical Link: Quasi-likelihood with variance function \(\text{Var}(Y) = \phi \mu^p\) (\(1 < p < 2\)).
  • Interpretation: Unifies zero probability estimation and continuous severity into a single convex likelihood, avoiding ad-hoc two-stage hurdle pipelines.

items.title: D. Tobit Left-Censoring Correction (Mroz Female Labor Supply)
items.text:
• Problem: 43.2% of women report 0 hours worked. Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) treats observed zeros as unconstrained choices, causing downward attenuation bias.
  • Algorithm: Expectation-Maximization within IRLS to estimate the latent unobserved propensity \(y^*\).
  • Interpretation: 
    Structural Parameter Comparison (Tobit EM-IRLS vs Standard OLS):
  exper  -> Tobit: +105.71 | OLS: +41.50 | OLS Attenuation: 60.7%
  kidslt6 -> Tobit: -497.70 | OLS: -611.61
    OLS underestimates the marginal return to labor experience by over 60% due to censoring attenuation; Tobit recovers the true structural elasticity.

items.title: Distributional, Hurdle & Survival Split Criteria
items.text:
This guide demonstrates mltreelib's specialized tree-splitting criteria on real-world benchmark datasets.

While standard decision trees rely on homoscedastic SSE or Gini impurity, real data often exhibits heavy zero-inflation, pure variance breaks, censoring floors, heterogeneous relative noise, or survival censoring.

items.title: 1. Tweedie Quasi-Deviance Splitting (gain="tweedie")
items.text:
Best for: Zero-inflated continuous quantities (\(y \ge 0\), e.g., insurance claim amounts, financial defaults, or event intensity).

For power parameter \(1 < p < 2\), variance scales with \(\mu^p\). The quasi-deviance is:

\[d(y, \mu) = 2 \left( \frac{y^{2-p}}{(1-p)(2-p)} - \frac{y \mu^{1-p}}{1-p} + \frac{\mu^{2-p}}{2-p} \right)\] \[\text{Gain}_{\text{Tweedie}} = \text{Dev}(P) - [\text{Dev}(L) + \text{Dev}(R)]\]

items.title: Benchmark: Fair's Affairs Dataset
items.text:
import csv
from mltreelib import ModelTree

with open("datasets/external/affairs.csv", "r") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))

cols = ["age", "yearsmarried", "religiousness", "education", "occupation", "rating"]
X = [[float(r[c]) for c in cols] for r in rows]
y = [float(r["affairs"]) for r in rows]

# 75% of rows are exactly zero
tree = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=25,
    gain="tweedie",
    tweedie_p=1.5,
    prune="none",
)
tree.fit(X, y, col_names=cols)

for s in tree.splits():
    print(f"Split on {s['col']} at {s['threshold']:.2f} (quasi-deviance gain = {s['gain']:.4f})")

items.title: 2. Heteroscedastic Gaussian NLL Splitting (gain="heteroscedastic")
items.text:
Best for: Detecting regime shifts in volatility, risk, or noise where the conditional mean remains unchanged (\(\Delta \mu = 0\)).

Standard MSE trees look only for shifts in the mean. The heteroscedastic Gaussian NLL deviance evaluates:

\[\text{Dev}(S) = W_S \ln(\hat{\sigma}_S^2 + \epsilon)\] \[\text{Gain}_{\text{Hetero}} = W_P \ln \hat{\sigma}_P^2 - \left[ W_L \ln \hat{\sigma}_L^2 + W_R \ln \hat{\sigma}_R^2 \right]\] 
from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Left regime has sigma=0.2, right regime has sigma=4.0 (both with E[Y|X] = 0)
tree = ModelTree(
    max_depth=2,
    min_rows=20,
    gain="heteroscedastic",
    prune="none",
)
tree.fit(X, y)

items.title: 3. Tobit Hurdle Splitting (gain="tobit")
items.text:
Best for: Left-censored continuous responses (e.g., hours worked censored at 0, purchase amount with non-buyers at 0).

Combines binary classification deviance (\(y_i > a\) vs \(y_i \le a\)) with Gaussian deviance on the positive slice (\(y_i > a\)):

\[\text{Gain}_{\text{Tobit}} = \text{Gain}_{\text{binomial}}(I(y > a)) + \text{Gain}_{\text{Gaussian}}(y \mid y > a)\]

items.title: Benchmark: Mroz Female Labor Supply
items.text:
tree = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=30,
    gain="tobit",
    tobit_threshold=0.0,
    prune="none",
)
tree.fit(X_mroz, y_hours, col_names=cols)

items.title: 4. Coefficient of Variation Reduction (gain="cv")
items.text:
Best for: Scale-heterogeneous continuous data where relative variation \(\text{CV} = \sigma / \mu\) drives homogeneity:

\[\text{CV}(S) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}_S}{|\hat{\mu}_S| + \epsilon}\] \[\text{Gain}_{\text{CV}} = \text{CV}(P) - \left[ \frac{W_L}{W_P} \text{CV}(L) + \frac{W_R}{W_P} \text{CV}(R) \right]\]

items.title: 5. Martingale Survival Residual Splitting (gain="martingale")
items.text:
Best for: Right-censored time-to-event outcomes with precomputed cumulative baseline hazard \(\hat{\Lambda}_0(T_i)\).

Evaluates variance reduction on martingale residuals \(M_i = E_i - \hat{\Lambda}_0(T_i)\):

\[\text{Gain}_{\text{Martingale}} = \text{SSE}_M(P) - [\text{SSE}_M(L) + \text{SSE}_M(R)]\]

items.title: Benchmark: Veteran Lung Cancer Trial
items.text:
tree = ModelTree(
    max_depth=2,
    min_rows=20,
    gain="martingale",
    prune="none",
)
tree.fit(X_covariates, martingale_residuals, col_names=cols)

items.title: Generic optimizer and real-data tuning
items.text:
mltreelib.solvers.optimize minimizes a callable scalar objective inside bounds. It is the public entry point for the shared optimization seam in the Rust core. One objective, bounds, budget, request, and result contract backs every method, so the result never changes shape when the method changes.

The library never substitutes another algorithm silently. Unknown methods raise ValueError. Incompatible problems return an unsupported result.

items.title: Python surface
items.text:
from mltreelib.solvers import optimize

def objective(point):
    return (point[0] - 0.3) ** 2 + (point[1] + 1.5) ** 2

result = optimize(
    objective,
    [(-2.0, 2.0), (-2.0, 2.0)],
    method="random_search",
    samples=500,
    max_evaluations=500,
    seed=42,
)
Argument Meaning objective Callable that takes one list of parameter values and returns one finite scalar. bounds One (lower, upper) pair per parameter. method Canonical method name. start Starting point. Warm-starts the search. max_evaluations Cap on objective calls. max_iterations Cap on solver iterations. tol Convergence tolerance used by the evolutionary methods. Other methods use their Rust method defaults. seed Seed for stochastic methods. gradient Optional callable returning one derivative per parameter. samples Candidate count for the sampling methods. initial_population Optional first candidates for population methods. constraints COBYLA callback returning a fixed-length sequence of finite residuals. constraint_kind Defaults to "inequality". COBYLA rejects "equality". local_method Basin hopping's inner solver. Defaults to "lbfgs_b".

The result reports:

Field Meaning best_x Best evaluated point, or an empty list when the method rejects the problem. best_value Objective value at best_x, or NaN when no objective value is available. iterations Solver iterations performed. evaluations User objective evaluations performed. status Termination status. converged True only for converged and tolerance. history Optional convergence history. max_constraint_violation Largest constraint violation at best_x. message Failure detail when the run did not succeed.

The API reference page Solvers & optimization holds the exact signatures and docstrings. Rust callers use the same contracts from mltreelib_core::generic; the Rust generic seam page lists every type, trait, and function with its doc comment.

items.title: Statuses
items.text:
Status Meaning converged The method reached its convergence test. tolerance The tolerance test ended the run. iteration_limit The iteration budget ended the run. evaluation_limit The evaluation budget ended the run. invalid_objective The objective returned a NaN or infinite value. numerical_failure The numerical kernel failed. infeasible No feasible point was found. unsupported The method cannot solve the requested problem. hard_error An unrecoverable error ended the run.

Budget exhaustion never reports success. A failed run never returns a converged status.

items.title: The optimizers
items.text: Method Status Needs Bounds Memory Use it for random_search available objective only finite box linear Honest baseline for every comparison. latin_hypercube available objective only finite box linear Stratified initialization for population methods. lbfgs_b available gradient or central differences box bounds linear Smooth bounded objectives with many parameters. bfgs available gradient or central differences unbounded only quadratic Small smooth problems where curvature pays off. nonlinear_cg available gradient or central differences unbounded only linear First-order competitor with no curvature history. nelder_mead available objective only box bounds quadratic Black-box local search and basin-hopping inner solves. powell available objective only box bounds quadratic Derivative-free search with different basin behaviour. simulated_annealing available objective only finite box linear Cheap global search over non-smooth objectives. cobyla available objective only box bounds quadratic in dimension, plus constraint models Nonlinear inequality constraints without gradients. basin_hopping available inner local solver depends on inner solver depends on inner solver Rugged landscapes with separated local minima. cmaes available objective only box bounds dense covariance plus population Continuous problems with coupled parameters. shade available objective only box bounds population and archive Differential evolution with adaptive mutation and crossover. nes available objective only box bounds population Evolution strategy with diagonal scales. ga available objective only box bounds population Real-coded genetic search with strict elitism.

items.title: Random Search
items.text: Samples uniformly inside the bounds and keeps the best candidate. It needs no gradient, so it runs against any objective. It is the baseline every other method must beat under an equal evaluation budget.

items.title: Latin hypercube
items.text: Stratifies every dimension independently into samples strata, draws one point per stratum, and shuffles the strata with the seeded generator. The marginal coverage of each dimension beats uniform sampling at the same budget, which makes it the better initializer for population methods.

items.title: L-BFGS-B
items.text: The bounded smooth local solver. Each iteration computes the generalized Cauchy point along the piecewise-linear projected-gradient path, approximately minimizes the quadratic model over the free variables, runs a line search, projects onto the bounds, and tests the projected gradient norm over the free variables only. It keeps the limited-memory curvature update, so large parameter vectors stay practical. Without binding bounds its result matches the existing solve_lbfgs path.

items.title: BFGS
items.text: Full-memory BFGS with a dense inverse-Hessian approximation. Memory grows quadratically with the parameter count, so it suits small problems. It solves the same unconstrained objective as L-BFGS, which makes the two directly comparable. It rejects finite bounds instead of clipping them.

items.title: Nonlinear conjugate gradient
items.text: Polak-Ribiere direction with a documented restart rule. It needs only the objective and the gradient, keeps memory linear in the parameter count, and carries no curvature history. A negative Polak-Ribiere coefficient restarts the search direction.

items.title: Nelder-Mead
items.text: Derivative-free simplex search. It replaces the worst vertex each iteration with reflection, expansion, contraction, or shrink. The initial simplex shape and the two tolerances are configurable in Rust. It clips simplex vertices to the box.

items.title: Powell
items.text: Derivative-free conjugate-direction search. It performs sequential one-dimensional minimizations along a maintained direction set, and every line-search evaluation stays inside the box.

items.title: Simulated annealing
items.text: Global trajectory search over a bounded domain. The proposal is a per dimension bounded random displacement, the cooling schedule is geometric by default, and the boundary policy is either resampling or reflection. Clipping is not offered because it piles proposal mass on bound-active points. The best incumbent is tracked separately from the current point, so the result never degrades. The method ships as a heuristic with no optimality claim.

items.title: COBYLA
items.text:
This derivative-free variant fits linear models over nearby evaluated points. It uses a box-shaped trust region and cyclic projection in place of Powell's original model subproblem solver. It keeps all evaluations inside the bounds. An infeasible result means the search found no feasible point. It does not prove that no feasible point exists.

result = optimize(
    lambda x: (x[0] - 2.0) ** 2 + x[1] ** 2,
    [(-5.0, 5.0)] * 2,
    method="cobyla",
    start=[1.5, 0.0],
    constraints=lambda x: [1.0 - x[0] ** 2 - x[1] ** 2],
    max_evaluations=200,
)

items.title: Basin hopping
items.text: A composition, not a numerical kernel. It perturbs the incumbent, runs an inner local solve through the same seam, and accepts the result with a constant-temperature Metropolis test. The step size is either fixed or adapted toward a target acceptance rate. Inner solve evaluations count against the outer budget, and a failed inner solve never erases the incumbent. Pass local_method to select lbfgs_b, bfgs, nonlinear_cg, nelder_mead, or powell. Use unbounded limits when the inner method is BFGS or nonlinear CG.

items.title: Evolutionary methods
items.text:
The generic entry point and standalone GLM fits share the same population kernels. Generic optimization clips candidates to the supplied bounds. If you pass initial_population, the adapter evaluates those candidates against the same budget and starts the kernel from the best candidate. It reports the best evaluated point even if the budget ends partway through a generation.

Use unbounded limits for bfgs and nonlinear_cg. Only cobyla accepts a nonlinear constraint callback.

items.title: Budgets and determinism
items.text: max_evaluations caps the number of objective calls and max_iterations caps the number of solver iterations. Both limits report their own status. Every stochastic method takes an explicit seed, and the same inputs, bounds, options, and seed produce the same result. An omitted seed uses the fixed default seed, so omitted seeds stay reproducible.

items.title: Constraint semantics
items.text: An inequality residual is nonnegative at a feasible point. COBYLA accepts residuals down to -1e-8 by default and reports the largest raw violation at the returned point. The Rust CobylaOptions can change the tolerance. COBYLA rejects equalities before it evaluates the objective.

items.title: Leaf solver decoupling
items.text:
Leaf building and solver selection are independent axes. A leaf declares the optimization problem it poses. A solver declares what it can solve. One compatibility lookup resolves a leaf, a response family, and a solver into a supported pairing or one precise rejection reason.

Solver Gradients Derivative-free L1 Monotone Box bounds Equality Nonlinear inequality Memory irls yes no yes yes no no no quadratic lbfgs yes no no no no no no linear ccd no yes yes yes no no no linear cmaes, shade, nes, ga no yes yes yes (GLM fits) yes (optimize) no no population

Rejected pairings name the missing capability, for example solver Lbfgs does not support L1 penalties.

Every fitted leaf persists two diagnostics: solver_used names the solver that ran, or that it did not apply, and leaf_problem_type names the objective the fit minimized. A closed-form leaf such as the weighted mean accepts any solver selection and reports the solver as not applicable instead of failing the fit.

items.title: Datasets
items.text:
The benchmark Parquet files under datasets/ are not tracked in git. Fetch the suite once per checkout:

uv run python scripts/fetch_datasets.py
uv run python scripts/fetch_datasets.py --only diabetes airfoil_self_noise

One dataset can also arrive on demand through the loader, which caches it under ~/.cache/mltreelib/datasets/:

from mltreelib.datasets import load_dataset

data = load_dataset("airfoil_self_noise")

datasets/MANIFEST.md lists every dataset with its OpenML identifier, task, target, size, and license.

items.text:
examples/optimize_generic.py tunes ModelTree hyperparameters on a local benchmark dataset and reports the holdout RMSE against a default tree. Both methods receive the same evaluation budget.

items.title: Canonical benchmark
items.text:
uv run python examples/benchmark_optimizers.py --budget 200 --offline --output-dir /tmp/mltreelib-optimizers

The runner writes JSON records and a Markdown summary. It covers analytic regression, synthetic landscapes, constrained problems, a binomial likelihood, tree tuning on Airfoil, and a split-threshold search. It records the domain because BFGS and nonlinear conjugate gradient require unbounded problems. It reports no objective gap for infeasible results or problems with no known optimum.

items.title: Hierarchical Leaf Retrain & Micro-Model Routing
items.text:
Tree partitions carve heterogeneous feature spaces into homogeneous sub-populations. While standard model trees fit models using the same features and targets at split and leaf time, complex empirical settings often require hierarchical model routing:

  1. A macro-tree splits on aggregated or cohort-level features (e.g. city, make, model year, fleet tier) to segment cohorts.
  2. An external micro-model retrains leaf nodes on granular entity-level telemetry (e.g. mileage, maintenance history, accident counts) using specialized distributional families (such as Gamma, Tweedie, or Tobit).
  3. Primary keys (id_col) track individual entities through leaf assignments without contaminating feature matrices.

Run the suite from the repository root to compare leaf fits while keeping the split fixed.

uv run python examples/suites/stump_leaf_retrain.py

Scripts: - examples/hierarchical_leaf_retrain.py — Macro cohort tree with micro telematics retrain. - examples/suites/stump_leaf_retrain.py — Industrial stump laboratory: Mean, Linear Ridge, Huber, Quantile, and Binomial on frozen regimes.

items.title: 1. Internal vs. External Retraining Modes
items.text:
The retrain() method supports two operational modes:

  • mode="internal": Mutates the tree's existing leaf models in-place, keeping the tree structure intact.
  • mode="external": Leaves the original tree untouched and returns a new ModelTree instance with updated leaf models fitted on new data or alternative feature subsets.
from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Step 1: Macro-level segmentation tree
macro_tree = ModelTree(max_depth=2, min_rows=2, leaf="mean")
macro_tree.fit(
    X_macro,
    y_baseline,
    col_names=["city_tier", "fleet_type"]
)

# Step 2: Retrain leaves externally with granular telemetry
micro_tree = macro_tree.retrain(
    X=df_telemetry,
    y=y_fine,
    mode="external",
    leaf="linear",
    leaf_family="gamma",
    leaf_features=["mileage", "service_count"],
    control={"l2": 1e-2, "max_iter": 25}
)

items.title: 2. Granular Leaf Feature Selection (leaf_features)
items.text:
You can decouple the split features from the leaf regression features using leaf_features (or retrain_cols):

  • Splitting Features: Used by internal tree nodes to route samples to the correct leaf (e.g. city_tier, fleet_type). These columns must be present in the retraining dataset.
  • Leaf Features: Selected subset of columns used inside each leaf node to fit local regressions (e.g. mileage, service_count).

If leaf_features is omitted, all non-identifier columns are used for leaf fitting.

items.title: 3. Entity Tracking with leaf_samples(X, id_col=...)
items.text:
To route entities and group downstream analyses by leaf assignments, pass id_col to leaf_samples():

# Group vehicle identification numbers (VINs) by leaf assignment
vin_groups = micro_tree.leaf_samples(df_telemetry, id_col="vin")

for leaf_id, vins in vin_groups.items():
    print(f"Leaf {leaf_id} manages {len(vins)} vehicles: {vins[:3]}...")

If id_col is None (default), leaf_samples() returns integer row indices 0..N-1.

items.title: 4. Family Control Knobs
items.text:
Algorithm controls for leaf fitting are passed via a flexible control dictionary or LeafControl:

control = {
    "l2": 1e-3,           # L2 ridge regularization penalty
    "max_iter": 30,       # Maximum Fisher scoring / IRLS iterations
    "tol": 1e-6,          # Convergence tolerance on parameter updates
    "extra": {            # Family-specific optional hyper-parameters
        "power": 1.5,     # Tweedie compound variance power p
        "censor_lower": 0 # Tobit left-censoring threshold
    }
}

retrained = macro_tree.retrain(
    X=df,
    y=y,
    mode="internal",
    leaf="linear",
    leaf_family="tweedie",
    control=control
)

items.title: 5. Stump Retrain Laboratory: Microsecond Loss Hot-Swapping
items.text:
Why Built & Use Case: In production streaming pipelines, rebuilding a tree's split topology requires scanning continuous histograms across all features (\(O(N \cdot P \log N)\)). However, if the macro spatial segmentation is stable, updating leaf parameters on incoming batches requires only \(O(N_L \cdot P^2)\) local convex optimizations, running in microseconds.

Real Dataset: Concrete Compressive Strength (Yeh 1998, Cement and Concrete Research; 1,030 mixtures). Hydration kinetics segment concrete into Early Curing (\(\le 14\) days) vs Mature Curing (\(> 14\) days).

from mltreelib import ModelTree, LeafControl

# Step 1: Base split search identifies optimal hydration regime (Age <= 14d vs > 14d)
stump = ModelTree(max_depth=1, min_rows=20, leaf="linear")
stump.fit(X, y, col_names=["Age", "Cement", "Water"])

# Step 2: Instantaneous Retraining (0.7ms - 20x speedup)
# A. Robust Huber M-estimator against sensor glitches
stump.retrain(X, y_polluted, control=LeafControl(leaf="huber"))

# B. Empirical Quantile safety corridors (10th-90th percentiles)
stump.retrain(X, y, leaf="quantile", tau=0.10)
q10 = stump.predict(X_test)
stump.retrain(X, y, leaf="quantile", tau=0.90)
q90 = stump.predict(X_test)

items.title: Honest trees & sample weights
items.text:
ModelTree supports sample-splitting honesty to reduce reuse of outcomes for split selection and leaf estimation, as well as observation weights for cost-sensitive learning and survey sampling.

Script: examples/honesty_weights.py (uv run python examples/honesty_weights.py).

items.title: Output
items.text:
== 1. Honest tree estimation (honesty=True) ==
  standard tree: 3 leaves, total leaf rows: 300
  honest tree  : 3 leaves, estimation leaf rows: 120 (structure used 40%)
    leaf 0: standard mean=0.004 (n=60) | honest mean=0.386 (n=50)
    leaf 1: standard mean=0.602 (n=60) | honest mean=1.474 (n=49)
    leaf 2: standard mean=1.797 (n=180) | honest mean=2.402 (n=21)

== 2. Weighted tree fitting (fit(x, y, w=...)) ==
  x0=0 target: eight rows at y=2.0, two rows at y=20.0
  unweighted prediction (equal weight): 5.600
  weighted prediction (10x rare weight) : 14.857

items.title: Honest estimation (honesty=True)
items.text:
In standard greedy decision trees, the same training observations select the splits and estimate leaf parameters (constants, linear slopes, and empirical quantiles). On noisy data, this double use introduces optimism bias and over-confident leaf distributions.

Honest estimation (adapted from Athey, Tibshirani, and Wager's grf) splits the dataset: - Structure sample (honesty_fraction, e.g. 0.4): evaluates split candidates, impurity reductions, and tree topology. - Estimation sample (1.0 - honesty_fraction, e.g. 0.6): flows down the fixed topology to fit leaf parameters and empirical t-digests.

from mltreelib import ModelTree

model = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    honesty=True,
    honesty_fraction=0.5,  # 50% structure, 50% estimation
)
model.fit(X, y)

Sample splitting reduces adaptive reuse of outcomes. It does not guarantee unbiased predictions or quantiles for every dataset, remove confounding, or replace independent evaluation. Fewer estimation rows can also make leaf estimates unstable. Check leaf support and compare performance on a held-out set. See Athey and Imbens (2016).

items.title: Sample weights (w, sample_weight, row_weights)
items.text:
Pass a 1D sequence of non-negative weights to ModelTree.fit():

from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Assign higher weight to rare or critical observations:
weights = [10.0 if is_critical(i) else 1.0 for i in range(len(X))]

model = ModelTree(max_depth=3, leaf="mean")
model.fit(X, y, sample_weight=weights)  # or w=weights / row_weights=weights

w weights observations across: - Impurity score and gain calculations during split search. - Leaf means and weighted least-squares linear fits. - Weighted IRLS for binomial (leaf_family="binomial") and Poisson (leaf_family="poisson") models.

items.title: Column / Feature weights (col_weights)
items.text:
Pass feature importance weights to scale candidate split gains and bias feature subsampling during col_sample:

# Scale split gain on column 0 by 2x, column 1 by 0.5x:
model = ModelTree(max_depth=3, col_weights=[2.0, 0.5])
model.fit(X, y)

items.title: Hyperparameter search (Optuna)
items.text:
The full ModelTree growth surface is a search space — and Optuna is the wheel we borrow for it. examples/hpo_optuna.py tunes depth, leaf size, ridge, leaf kind, criterion, the split grid, categorical search, the imbalance knobs and pruning on a seeded TPE study:

uv run --with pandas --with optuna python examples/hpo_optuna.py 40

The objective is plain — fit, score, return RMSE. Every suggestion maps 1:1 to a ModelTree keyword:

params = dict(
    max_depth=trial.suggest_int("max_depth", 1, 8),
    min_rows=trial.suggest_int("min_rows", 5, 200, log=True),
    l2=trial.suggest_float("l2", 1e-3, 10.0, log=True),
    leaf=trial.suggest_categorical("leaf", ["linear", "mean"]),
    leaf_cols=trial.suggest_categorical("leaf_cols", ["all", "path"]),
    gain=trial.suggest_categorical("gain", ["sse", "sdr"]),
    split_precision=trial.suggest_categorical("split_precision", [None, 0.1, 0.01]),
    cat_search=trial.suggest_categorical("cat_search", ["cumulative", "single_vs_rest", "both"]),
    alpha=trial.suggest_float("alpha", 0.0, 0.2),
    imbalance_penalty=trial.suggest_float("imbalance_penalty", 1e-3, 100.0, log=True),
    prune=trial.suggest_categorical("prune", ["none", "bic", "mdl"]),
)
m = ModelTree(**params)
m.fit(xtr, ytr, dtypes=dtypes)
return Metrics().regression(yte, m.predict(xte))["rmse"]

items.title: A real study (airfoil_self_noise, 40 seeded TPE trials)
items.text:
trials: 40   best rmse: 1.848
best settings (the elo_round SETTINGS shape):
    max_depth=8,
    min_rows=6,
    l2=5.8545958517512275,
    leaf='linear',
    leaf_cols='all',
    gain='sse',
    split_precision=None,
    cat_search='both',
    alpha=0.030185289276873507,
    imbalance_penalty=0.05567092885866246,
    prune='bic',
trial #38  (seeded TPE, airfoil 80/20)

Two findings worth keeping: TPE independently rejected the split grid (split_precision=None) for this fit, and it picked prune='bic' with a small imbalance penalty — cost pruning and balance tuning, chosen by the search rather than by hand.

The winner prints in the exact SETTINGS dict shape the Elo rounds record — paste it into examples/elo_round.py to score a tuned flavor on the full field. That is the intended loop: search per-dataset, then let the round measure what the settings are actually worth across 18 datasets (ELO — Running a round).

Examples — next: Metrics & plots

items.title: Significance Testing Gate — split_test="chow"
items.text:
The Chow structural break test evaluates whether splitting a node into two children yields a statistically significant parameter shift over the pooled node model:

model = ModelTree(split_test="chow", split_alpha=0.05, bonferroni=True, verbose=2)
model.fit(x, y)
  • When fitting pure noise, chow=stop halts growth immediately (1 leaf), avoiding false splits without needing aggressive manual tuning.
  • bonferroni=True divides split_alpha by the number of candidate cuts tested at the node, correcting for multiple testing.

items.title: Honesty — honesty=True
items.text:
In the spirit of generalized random forests (grf), honesty splits the training rows into two independent samples: - Structure rows (honesty_fraction=0.5 by default) determine split candidate scoring, significance gating, and tree structure. - Estimation rows determine leaf parameters and fitted responses.

This reduces reuse of outcomes for selecting splits and estimating leaves. It does not eliminate overfitting or replace independent evaluation.

items.title: NA Surrogate Splits — maxsurrogate
items.text: maxsurrogate=k (following rpart lineage) stores up to \(k\) surrogate splits at each internal node that mimic the primary partition. When predicting a test row missing the primary split feature, the primary surrogate routes the row instead of defaulting to a static branch.

items.title: Feature Screening — preselect
items.text: Before tree growth begins, candidate features can be filtered via screening: - "winnow": Univariate linear correlation screening. - "boruta": Comparison against shadow randomized permutations. - "unitree": Univariate shallow surrogate trees scored by explained variation \(R^2\).

items.title: Metrics & plots
items.text:
Every evaluation surface and every chart, demonstrated on real data (bank churn, with the tree's predictions as scores). Script: examples/metrics_showcase.py.

pip install mltreelib[plotting]        # matplotlib + pygraphviz + seaborn
uv run python examples/metrics_showcase.py

items.title: The full surface, in one run
items.text: The script fits ModelTree on raw categorical labels and evaluates a held-out slice. It computes its comparison baseline from the training outcomes. The break-down chart uses a separately fitted numeric-only model because break_down rejected raw strings in a tested mixed row. A threshold of 0.5 is illustrative; select operational thresholds on validation data. The evaluation pathway demonstrates that sequence with reproducible synthetic data.

items.title: The chart surface
items.text:
All sixteen charts from mltreelib.plots render as click-to-zoom figures in Visualization Guide:

chart what it answers plot_roc / plot_pr discrimination; PR is the honest view on class imbalance plot_cumulative_gain / plot_lift targeting efficiency: "top decile captures X% at Y× lift" plot_ks maximum separation distance between classes + Score@KS plot_decile scorecard decile profile: event rate bars + cumulative capture plot_calibration / plot_response probability reliability vs. diagonal and decile response plot_double_lift head-to-head model comparison along one ranking (CAS) plot_psi score/feature stability and population shift between two periods plot_confusion_matrix classification error distribution across class boundaries plot_residuals regression fit diagnostics: actual vs. predicted and equality line plot_importance variable importance shares of total split gain plot_breakdown DALE-style waterfall attribution of one observation plot_variance_shares realized variance shares against ground truth plot_decomposition 4-panel additive time-series decomposition (trend/season/residual)

Each chart takes ax= and returns Axes, so any panel composes. The library itself never imports matplotlib — this layer is opt-in via the [plotting] extra. Every number on this page comes from the script; the API shapes are in Metrics.

items.title: Native Missing Data Routing & Surrogate Splits
items.text:
This guide details mltreelib's first-class handling of missing tabular data (None and NaN), evaluating learned missing split directions and surrogate splits on industrial telemetry without synthetic imputation.

Script: examples/suites/missing_routing_benchmark.py (uv run python examples/suites/missing_routing_benchmark.py).

items.title: 1. Domain Context & The Imputation Failure Mode
items.text:
In mission-critical sensor telemetry (such as heavy truck fleet diagnostics, aerospace health monitoring, and clinical vital tracking), missing values occur regularly due to intermittent sensor disconnections, telemetry dropouts, or power cycles.

Standard tabular workflows apply global mean, median, or MICE imputation before fitting. Imputation introduces three dangerous failure modes: 1. Covariance Distortion: Imputing a constant mean collapses the conditional variance of missing sensors and creates artificial point-mass spikes in the distribution. 2. Destruction of Missingness Signal: In engineering systems, the fact that a sensor stopped reporting is often highly correlated with system failure. Imputation erases this indicator. 3. Serving-Time Dependency: In production, streaming scoring pipelines must maintain online imputation buffers across dozens of historical distributions.

mltreelib eliminates imputation completely through Native Rust-Level Missing Routing: - Learned Missing Direction (missing_left): During node partition search, candidate splits score sending missing records to the left branch versus the right branch, selecting the direction that minimizes node deviance or SSE. - Surrogate Splits (maxsurrogate=N): When a primary split feature is missing at prediction time, the tree inspects pre-computed correlated surrogate features to route the sample along the optimal path. - NA-Indicator Linear Leaves: Linear leaves fit dedicated indicator coefficients \(\beta_{\text{NA}, j}\) for absent features, preserving local linear slopes for observed predictors.

flowchart TD
    A["Incoming Feature Vector\n[x1, x2, ..., xk]"] --> B{"Is Primary Split Feature\nx_j Observed?"}

    B -- "Observed" --> C{"Predicate Test:\nx_j <= Threshold?"}
    C -- "True" --> Left["Left Child Node"]
    C -- "False" --> Right["Right Child Node"]

    B -- "Missing (None / NaN)" --> D{"Are Surrogate Splits\nConfigured & Available?"}

    D -- "Surrogate Feature Available" --> E{"Surrogate Predicate Test:\nx_surrogate <= Threshold?"}

items.title: 2. Benchmark Study: Scania Truck Air Pressure System (APS) Failure
items.text:
We evaluate native routing against standard mean imputation on the Scania APS Failure benchmark (76,000 industrial truck diagnostic records, 171 sensor channels).

from mltreelib import Metrics, ModelTree, load_dataset

# 1. Load Scania truck telemetry benchmark
data = load_dataset("APSFailure")
target = "AirPressureSystemFailure"
features = [
    "aa_000", "ab_000", "ac_000", "ad_000", "ae_000", "af_000",
    "ag_000", "ag_001", "ag_002", "ag_003", "ag_004", "ag_005"
]
n_sample = 12000

y_raw = data["columns"][target][:n_sample]
y = [1 if v in ("pos", "1", 1) else 0 for v in y_raw]
X = [[data["columns"][c][i] for c in features] for i in range(n_sample)]

split = 8000
X_train, y_train = X[:split], y[:split]
X_test, y_test = X[split:10000], y[split:10000]

# 2. Fit ModelTree with Native Missing Routing and 2 Surrogates per node
tree_native = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=50,
    maxsurrogate=2,
    leaf="mean",
    leaf_family="binomial",
    gain="deviance",
)
tree_native.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=features)

# 3. Evaluate on held-out test telemetry
probs = tree_native.predict_proba(X_test)
metrics = Metrics()
pr = metrics.pr_curve(y_test, probs)
roc = metrics.roc_curve(y_test, probs)

print(f"Native Routing -> Average Precision: {pr['average_precision']:.4f}, ROC-AUC: {roc['auc']:.4f}")

items.title: Key Quantitative Findings
items.text:
1. High Missingness Tolerance (Panel 1): Key diagnostic sensors like ab_000 exhibit 77.4% missingness in production telemetry. Standard imputation collapses 77% of this channel to a single scalar value, destroying its variance.
  2. Superior Precision-Recall (Panel 2): Native missing routing achieves 0.5924 Average Precision, outperforming the mean imputation baseline by +3.8%.
  3. Calibrated Probabilities on Incomplete Telemetry (Panel 4): On 1,606 test records with at least one missing sensor, ModelTree achieves a 0.0153 Brier score, maintaining reliable probability calibration without collapsing to the prior mean.

items.title: Missing data routing & surrogate splits
items.text:
In mltreelib, missing data is a first-class citizen. ModelTree supports missing predictor values (None and NaN) in the workflows below. Input validation and missing-target behavior vary by operation. Check the contract for the selected estimator.

ModelTree resolves missing data through three mechanisms: 1. Learned missing directions (missing_left): during split search, the tree evaluates both sending missing values left vs. right, selecting whichever branch minimizes error. 2. Surrogate splits (maxsurrogate=N): when a split feature is missing at prediction time, the highest-agreement surrogate split directs the sample. 3. NA indicator coefficients in linear leaves: linear leaves estimate dedicated indicator coefficients for missing predictors so within-leaf regressions remain valid.

Script: examples/missing_routing.py (uv run python examples/missing_routing.py).

items.title: 1. Learned split directions (missing_left)
items.text:
For every candidate numeric or categorical split, the partition search evaluates: - Send observed values matching the predicate to the left branch. - Send observed values failing the predicate to the right branch. - Score placing None values on the left branch vs. placing None values on the right branch.

The configuration minimizing SSE or deviance is stored as missing_left: bool. When an unseen record with None arrives, it routes along this learned direction.

items.title: 2. Surrogate splits (maxsurrogate=N)
items.text:
When maxsurrogate >= 1, the tree identifies correlated secondary features whose splits best mimic the primary split partition:

from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Compute up to 2 surrogate splits per internal node:
model = ModelTree(max_depth=3, maxsurrogate=2)
model.fit(X, y)

At prediction time, if the primary split feature is missing, the highest-ranking surrogate is checked. Only if all surrogate features are also missing does the tree fall back to missing_left.

items.title: 3. NA-indicator leaf regression
items.text:
When leaf="linear", the leaf fits a coefficient for each observed feature plus an indicator term \(\beta_{\text{NA}, j}\) for whether feature \(j\) was missing:

\[\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \sum_{j \in \text{obs}} \beta_j x_j + \sum_{j \in \text{missing}} \beta_{\text{NA}, j}\]

This allows leaves to make continuous linear adjustments when predictors are partially missing without collapsing to a simple global mean.

items.title: Model building & predictions
items.text:
Every parameter and nuance the tree handles, on one big, tedious dataset — the bundled diamonds parquet (53,940 rows, mixed numeric/categorical, missing cells) — with deeper trees than the quickstart.

Script: examples/model_building.py. Fits use the shipped defaults (linear leaves + small ridge — closed-form fast). Regularization gets its own dedicated example later.

diamonds: 53940 rows x 26 cols (deeper trees below)

coarser leaves min_rows=500            rmse=     555.6  r2=      0.980  leaves=  57
leaf="mean"                            rmse=     884.5  r2=      0.950  leaves= 150
leaf="linear", leaf_cols="path"        rmse=    1137.5  r2=      0.918  leaves= 127

row weights (2x carat<1)               rmse=     884.5  r2=      0.950  leaves= 150
winnow kept 15/26 columns (dropped: [1, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25])
min_relevance=0.05 (winnowed fit)      rmse=     898.1  r2=      0.949  leaves= 134

predictions with missing carat: [1175.4, -1371.3, 1042.0]

items.title: Growth knobs — max_depth, min_rows, min_gain
items.text: Deeper is not better: depth 12 chases noise (598.6 vs 577.0), and coarser leaves win outright (555.6 with min_rows=500) — on 54k rows the tree prefers fewer, steadier leaves. min_gain is the numerical noise floor.

items.title: Leaf models — and why the default keeps ridge
items.text:
leaf="mean" fits piecewise constants (884.5); leaf="linear" fits piecewise slopes and wins here (577.0). leaf_cols="path" restricts leaf regressions to the columns used on the path — fewer coefficients, less variance, more bias (1137.5).

Then the important one: l1=0, l2=0 explodes (r² = −40499). Pure-OLS leaves on raw, collinear scales produce wild coefficients and nine-million-dollar predictions. The small default ridge is not cosmetic — it is load-bearing, and it is closed-form (fast). This is exactly why regularization earns its own upcoming example.

items.title: Row weights
items.text: fit(x, y, w) — upweighting small stones (2x carat<1) shifts the fitted leaf values toward the weighted rows without touching the structure.

items.title: Winnowing — min_relevance / winnow()
items.text:
res = winnow(xtr, ytr, min_relevance=0.05)   # {"kept": [...], "relevance": [...]}

Univariate relevance screening drops 11 of 26 columns (mostly one-hot levels) before the split search; the winnowed fit keeps its accuracy on half the columns (898.1). Same screen runs inside fit when min_relevance is set.

items.title: Monotone constraints
items.text: A domain fact: price never falls as carat rises. monotone=[…, +1, …] enforces it at split choice and in leaf coefficients — costing almost nothing here (601.8 vs 577.0) because the fact is true.

items.title: Interaction groups
items.text: interaction_groups=[[carat…], [rest…]] — every root-to-leaf path may split only one group (LightGBM-style interaction constraints). Small cost (583.7), bounded interaction structure.

items.title: Missing values are first-class
items.text:
Predicting with a missing carat cell just works — the learned NA direction and indicator terms answer:

predictions with missing carat: [1175.4, -1371.3, 1042.0]

(The negative one is honest linear-leaf extrapolation in an unobserved direction, not a crash — see Inspection for the leaf coefficients behind it.)

items.title: Distributional leaves — leaf_family
items.text:
Binary targets and counts get a family instead of a Gaussian mean: leaf_family="binomial" (logit link) for 0/1 targets and "poisson" (log link) for nonnegative counts or rates. Pair them with gain="deviance" so the split search scores the fitted likelihood, not squared error. Predictions stay on the response scale — predict_proba returns P(class 1), and cdf(x, value) returns the fitted distribution's P(Y <= value) (distinct from the empirical quantile).

Script: examples/leaf_family.py.

binomial P(1): [0.25, 0.75]
binomial P(Y <= 0): [0.75, 0.25]
poisson means: [1.0, 2.0, 4.0]
poisson P(Y <= 0): [0.367879, 0.018316]
categorical + NA P(1): [0.0, 1.0, 1.0]

The exact grouped MLEs recover the planted log-odds and log-rates; categorical levels and missing values route through the same native handlers as Gaussian trees. Linear coefficients are on the link scale (logit / log); predict/predict_proba convert back to response means.

Next: Inspection for the metrics and structure reports, or Visualization to draw the tree.

items.title: PCA Rotations — Simple Structure, Orthomax Family & Oblique Promax
items.text:
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) decomposes high-dimensional feature spaces into orthogonal axes that maximize explained variance. However, raw principal component loadings are dense, unaligned with natural domain concepts, and hard to interpret.

mltreelib.ComponentModel provides a pure Rust implementation of factor and PCA rotations mirroring the classic R statistical foundations (stats::varimax, stats::promax, and the Orthomax family), resolving rotational indeterminacy to discover Thurstone's simple structure.

Run the educational example and benchmark suite directly:

uv run python examples/pca_rotations_educational.py
uv run python examples/suites/component_benchmarks.py

Executable Reference Scripts: - examples/pca_rotations_educational.py — Cognitive aptitude battery case study, Thurstone's simple structure criteria, and loading matrix comparisons. - examples/suites/component_benchmarks.py — Suite 10: Quantitative benchmark across PCA rotations, ZCA/PCA whitening, and NMF solvers (MU, ALS, HALS). - docs/examples/component-benchmarks.md — Comprehensive documentation for Suite 10 component benchmarks.

items.title: Why PCA Rotations Were Built (The Interpretability Problem)
items.text:
Standard PCA computes eigenvectors \(\mathbf{V} = [\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k]\) of the empirical covariance matrix \(\mathbf{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{N} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}\) corresponding to the largest eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_k\):

\[\max_{\mathbf{v}_j} \mathbf{v}_j^T \mathbf{\Sigma} \mathbf{v}_j \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{v}_j^T \mathbf{v}_j = 1, \quad \mathbf{v}_j^T \mathbf{v}_l = 0 \; (l \ne j)\]

This mathematical criterion produces severe interpretability issues in real-world data:

  1. Dense Global Loadings: The first principal component (PC1) maximizes global variance. Consequently, almost all variables exhibit non-zero loadings of similar magnitude (the classic "general factor", such as general intelligence \(g\), general company size, or overall user activity).
  2. Artificial Bipolarity: Higher components (PC2, PC3, ...) are constrained to be globally orthogonal to PC1. This forces negative and positive loadings across unrelated features that are mathematical artifacts of orthogonality rather than genuine domain phenomena.
  3. Rotational Indeterminacy: The subspace spanned by \(k\) components is invariant under any invertible rotation matrix \(\mathbf{T}\): $\(\hat{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{Z} \mathbf{V}^T = (\mathbf{Z} \mathbf{T}) (\mathbf{V} \mathbf{T})^{-T} = \mathbf{Z}^* (\mathbf{V}^*)^T\)$ When \(\mathbf{T}\) is orthogonal (\(\mathbf{T}^T \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{I}\)), the reconstructed subspace and the total variance explained remain 100% identical. The rotation simply chooses new coordinate axes within the same subspace to make the factor loadings human-interpretable.

items.title: Thurstone's Simple Structure Criteria (1947)
items.text:
In Multiple-Factor Analysis (1947), Louis Leon Thurstone formalized five criteria for an interpretable coordinate system:

  1. Each variable (row of \(\mathbf{V}^*\)) must have at least one loading close to zero.
  2. For each factor (column of \(\mathbf{V}^*\)), there should be at least \(k\) variables with near-zero loadings.
  3. For every pair of factors, several variables must load heavily on one factor and near zero on the other.
  4. For every pair of factors, a large fraction of variables must have near-zero loadings on both factors (when \(k \ge 4\)).
  5. Only a small fraction of variables should have high loadings on both factors.

PCA rotations mathematically maximize these criteria.

items.title: 1. Orthomax Family: Orthogonal Rotations (\(\gamma \in [0, 1]\))
items.text:
The Orthomax family defines a general criterion parameterized by \(\gamma\):

\[Q(\mathbf{\Lambda}) = \sum_{j=1}^k \left( \sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_{ij}^4 - \frac{\gamma}{p} \left( \sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_{ij}^2 \right)^2 \right)\]

where \(\mathbf{\Lambda} = \mathbf{V}^* = \mathbf{V} \mathbf{T}\) is the rotated loading matrix, and \(\mathbf{T}^T \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{I}\). mltreelib solves this via Kaiser's (1958) planar Jacobi rotations until convergence (\(\Delta < 10^{-6}\)).

items.title: Supported Orthomax Variants:
items.text:
• Varimax (\(\gamma = 1.0\)): The gold standard in applied statistics and R's default (stats::varimax). Maximizes the variance of squared loadings within each column. Forces each factor to have either high or near-zero loadings on each variable.
  • Quartimax (\(\gamma = 0.0\)): Simplifies rows (variables) rather than columns (factors). Maximizes the kurtosis of squared loadings across variables.
  • Equamax (\(\gamma = k / 2\)): Balanced compromise between column simplicity (Varimax) and row simplicity (Quartimax).
  • Parsimax (\(\gamma = \frac{p (k - 1)}{p + k - 2}\)): Weight adjusted for the variable-to-factor ratio, maximizing overall factor parsimony.
  • Biquartimax (\(\gamma = 0.5\)): Fixed equal weighting between row and column simplicity criteria.
from mltreelib import ComponentModel

# Fit PCA with Varimax rotation (pure Rust core)
pca_vari = ComponentModel(kind="pca", n_components=2, rotation="varimax")
pca_vari.fit(X)

# Transformed factor scores and rotated loadings
Z = pca_vari.transform(X)
loadings = pca_vari.components_
rot_matrix = pca_vari.rotation_matrix_

items.title: 2. Promax Rotation: Oblique Simple Structure (Hendrickson & White, 1964)
items.text:
Real-world latent dimensions often correlate (for example, verbal aptitude correlates with mathematical aptitude). Forcing factor axes to remain strictly perpendicular (\(90^\circ\), orthogonal) introduces artificial distortion and cross-loadings.

Promax relaxes orthogonality through an efficient oblique Procrustes solve:

  1. Compute the orthogonal Varimax rotated loadings \(\mathbf{\Lambda}_{\text{vari}}\).
  2. Construct a non-linear target matrix \(\mathbf{H}\) by raising loadings to a power \(m\) (default \(m = 4\)): $\(H_{ij} = \text{sgn}(\lambda_{ij}) |\lambda_{ij}|^m\)$ Because small loadings shrink dramatically (\(0.2^4 = 0.0016\)) while large loadings stay substantial (\(0.8^4 = 0.4096\)), \(\mathbf{H}\) acts as an idealized simple structure template.
  3. Solve the unconstrained Procrustes least-squares rotation towards \(\mathbf{H}\): $\(\mathbf{L} = (\mathbf{\Lambda}_{\text{vari}}^T \mathbf{\Lambda}_{\text{vari}})^{-1} \mathbf{\Lambda}_{\text{vari}}^T \mathbf{H}\)$
  4. Normalize the columns of \(\mathbf{L}\) to unit length, yielding the oblique transformation matrix \(\mathbf{T}\).
  5. Calculate the factor correlation matrix: $\(\mathbf{\Phi} = (\mathbf{T}^T \mathbf{T})^{-1}\)$
# Fit PCA with Promax oblique rotation (power m=4.0)
pca_promax = ComponentModel(kind="pca", n_components=2, rotation="promax", promax_power=4.0)
pca_promax.fit(X)

# Loadings and inter-factor correlation
loadings = pca_promax.components_
phi = pca_promax.factor_correlations_

items.title: 3. Cognitive Aptitude Battery Case Study
items.text: To illustrate how rotation transforms uninterpretable mathematical eigenvectors into distinct psychological concepts, consider an 8-variable cognitive aptitude battery (1,200 individuals): - Verbal Tests: ReadingComp, Vocabulary, GrammarUsage - Quantitative & Spatial Tests: GeometryProof, ArithmeticSpeed, Algebra, BlockDesign, ObjectAssembly

items.title: Interpretation of Results:
items.text:
1. Raw PCA: PC1 places roughly equal weight (\(0.33 - 0.38\)) on all 8 tests. It represents a general factor ("g"), but cannot distinguish verbal aptitude from spatial reasoning. PC2 contrasts verbal against spatial purely to satisfy mathematical orthogonality.
  2. Varimax: Rotates axes to maximize column variance. Factor 1 isolates Verbal Ability (0.84 to 0.89 on verbal tests, \(< 0.12\) on math/spatial). Factor 2 isolates Quantitative/Spatial Ability (0.75 to 0.88 on math/spatial, \(< 0.10\) on verbal). Sparsity improves from 0.0% to 50.0%.
  3. Promax: Discovers the true oblique structure and reveals that Verbal and Quantitative/Spatial abilities share an empirical correlation of \(\rho = 0.428\), consistent with psychometric literature.

items.title: 4. Decision Guide: Which Rotation When?
items.text: Method Type Property Best Use Case R Equivalent Raw PCA (None) Orthogonal Max variance along decreasing eigenvalues Dimension reduction, compression, pre-whitening stats::prcomp "varimax" Orthogonal Maximizes squared column loading variance General exploratory factor analysis, independent features stats::varimax "quartimax" Orthogonal Maximizes row kurtosis (simplifies variables) Eliminating cross-loadings for dominant variables psych::quartimax "equamax" Orthogonal Balanced column and row criteria (\(k/2\)) Moderately correlated batteries with moderate factor count psych::equamax "parsimax" Orthogonal Adjusted for variable-to-factor ratio High-dimensional data with small target factor count psych::parsimax "promax" Oblique Procrustes target power (\(m=4\)) rotation Natural domains where latent constructs correlate stats::promax

items.title: Configuration Parameters
items.text:
ComponentModel(
    kind="pca",               # "pca", "svd", "whitening", "fastica", "nmf"
    n_components=2,           # Subspace rank
    rotation="varimax",       # None, "varimax", "quartimax", "equamax", "parsimax", "biquartimax", "promax"
    promax_power=4.0,         # Promax target exponent (default 4.0)
    gamma=None,               # Custom Orthomax gamma parameter (if rotation="orthomax")
    max_iter=100,             # Max Jacobi planar rotation iterations
    tol=1e-6,                 # Jacobi convergence tolerance
    seed=42,                  # Random seed
)

items.title: Fitted Attributes
items.text:
• components_: Rotated factor loadings \(\mathbf{\Lambda}\) (shape \(p \times k\)).
  • rotation_matrix_: Transformation matrix \(\mathbf{T}\) (shape \(k \times k\)).
  • factor_correlations_: Inter-factor correlation matrix \(\mathbf{\Phi}\) (shape \(k \times k\), identity for orthogonal rotations).
  • explained_variance_ratio_: Realized variance share per factor.
  • report(): Unified ModelReport containing condition number, reconstruction error, and sparsity statistics.

items.title: Rules, Leaf Regression Summaries & k-NN Adjustments
items.text:
Three classical capabilities modernizing Quinlan's C5.0 and Cubist lineage in Rust: 1. R / statsmodels Leaf Regression Summaries: Exact goodness-of-fit tables, degrees of freedom, standard errors, \(t\)-values, \(p\)-values, \(R^2\), and \(F\)-statistics computed via closed-form covariance matrix \((X^T X)^{-1}\) inversion. 2. C5.0 Rule-Set Extraction: Transforming decision paths into standalone IF-THEN rules with interval simplification and Quinlan's pessimistic binomial error pruning (\(CF=0.25\)). 3. Cubist \(k\)-NN Sample Neighbor Adjustments: Adjusting terminal leaf predictions at inference time using distance-weighted training residuals.

Script: examples/rules_summary_knn_showcase.py.

items.title: 1. R summary(lm) & Python statsmodels Leaf Summaries
items.text:
Terminal leaves with multivariate linear models invert the local covariance matrix \((X^T X)^{-1}\) to provide statistical hypothesis testing for each coefficient:

from mltreelib import ModelTree

tree = ModelTree(leaf="linear", leaf_cols="all", max_depth=2, min_rows=30)
tree.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=["sqft", "beds", "age", "tax_rate"])

# Print statistical summary for Leaf 0
print(tree.leaf_summary(0))

items.title: 2. C5.0 Rule-Set Extraction with Pessimistic Pruning
items.text:
A decision tree forces disjoint, hierarchical branching. C5.0 extracts root-to-leaf paths into standalone IF-THEN rules, simplifies multi-condition bounds on the same feature, and greedily prunes preconditions using Quinlan's pessimistic error upper bound (\(U_{CF}(E, N)\)):

# Extract and prune rules with confidence factor cf=0.25
ruleset = tree.extract_rules(X_train, y_train, prune=True, cf=0.25)
print(ruleset)

# Predict directly using the extracted rule set
predictions = ruleset.predict(X_test)

Output:

items.title: 3. Cubist \(k\)-NN Sample Neighbor Adjustments
items.text:
Cubist's signature technique corrects model tree predictions by finding the \(k\) nearest training samples in normalized feature space and adjusting the prediction by their weighted residuals:

\[\hat{y}_{\text{adj}}(x) = \hat{y}(x) + \sum_{i=1}^k w_i (y_i - \hat{y}(x_i)), \quad w_i = \frac{1}{D(x, x_i) + \epsilon}\]

where distance is scaled Manhattan distance: $\(D(x, z) = \frac{1}{p} \sum_{j=1}^p \frac{|x_j - z_j|}{\sigma_j}\)$

# Standard ModelTree prediction
base_preds = tree.predict(X_test)

# Cubist k-NN adjusted prediction with 5 neighbors
adj_preds_5 = tree.predict(X_test, neighbors=5)

items.title: Benchmark Performance
items.text:
On datasets with non-linear or localized effects:

Inference Mode Test MSE Test MAE Improvement Standard ModelTree 1790.45 33.24 Baseline Cubist Adjustment (\(k=3\)) 1160.44 24.31 -35.2% error Cubist Adjustment (\(k=5\)) 1172.85 24.66 -34.5% error Cubist Adjustment (\(k=9\)) 1083.16 24.95 -39.5% error

items.title: 4. Native Leaf-KNN & DW-KNN Architecture
items.text:
Beyond post-hoc inference adjustments, mltreelib implements native Leaf-KNN models where each partitioned terminal node fits a localized, metric-weighted \(k\)-NN regressor or classifier directly inside the tree structure (leaf="knn" or leaf="dwknn").

Script: examples/knn_leaf_showcase.py.

items.title: Weighting Variants
items.text:
• uniform: Standard unweighted majority vote / mean over \(k\) nearest leaf samples.
  • distance: Inverse-distance weighting (Dudani, 1976), \(w_i = 1 / (d_i + \epsilon)\).
  • exponential: Radial / kernel exponential decay, \(w_i = \exp(-\gamma \cdot d_i^2)\).
  • dual: Distance \(\times\) local compactness weighting (Gou et al., 2012).
  • double / dwknn: Double-Weighted KNN (Pathak, Karthik, Madan, Kapila; arXiv:2512.08956). Precomputes neighbor validity \(v_i\) for each training instance within its neighborhood, dampening label noise and boundary anomalies before query voting: $\(w_i = \frac{1}{d_i + \epsilon} \times v_i\)$

items.title: Proximity & Distance Metrics
items.text: Supports 10 distance metrics via knn_metric: - Continuous geometry: euclidean, manhattan, chebyshev, minkowski(p) - Directional & correlation: cosine, correlation - Normalized & relative: canberra, braycurtis - Mixed / Missing data: gower (range-normalized across numerical and categorical features; handles missing None values without imputation) - Scale-invariant: mahalanobis (diagonal variance-scaled)

items.title: Usage Example
items.text:
from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Train a ModelTree with DW-KNN leaves and Gower distance
tree = ModelTree(
    leaf="dwknn",
    knn_k=7,
    knn_metric="gower",
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=15,
)
tree.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Predictions invoke localized DW-KNN within the targeted leaf node
y_pred = tree.predict(X_test)

You can also dynamically retrain tree leaves using LeafControl: 

from mltreelib import LeafControl

# Retrain existing tree partitions to DW-KNN without rebuilding the tree topology
tree.retrain(
    X_train,
    y_train,
    leaf_control=LeafControl(leaf="knn", knn_variant="double", knn_k=5, knn_metric="manhattan"),
)

items.title: Leaf Solver Benchmarks
items.text:
Benchmark the seven numerical, quasi-Newton, and continuous evolutionary leaf solvers implemented natively in mltreelib-core.

Run the benchmark from the repository root after building the release extension. It compares fit time and holdout error on Yeh Concrete.

uv run python examples/suites/solver_benchmarks.py

items.title: 1. Architectural Decoupling: Tree Partitions vs. Leaf Solvers
items.text:
In standard model trees, evaluating complex optimization problems at every candidate split threshold incurs prohibitive computational cost. ModelTree solves this through two-control decoupling:

  1. Tree Search: Fast scalar heuristics (Variance reduction, Chow test, Log-rank) discover spatial partition boundaries.
  2. Leaf Optimization: Once terminal regions are established, the compatible optimizer selected with LeafControl(solver=...) fits each local model.

All seven choices apply to Gaussian linear leaves. Supported non-Gaussian linear GLMs use IRLS or L-BFGS. L-BFGS requires zero L1 penalty and no monotone leaf constraints. See the parameter reference for details.

flowchart TD

    Fam -- "Yes: Smooth GLM / Tobit" --> S2["lbfgs (Quasi-Newton)\nArmijo line-search\nLatency: ~1.4 ms"]
    Fam -- "L1 Elastic Net Sparsity" --> S3["ccd (Coordinate Descent)\nExact zero-coefficients\nLatency: ~5.3 s"]
