items.title: 2. The Seven Solvers in mltreelib-core
items.text: Solver (leaf_solver) Mathematical Paradigm Gradient Required? Primary Strengths Recommended Setting "irls" Cholesky / Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares Yes Direct weighted least squares via faer, with iterative reweighting for supported GLMs. Gaussian ridge or a supported GLM. "lbfgs" Quasi-Newton L-BFGS with Armijo line search Yes Superlinear convergence on smooth likelihoods (Gaussian, Binomial, Poisson, Gamma, Tobit, Tweedie). Default for non-Gaussian GLM families and censored regression. "ccd" Cyclic Coordinate Descent Yes (Subgradient) Exact soft-thresholding producing true zero-coefficient sparsity under \(L_1\) penalty. High-dimensional feature selection and sparse leaves. "shade" Success-History Adaptive Differential Evolution No Continuous mutation scale (\(F\)) and crossover rate (\(CR\)) adaptation with external archive. Rugged, discontinuous, or multi-modal loss surfaces. "cmaes" Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy No Learns second-order dependency landscape without explicit Hessian inversion. Ill-conditioned parameter spaces with strong feature correlations. "ga" Real-Coded Genetic Algorithm No Simulated Binary Crossover (SBX) and polynomial mutation across diverse populations. Broad global exploration of complex parameter bounds. "nes" Separable Natural Evolution Strategies No Monte Carlo natural gradient updates along estimated search directions. Fast derivative-free parameter tuning in moderate dimensions.

items.title: 3. Empirical Benchmark on Real Data
items.text:
We benchmark all seven solvers on the Yeh (1998) Concrete Compressive Strength dataset (1,030 rows, 8 features; 80% train / 20% test).

Exact Cholesky (irls)Quasi-Newton (lbfgs)Adaptive Evolutionary (shade)Coordinate Descent (ccd) 
from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Analytical closed-form normal equations
tree = ModelTree(max_depth=0, leaf="linear", leaf_solver="irls", l2=0.01)
tree.fit(X_train, y_train)

from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Quasi-Newton L-BFGS with two-loop recursion
tree = ModelTree(max_depth=0, leaf="linear", leaf_solver="lbfgs", l2=0.01)
tree.fit(X_train, y_train)

from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Success-history based adaptive differential evolution (derivative-free)
tree = ModelTree(max_depth=0, leaf="linear", leaf_solver="shade", l2=0.01, seed=42)
tree.fit(X_train, y_train)

from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Cyclic coordinate descent with soft thresholding for L1 sparsity
tree = ModelTree(max_depth=0, leaf="linear", leaf_solver="ccd", l1=0.1, l2=0.01)
tree.fit(X_train, y_train)

items.title: Benchmark Results (Standalone Global Fit, max_depth=0)
items.text: Solver Family Latency (ms) Holdout Test RMSE (MPa) Test \(R^2\) Convergence Character irls Analytical Cholesky 1.17 ms 10.224 0.631 Exact analytical optimum in 1 step. lbfgs Quasi-Newton 1.37 ms 10.224 0.631 Converges in 14 iterations to machine precision. shade Continuous DE 33.24 ms 10.269 0.627 Reaches 99.6% of exact analytical optimum without gradients. ga Genetic Algorithm 57.77 ms 10.360 0.621 Robust global convergence across 100 generations. cmaes Evolutionary Covariance 13.23 ms 11.423 0.539 Fast adaptation; sensitive to raw unstandardized scale. nes Natural Gradient 13.13 ms 16.919 -0.011 Fast step updates; requires standardized inputs. ccd Cyclic Coordinate Descent 5,720 ms 10.224 0.631 Exact analytical match; coordinate sweeps on raw scale.

items.title: Key Observations:
items.text:
1. Analytical & Quasi-Newton Supremacy on Convex Surfaces: irls (1.17 ms) and lbfgs (1.37 ms) define the Pareto frontier for smooth convex losses. Both reach identical test RMSE (10.224 MPa) at microsecond speed.
  2. Derivative-Free Precision with SHADE: shade achieves 10.269 MPa (within 0.4% of the exact analytical minimum) in only 33 ms without evaluating a single gradient or Hessian. This makes it ideal for non-differentiable penalties, multi-objective fitness, or discontinuous loss landscapes.
  3. Tree-Decoupled Leaf Performance (max_depth=2, 4 Leaves): When deployed inside a partitioned model tree:
  4. irls: 4.34 ms total fit time \(\to\) 7.183 MPa RMSE (\(R^2 = 0.818\)).
  5. lbfgs: 2.80 ms total fit time \(\to\) 7.183 MPa RMSE (\(R^2 = 0.818\)).
  6. shade: 38.94 ms total fit time \(\to\) 7.606 MPa RMSE (\(R^2 = 0.796\)).

items.title: 5. Production Recommendations
items.text:
When to Select Each Solver

  • Use irls for standard linear ridge regression (leaf="linear") on Gaussian continuous targets. It uses Rust's faer dense Cholesky solver with minimal overhead.
  • Use lbfgs for GLMs (leaf_family="binomial", "poisson", "gamma", "tweedie", "tobit").
  • Use ccd when sparse leaves are mandatory (\(L_1 > 0\)) to eliminate irrelevant features inside leaf equations.
  • Use shade when fitting custom non-smooth losses, quantile objectives with heavy outliers, or discontinuous simulation simulators.

items.title: References
items.text:
• Nocedal, J., & Wright, S. J. (2006). Numerical Optimization. Springer.
  • Tanabe, R., & Fukunaga, A. S. (2014). "Improving the search performance of SHADE using linear population size reduction." IEEE CEC, 1658-1665.
  • Hansen, N. (2016). "The CMA evolution strategy: A tutorial." arXiv preprint arXiv:1604.00772.

items.title: Exotic Statistical, Metric & Fair Splitting Criteria (Spec 12 Suite)
items.text:
This guide demonstrates mltreelib's exotic statistical hypothesis testing, optimal transport, and metric splitting criteria.

To enable direct head-to-head comparison and verifiable properties, all criteria are evaluated on the exact same dataset for the exact same task (Credit Portfolio Risk Valuation). As new phases are developed, they are integrated directly into this unified benchmarking framework.

items.title: Shared Benchmark Task: Credit Portfolio Risk Valuation
items.text:
We generate a unified financial risk dataset (\(N = 300\)) where each observation represents an account with: - score: Continuous risk score \(\in [-2.0, 2.0]\) with an underlying structural break at \(0.0\). - zip_code: High-cardinality noise categorical feature (50 zip code levels with zero true signal). - tier_flag: Low-cardinality binary signal factor (\(\{0, 1\}\)). - gender: Protected demographic attribute (\(S \in \{0, 1\}\)). - gender_proxy: Unfair proxy feature with high correlation to gender. - fair_merit: Independent financial merit score.

Target modalities derived from the same underlying portfolio distribution: 1. Scalar Target (\(y \in \mathbb{R}\)): Portfolio loss / return. 2. Distribution Target (\(Y \in \mathbb{R}^{20}\)): 20-point quantile curve of future loss distributions. 3. Embedding Vector Target (\(Y \in \mathbb{R}^5\)): 5-dimensional risk embedding vector.

items.title: 1. Baseline: Standard CART (gain="sse")
items.text:
Standard recursive partitioning greedily maximizes variance reduction:

\[\text{Gain}_{\text{SSE}} = \text{SSE}(P) - [\text{SSE}(L) + \text{SSE}(R)]\]

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Standard CART with variance reduction
tree_cart = ModelTree(max_depth=1, min_rows=15, gain="sse", prune="none")
tree_cart.fit(X, y_scalar, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_cart.root_split())

items.title: Visual Execution Output
items.text:
Split: {'col': 'score', 'threshold': -0.012, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 1222.8814}
Note:  Greedily isolates variance; susceptible to Loh's cardinality trap on high-level factors.

items.title: 2. Phase 12A: Model-Based Recursive Partitioning (gain="mob")
items.text:
Best for: Detecting parameter instability or structural breaks along continuous covariates without refitting linear models across thousands of candidate cutpoints.

Fits the leaf linear regression once at the parent node, calculates individual score residuals \(\psi_i = \nabla_\theta \ell_i(\hat{\theta})\), and evaluates empirical fluctuation processes via the supLM test statistic:

\[\max_{t \in [\underline{t}, \bar{t}]} \frac{\|W(t)\|^2}{t(1-t)}\]

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# MOB parameter instability test
tree_mob = ModelTree(
    gain="mob",
    split_test="mob",
    max_depth=1,
    min_rows=15,
    leaf="linear",
    prune="none",
)
tree_mob.fit(X, y_scalar, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_mob.root_split())
print("Diagnostics:", tree_mob.split_diagnostics()[0])

items.title: Visual Execution Output
items.text:
Split:       {'col': 'score', 'threshold': -1.495, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 212.9632}
Diagnostics: {'p_value': 0.0000e+00, 'test_stat': 212.9632, 'test_name': 'mob'}
Note:        Evaluates structural break in linear slopes; avoids combinatorial refits.

items.title: 3. Phase 12B: Conditional Inference Trees (gain="ctree")
items.text:
Best for: Tabular datasets with mixed scale and high-cardinality factors (e.g. zip codes, store IDs, diagnoses) where CART suffers from selection bias.

CTree separates variable selection from splitpoint selection using permutation rank tests. Under \(H_0\), test statistics follow standardized \(\chi^2\) distributions regardless of cardinality:

\[c_j = z_j^2 \sim \chi^2_1 \quad (\text{numeric}), \qquad c_j = \frac{\text{SSB}}{V_Y} \sim \chi^2_{C - 1} \quad (\text{categorical})\]

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# CTree unbiased permutation rank test
tree_ctree = ModelTree(
    gain="ctree",
    split_test="ctree",
    max_depth=1,
    min_rows=15,
    prune="none",
)
tree_ctree.fit(X, y_scalar, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_ctree.root_split())

items.title: Visual Execution Output
items.text:
Split: {'col': 'score', 'threshold': 0.011, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 141.5636}
Note:  Strictly unbiased variable selection; rejects 50-level noise feature 'zip_code'.

items.title: 4. Phase 12C: Metric & Kernel Splitting (gain="energy_distance" & gain="mmd")
items.text:
Best for: Multi-output targets, embeddings, representations, and complex distribution targets \(Y \in \mathbb{R}^D\) where scalar variance is undefined.

  • Energy Distance (Székely & Rizzo): $\(\text{Gain}_{\mathcal{E}} = \frac{W_L W_R}{W_L + W_R} \left( 2 \mathbb{E}\|Y_L - Y_R\| - \mathbb{E}\|Y_L - Y_L'\| - \mathbb{E}\|Y_R - Y_R'\| \right)\)$
  • Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD / Gretton et al.): $\(\text{Gain}_{\text{MMD}} = \frac{W_L W_R}{W_L + W_R} \left( \mathbb{E}[k(Y_L, Y_L')] + \mathbb{E}[k(Y_R, Y_R')] - 2 \mathbb{E}[k(Y_L, Y_R)] \right)\)$

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# Energy Distance on 5D vector embeddings
tree_energy = ModelTree(gain="energy_distance", max_depth=1, min_rows=15, prune="none")
tree_energy.fit(X, y_vectors, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

# MMD with RBF Kernel
tree_mmd = ModelTree(gain="mmd", mmd_kernel="rbf", max_depth=1, min_rows=15, prune="none")
tree_mmd.fit(X, y_vectors, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Energy Split:", tree_energy.root_split())
print("MMD Split:   ", tree_mmd.root_split())

items.title: Visual Execution Output
items.text:
Energy Split: {'col': 'score', 'threshold': 0.011, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 903.1499}
MMD Split:    {'col': 'score', 'threshold': 0.011, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 58.1626}
Note:         Optimizes multi-target embeddings without parametric assumptions; detects covariance shifts.

items.title: 5. Phase 12D.1: Wasserstein-2 Optimal Transport (gain="wasserstein")
items.text:
Best for: Target outcomes that are continuous distributions, quantile functions, or probability histograms (e.g., regional daily temperature profiles, financial yield curves, pollution distributions).

Maximizes Fréchet barycenter dispersion reduction:

\[\text{Gain}_{\mathcal{W}_2}(L, R) = \frac{W_L W_R}{W_L + W_R} \frac{1}{D} \sum_{d=0}^{D-1} (\bar{Y}_L[d] - \bar{Y}_R[d])^2\]

Leaves output the predicted Fréchet barycenter distribution via predict_vector.

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# Wasserstein-2 Optimal Transport on 20-point quantile curves
tree_wass = ModelTree(gain="wasserstein", max_depth=1, min_rows=15, prune="none")
tree_wass.fit(X, y_quantiles, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_wass.root_split())

# Predict Fréchet barycenter distribution for new profiles
barycenter_preds = tree_wass.predict_vector([X[0]])
print(f"Leaf Fréchet Barycenter (len={len(barycenter_preds[0])}):", [round(v, 2) for v in barycenter_preds[0][:5]], "...")

items.title: Visual Execution Output
items.text:
Split: {'col': 'score', 'threshold': 0.011, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 1221.0445}
Leaf Fréchet Barycenter (len=20): [-3.42, -3.11, -2.89, -2.71, -2.55] ...
Note: Directly splits and outputs continuous distribution curves.

items.title: 6. Phase 12D.2: Fairness-Constrained Splitting (gain="fair")
items.text:
Best for: High-stakes automated decisions (credit approval, hiring, insurance underwriting) subject to demographic parity compliance bounds.

Penalizes split quality by Total Variation disparity across protected attribute \(S\):

\[\text{Gain}_{\text{fair}} = \text{BaseGain}(L, R) - \lambda \cdot \text{Impurity}_{\text{parent}} \cdot |P(S=1 \mid L) - P(S=1 \mid R)|\]

When \(\lambda > 0\), candidate splits that create disparate impact on protected groups are penalized, forcing the tree to select clean, fair merit features.

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# Demographic Parity Fair Tree (lambda = 1.0 on protected column 3 'gender')
tree_fair = ModelTree(
    gain="fair",
    fairness_penalty=1.0,
    protected_col=3,
    max_depth=1,
    min_rows=15,
    prune="none",
)
tree_fair.fit(X, y_scalar, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_fair.root_split())

items.title: Visual Execution Output
items.text:
Split: {'col': 'score', 'threshold': 0.107, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 1191.7879}
Note:  Penalizes proxy discrimination; narrows selection rate gap between protected groups.

items.title: 7. Phase 12E.1: Hellinger Distance Splitting (gain="hellinger")
items.text:
Best for: Highly imbalanced classification regimes (e.g. fraud detection, rare failure analysis) where rare positive events represent < 5% of data.

Evaluates the skew-invariant Hellinger affinity divergence between child partitions without suffering from the probability floor collapse of Gini or Shannon entropy:

\[H^2(L, R) = \sum_{k=1}^C \left(\sqrt{p_{L, k}} - \sqrt{p_{R, k}}\right)^2\]

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# Hellinger Distance on rare catastrophic risk event (~5% prevalence)
tree_hellinger = ModelTree(gain="hellinger", max_depth=1, min_rows=5, prune="none")
tree_hellinger.fit(X, y_rare, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_hellinger.root_split())

items.title: Visual Execution Output
items.text:
Split: {'col': 'score', 'threshold': -1.409, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 70.7933}
Note:  Skew-invariant divergence; cleanly isolates rare tail catastrophe without score collapse.

items.title: 8. Phase 12E.2: Maximally Selected Rank Statistics (gain="maxstat")
items.text:
Best for: Continuous targets with nonlinear monotone distortion or outliers where order preservation matters more than squared distance.

Maximizes the standardized two-sample linear rank statistic \(T^2(s) = S_L^2 / \text{Var}(S_L)\) with strict invariance under monotonic scalings:

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# MaxStat Rank Splitting
tree_maxstat = ModelTree(gain="maxstat", max_depth=1, min_rows=15, prune="none")
tree_maxstat.fit(X, y_scalar, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_maxstat.root_split())

items.title: Visual Execution Output
items.text:
Split: {'col': 'score', 'threshold': -0.012, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 149.2552}
Note:  Standardized two-sample linear rank divergence; invariant to monotone target scalings.

items.title: 9. Phase 12F: SPORF Oblique Splitting (sporf_d=2)
items.text:
Best for: Non-axis-aligned data regimes where true boundaries are diagonal hyperplanes (\(w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 \le c\)).

Sparse Projection Oblique Randomer Forest (Tomita et al. 2020) evaluates random linear combinations of \(d\) features with random signs:

\[Z = \sum_{k=1}^d \alpha_k X_{j_k}, \quad \alpha_k \in \{-1, +1\}\]

When an oblique projection beats the best univariate axis split, it is selected and exposed with full algebraic transparency in root_split()["oblique"]:

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# SPORF: 2-feature oblique projections (30 candidate hyperplanes)
tree_sporf = ModelTree(sporf_d=2, sporf_projections=30, max_depth=1, min_rows=15, seed=42, prune="none")
tree_sporf.fit(X, y_scalar, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

root = tree_sporf.root_split()
print("Split:", root)
print("Oblique Equation:", root["oblique"]["equation"])

items.title: Visual Execution Output
items.text:
Split: {'col': '-1.00*score -1.00*gender_proxy <= -1.2379', 'threshold': -1.238, 'gain': 3263.2392, 'oblique': {'cols': ['score', 'gender_proxy'], 'weights': [-1.0, -1.0], 'equation': '-1.00*score -1.00*gender_proxy <= -1.2379'}}
Oblique Equation: -1.00*score -1.00*gender_proxy <= -1.2379
Note:  Evaluates random linear combinations of 2 features; eliminates diagonal staircasing.

items.title: 10. Phase 12G: Equalized Odds Fairness Penalty (fairness_metric="equalized_odds")
items.text:
Best for: Regulatory and credit compliance where decision error rates (True Positive Rate and False Positive Rate) must not disproportionately penalize a protected demographic subgroup:

\[\text{Disparity}_{\text{EO}} = \frac{1}{2} \left( |\text{TPR}_1 - \text{TPR}_0| + |\text{FPR}_1 - \text{FPR}_0| \right)\] \[\text{Gain}_{\text{Fair}} = \max\left(0, \, \text{Gain}_{\text{Raw}} - \lambda \cdot \text{SSE}_{\text{parent}} \cdot \text{Disparity}_{\text{EO}}\right)\]

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# Equalized Odds constrained splitting (protected attribute = col 3 'gender')
tree_eo = ModelTree(
    fairness_penalty=1.0,
    fairness_metric="equalized_odds",
    protected_col=3,
    max_depth=1,
    min_rows=15,
    prune="none",
)
tree_eo.fit(X, y_fair, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_eo.root_split())

items.title: Visual Execution Output
items.text:
Split: {'col': 'fair_merit', 'threshold': 50.005, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 1816.0941}
Note:  Penalizes TPR and FPR disparate error rates; suppresses unfair proxy and selects fair_merit (EO gap=0.000).

items.title: 11. Phase 12H: Extremely Randomized Splits / ExtraTrees (extratrees=True)
items.text:
Best for: Fast \(O(1)\) split evaluation during tree bagging and ensemble training, avoiding the \(O(N \log N)\) sorting and exhaustive cutpoint scan per continuous feature:

\[s \sim \text{Uniform}(\min X_j, \max X_j)\]

items.title: Code Run

tree_et = ModelTree(
    extratrees=True,
    seed=42,
    max_depth=1,
    min_rows=15,
    prune="none",
)
tree_et.fit(X, y_scalar, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_et.root_split())

Split: {'col': 'tier_flag', 'threshold': 0.147, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 2410.5738}
Note:  Evaluates exactly 1 random cut per continuous feature in O(1) time without sorting.

items.title: 12. Phase 12I: EBM FAST Interaction Screening (ebm_fast=True)
items.text:
Best for: Discovering non-linear pairwise interactions across all \(P(P-1)/2\) feature pairs without combinatorial model fitting:

\[\text{InteractionGain}(j, k) = \frac{\sum_{a,b \in \{0, 1\}} N_{ab} (\bar{y}_{ab} - \hat{y}_{\text{add}})^2}{\text{SSE}_{\text{parent}}}\]

items.title: Code Run

from mltreelib import fast_interaction_screen

# Standalone FAST screening over all candidate pairs
screened = fast_interaction_screen(X, y_inter, col_names=col_names, top_k=3, min_samples=15)
print("Top Screened Pairs:", [(s['col1_name'], s['col2_name'], s['score']) for s in screened])

# Tree fitted with FAST interaction constraint
tree_fast = ModelTree(ebm_fast=True, max_depth=2, min_rows=15, prune="none")
tree_fast.fit(X, y_inter, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

items.title: Explainable Decision Stumps & Leaf Retraining
items.text:
A single decision stump (max_depth=1) splits feature space into two transparent regimes, then fits independent models inside each leaf. This pattern replicates the high-explainability output of Quinlan's Cubist and C5.0 — models senior executives, actuaries, and clinical leaders understand in seconds.

With tree.retrain(...), leaf models can be refitted across families (linear, huber, quantile, binomial, poisson) on frozen partitions in microseconds, completely decoupling split finding from leaf estimation.

Script: examples/practical_stump_showcase.py.

items.title: Real-World Case: Healthcare Insurance Expenses
items.text:
Using the TabArena healthcare_insurance_expenses benchmark (1,338 patients with age, bmi, children, smoker predicting medical charges):

from mltreelib import ModelTree, LeafControl
from mltreelib.datasets import load_dataset

d = load_dataset("healthcare_insurance_expenses")
cols = ["age", "bmi", "children", "smoker"]
x = [[d["columns"][c][i] for c in cols] for i in range(d["n_rows"])]
y = d["columns"]["charges"]

stump = ModelTree(max_depth=1, min_rows=20, leaf="linear", l2=1e-3, leaf_digest=True)
stump.fit(x, y, dtypes=["numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "categorical"])

items.title: Practical Insights Delivered Instantly
items.text:
1. Identical Aging Velocity:
  2. Non-smokers: +$265.29 / year
  3. Smokers: +$264.93 / year

  4. Both populations accumulate baseline medical risk at identical rates (~$265 annually).

  5. Compounding Metabolic Risk:

  6. Non-smokers: +$5.28 / BMI unit (essentially flat).
  7. Smokers: +$1,438.73 / BMI unit (270× steeper!).

  8. In smokers, high BMI triggers catastrophic cardiovascular and pulmonary claims. A flat linear model would average these slopes (~$330/BMI) and miss the entire interaction.

  9. Base Claim Shift:

  10. Non-smoker average: $8,434
  11. Smoker average: $32,050 (nearly 4× higher).

items.title: Frozen-Topology Retraining (tree.retrain)
items.text:
Re-partitioning 1,338 rows across feature candidates takes ~38 ms. But once split boundaries are set, leaf models can be swapped and refitted in < 1 ms:

# 1. Robust Huber M-estimator (outlier bill resistance)
stump.retrain(x, y, leaf="huber")

# 2. Actuarial Quantile Bands (10th, 50th, 90th percentile reserves)
stump.retrain(x, y, leaf="linear", l2=1e-3, leaf_digest=True)
q10 = stump.quantile(test_cases, 0.10)
q50 = stump.quantile(test_cases, 0.50)
q90 = stump.quantile(test_cases, 0.90)

# 3. Regularized Ridge Leaves (shrinkage under small sample partitions)
stump.retrain(x, y, leaf="linear", l2=10.0)

# 4. Piecewise Constant CART baseline
stump.retrain(x, y, control=LeafControl(leaf="mean"))

items.title: Architectural Extensibility
items.text: By decoupling routing from leaf estimation: - The tree handles global discrete partitioning (discovering regime boundaries). - The leaves handle local estimation (OLS, GLM, Huber, Quantiles, and future kNN, SVM, or Neural leaves). - Leaf models can be updated in production or fine-tuned on recent data without altering approved business rules.

items.title: Suite 9: Survival & Competing Risks Trees
items.text:
This suite implements non-parametric Survival Trees and Competing Risks Trees in pure Rust (mltreelib-core) with thin Python bindings (mltreelib). It partitions heterogeneous survival cohorts into interpretable prognostic subgroups while rigorously accounting for right-censoring and multi-cause competing risks.

Companion executable script: - examples/suites/survival_and_competing_risks.py (uv run python examples/suites/survival_and_competing_risks.py)

items.title: 1. Survival Tree Structure & Decision Topology
items.text:
In survival analysis, observations are right-censored: study termination or patient dropout masks the true event time \(T_i^*\). The observed pair is \((T_i, E_i)\) where \(T_i = \min(T_i^*, C_i)\) and \(E_i = I(T_i^* \le C_i)\).

In competing risks, an observation can experience one of \(J\) distinct, mutually exclusive event types (\(E_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, J\}\), where \(E_i = 0\) denotes right-censoring).

items.title: High-Level Workflow Architecture
items.text:
flowchart TD
    Data["Cohort Ingestion: (X, (T, E))"] --> TargetType{"Target Setting"}

    TargetType -- "Single Event (E in {0, 1})" --> SingleEvent["Right-Censored Survival"]
    SingleEvent --> SplitCrit1["Split Criterion:\nlogrank | tarone_ware | peto | martingale | survival_brier | rmst"]
    SplitCrit1 --> LeafEst1["Leaf Estimators:\nKaplan-Meier S(t)\nNelson-Aalen Lambda(t)\nAFT / Cure / Spline"]

    TargetType -- "Competing Risks (E in {0, 1, ..., J})" --> CompRisks["Multi-Cause Competing Risks"]
    CompRisks --> SplitCrit2["Split Criterion:\ngray (Subdistribution Log-Rank)\ntarget_cause = c"]
    CompRisks --> LeafEst2["Leaf Estimators:\nAalen-Johansen CIF F_c(t)\nCause-Specific Hazard Lambda_c(t)"]

    LeafEst1 --> SimplexCheck["Verify Monotonicity:\nS(t) non-increasing"]
    LeafEst2 --> SimplexCheck2["Verify Simplex Invariant:\nsum_c F_c(t) + S(t) == 1.0"]

items.title: Native ModelTree Architecture & Graphviz Topology
items.text:
Rather than an abstract diagram, mltreelib exports the exact mathematical graph structure directly via ModelTree.to_dot(). You can render this directly with Graphviz (dot -Tsvg):

import subprocess
from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Export and render native ModelTree graphviz DOT representation
dot_graph = tree.to_dot()
subprocess.run(["dot", "-Tsvg", "-o", "docs/assets/suite9_survival_tree_model.svg"], input=dot_graph, text=True)

The resulting native decision topology shows split predicates, node sample counts \(N\), node deviances, and leaf response constants:

items.title: Individual Leaf Survival & Competing Risks Profiles
items.text: Behind each terminal node in the tree lives a complete multi-state survival distribution. The panel below illustrates the distinct Kaplan-Meier survival curves \(S(t)\) and Aalen-Johansen Cumulative Incidence Functions \(F_1(t)\) (Relapse) and \(F_2(t)\) (Competing Mortality) across all 5 leaves:

items.title: Why the Partitions Formed:
items.text:
1. Leaf 1 (Rule 4: biomarker <= -0.155 & age <= 5.751) — Favorable Long-Term (\(N=111\), Median = 5.68 yrs): Younger patients with low biomarker levels have minimal hazard. Primary relapse incidence \(F_1(t)\) plateaus below 10%, while competing mortality remains negligible, sustaining high long-term survival.
  2. Leaf 2 (Rule 1: biomarker <= -0.155 & age > 5.751) — Moderate-Low Risk (\(N=161\), Median = 1.99 yrs): Older patients with low biomarker levels experience moderate relapse (32.3%), but their competing risk mortality \(F_2(t)\) accumulates steadily due to age-related hazards, pulling overall survival down to a 1.99-year median.
  3. Leaf 3 (Rule 3: -0.155 < biomarker <= 1.471 & age <= 6.168) — Intermediate Risk (\(N=135\), Median = 2.97 yrs): Intermediate biomarker levels in younger cohorts produce a moderate, delayed relapse accumulation (24.4%), yielding a stable 2.97-year median survival.
  4. Leaf 4 (Rule 2: -0.155 < biomarker <= 1.471 & age > 6.168) — Elevated Risk (\(N=152\), Median = 1.62 yrs): Older patients with intermediate biomarker levels face a dual-hazard scenario: accelerated relapse incidence (48.0%) combined with substantial competing mortality (\(F_2(t) \approx 45\%\)).
  5. Leaf 5 (Rule 5: biomarker > 1.471) — Extreme Early Relapse (\(N=41\), Median = 0.76 yrs): High biomarker levels trigger a catastrophic relapse spike (\(F_1(t) = 85.4\%\) within the first 12 months). The tree immediately isolates this high-risk cluster at the root split, dropping median survival to 0.76 years.

items.title: 2. The 9 Survival Split Criteria
items.text:
Configure the split criterion using the gain parameter in ModelTree:

tree = ModelTree(max_depth=3, min_rows=20, gain="pseudo_value")
Criterion (gain=) Mathematical Formula Weighting Function \(w(t_j)\) Best Used For "logrank" Two-sample Mantel-Haenszel score: \(Z = \frac{\sum_j (d_{1j} - e_{1j})}{\sqrt{\sum_j V_j}}\) \(w(t_j) = 1\) Proportional hazards settings where treatment or risk effect is uniform over time. "tarone_ware" Weighted log-rank score test \(w(t_j) = \sqrt{n_j}\) (square root of risk set size) Moderate non-proportional hazards; balances sensitivity between early and late event horizons. "peto" Peto-Prentice weighted score test \(w(t_j) = \tilde{S}(t_j-)\) (Kaplan-Meier survival at previous time) High-risk early divergence; prioritizes splits that separate immediate mortality or early customer drop-off. "martingale" \(O(N)\) streaming scan on Cox null martingale residuals: \(M_i = E_i - \hat{\Lambda}_0(T_i)\) Residual difference: \(\Delta \text{SSE} = \frac{S_L^2}{N_L} + \frac{S_R^2}{N_R} - \frac{S^2}{N}\) Large-scale datasets where \(O(N \log N)\) sorting per candidate split is too slow. Splits at the speed of regression trees. "pseudo_value" Jackknife pseudo-observations \(\theta_i = N \hat{S}(t) - (N-1)\hat{S}_{-i}(t)\) Standard regression variance reduction Fast \(O(N)\) streaming splits on survival probability or restricted mean survival time. "rmst" Restricted Mean Survival Time area divergence: \(\Delta \text{RMST} = \int_0^\tau S_L(t) dt - \int_0^\tau S_R(t) dt\) Integrated area difference: \(\frac{N_L N_R}{N_L + N_R} (\text{RMST}_L - \text{RMST}_R)^2\) Crossing hazards settings where log-rank statistics lose statistical power. "aft_deviance" Parametric AFT log-likelihood deviance reduction Likelihood ratio reduction \(\Delta D\) Parametric survival model trees targeting smooth log-linear survival functions. "gray" Gray's (1988) subdistribution score test for cause \(c\) Subdistribution weight: \(w(t_j) = \frac{n_j - d_j}{n_j} \cdot \dots\) Competing risks (\(E_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, J\}\)). Evaluates cumulative incidence separation for target_cause. "survival_brier" Minimizes IPCW integrated Brier loss at quartile time horizons Integrated squared residual: \(\sum_k \text{BS}(t_k)\) Calibration-first trees where calibrated probability estimates \(S(t)\) matter more than rank-ordering.

items.title: 3. Leaf Estimators & Invariants
items.text:
Inside each leaf, mltreelib-core computes non-parametric step functions:

  1. Kaplan-Meier Survival Estimator: $\(\hat{S}(t) = \prod_{t_j \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_j}{n_j}\right)\)$

  2. Nelson-Aalen Cumulative Hazard: $\(\hat{\Lambda}(t) = \sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{n_j}\)$

  3. Aalen-Johansen Cumulative Incidence Function (CIF): For cause \(c \in \{1, \dots, J\}\): $\(\hat{F}_c(t) = \sum_{t_j \le t} \hat{S}(t_{j-1}) \frac{d_{cj}}{n_j}\)$ where \(d_{cj}\) is the number of cause-\(c\) events at time \(t_j\).

  4. The Simplex Invariant: At any time \(t \ge 0\), the sum of all cause-specific cumulative incidence probabilities plus overall survival equals exactly 1: $\(\sum_{c=1}^J \hat{F}_c(t) + \hat{S}(t) \equiv 1.0\)$ The engine enforces and tests this invariant down to machine precision (\(1.33 \times 10^{-15}\)).

items.title: Frontier Leaf Models
items.text:
Standard survival tree libraries fit flat step functions in leaves. mltreelib supports parametric and semi-parametric model leaves:

  • Parametric AFT Leaves (leaf_family="aft"): Fits smooth continuous accelerated failure time distributions inside leaves: $\(\ln T = \mu(X) + \sigma \epsilon\)$ Knobs: aft_dist="weibull" | "lognormal" | "loglogistic". When paired with leaf="linear", the survival curve \(S(t \mid x)\) varies smoothly with continuous covariates within the leaf partition.
  • Mixture Cure Rate Leaves (leaf_family="cure"): Models populations where a fraction \(\pi\) are cured and will never experience the event: $\(S_{\text{pop}}(t) = \pi + (1 - \pi) S_{\text{uncured}}(t)\)$ Knob: cure_fraction=0.2. As \(t \to \infty\), the survival curve plateaus at \(\pi > 0\).
  • Restricted Cubic Splines Leaves (leaf_family="spline"): Fits Royston-Parmar flexible spline log cumulative hazard functions: $\(\ln \Lambda(t \mid x) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 \ln t + \sum_{k=1}^K \gamma_{k+1} v_k(\ln t) + \beta^T x\)$ Knob: spline_knots=3. Eliminates discrete stepping while avoiding rigid parametric distribution assumptions.

items.title: 4. Fitting & Predictions API
items.text:
Fit trees using the standard 2-tuple target (durations, events):

from mltreelib import ModelTree

# 1. Competing risks tree isolating Cause 1 (Relapse) with Gray's test
tree = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=25,
    gain="gray",
    target_cause=1,
)
tree.fit(X_train, (dur_train, ev_train))

# 2. Frontier parametric AFT tree with smooth Weibull linear leaves
tree_aft = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=15,
    gain="rmst",          # Area divergence splitting under non-proportional hazards
    leaf_family="aft",    # Parametric AFT distribution
    aft_dist="weibull",   # "weibull", "lognormal", or "loglogistic"
    leaf="linear",        # Linear covariate response inside each leaf
)
tree_aft.fit(X_train, (dur_train, ev_train))

items.title: 5. Model Evaluation with Modern Calibration Metrics
items.text:
Evaluate models with classical IPCW concordance and frontier calibration metrics:

from mltreelib import (
    Metrics,
    d_calibration,
    integrated_calibration_index,
    one_calibration,
    competing_risks_calibration,
)

# 1. Classical Discrimination & Calibration
metrics = Metrics()
cif_all_c1 = tree.predict(X_test, kind="cif", times=time_horizons, cause=1)
cif_all_c2 = tree.predict(X_test, kind="cif", times=time_horizons, cause=2)
risk_all_c1 = tree.predict(X_test, kind="risk", cause=1)
risk_all_c2 = tree.predict(X_test, kind="risk", cause=2)

report = metrics.competing_risks(
    durations=dur_test,
    events=ev_test,
    cif_curves={1: cif_all_c1, 2: cif_all_c2},
    risk_scores={1: risk_all_c1, 2: risk_all_c2},
    times=time_horizons,
)

print(f"Cause 1 Harrell C:  {report['cause_c_indices'][1]:.4f}")
print(f"Cause 1 Uno IPCW C: {report['cause_uno_c_indices'][1]:.4f}")
print(f"Cause 1 IBS:        {report['cause_ibs'][1]:.4f}")
print("Brier at horizons: ", {k: round(v, 4) for k, v in report['brier_at_horizons'][1].items()})

# 2. D-Calibration (Haider et al. 2020)
# Evaluates whether event occurrences are uniformly distributed across probability bins
surv_test_h = [row[1] for row in tree.predict(X_test, kind="survival", times=time_horizons)] # at t=2.0 yr
d_rep = d_calibration(dur_test, ev_test, surv_test_h, n_bins=10)
print(f"D-Calibration: Chi2 = {d_rep['chi2_stat']:.3f}, p-value = {d_rep['p_value']:.4f}, Calibrated = {d_rep['is_calibrated']}")

# 3. Integrated Calibration Index (ICI) (Austin et al. 2020)
# IPCW-weighted mean absolute calibration error at horizon t_0
ici_rep = integrated_calibration_index(dur_test, ev_test, surv_test_h, horizon=2.0)
print(f"ICI: {ici_rep['ici']:.4f}, E50: {ici_rep['e50']:.4f}, E90: {ici_rep['e90']:.4f}, Emax: {ici_rep['emax']:.4f}")

# 4. 1-Calibration Slope & Intercept
one_rep = one_calibration(dur_test, ev_test, surv_test_h, horizon=2.0)
print(f"1-Calibration: Intercept = {one_rep['intercept']:.3f}, Slope = {one_rep['slope']:.3f}")

# 5. Competing Risks Multi-Cause Calibration (Alberge et al. 2026)
cr_rep = competing_risks_calibration(
    dur_test,
    ev_test,
    {1: [r[1] for r in cif_all_c1], 2: [r[1] for r in cif_all_c2]},
    horizon=2.0,
)
print(f"Competing Risks: Cause 1 ICI = {cr_rep['cause_ici'][1]:.4f}, Cause 2 ICI = {cr_rep['cause_ici'][2]:.4f}")

items.title: 7. Assumptions & Limitations
items.text:
1. Conditionally Independent Censoring: \(T_i^* \perp C_i \mid X_i\). If unobserved health deterioration causes patients to drop out, Kaplan-Meier leaf estimates will overestimate survival.
  2. Competing Risks vs. Censoring: Do not treat competing events (e.g., organ transplant, accidental death) as right-censoring. Doing so overestimates the cumulative incidence of the primary event by 15–30%. Use gain="gray" and kind="cif".
  3. Cumulative Hazard vs. Instantaneous Hazard Rate: predict(kind="hazard") computes \(\hat{\Lambda}(t) = \int_0^t \lambda(u) du\) (dimensionless accumulated expected event count). It does not compute instantaneous hazard rate \(\lambda(t) = \frac{d\Lambda(t)}{dt}\).
  4. Tail Extrapolation: Beyond \(\max(T_i)\) in a leaf, non-parametric step curves remain flat at their last estimated value. For continuous tail extrapolation, use parametric AFT leaves (leaf_family="aft").

items.title: 8. Research Foundations & Benchmark Reproductions
items.text:
The implementation reproduces eleven key findings from classical (1988–2014) and frontier (2020–2026) survival analysis literature:

Reference & Paper Link Topic & Method Benchmark Dataset Original Paper Finding mltreelib Reproduction Result LeBlanc & Crowley (1992), (1993) Martingale residual splitting (\(O(N)\) streaming scan) Veterans' Lung Cancer (\(N=137\), 128 deaths) Primary prognostic split occurs on Karnofsky score \(\le 40\), yielding 3.1x mortality hazard jump. ModelTree(gain="martingale", max_depth=2) isolates primary cut at karno <= 40. Yields median survival of 30 days vs 111 days. Gray (1988) K-sample subdistribution log-rank test for competing risks Mayo Clinic PBC (\(N=312\): 125 deaths, 29 liver transplants, 158 censored) Naive Kaplan-Meier overestimates 10-year death probability at 52.4% because it treats transplants as independent censoring. gain="gray", target_cause=1 correctly estimates 10-year death CIF at 38.6%, eliminating the 13.8% risk overestimation. Fine & Gray (1999) Subdistribution hazards model Mayo Clinic PBC cohort Serum bilirubin and albumin are dominant predictors of primary liver failure mortality. Tree rules isolate bili > 3.2 and albumin <= 3.1 with high subdistribution hazard and rapid CIF accumulation. Ishwaran et al. (2014) Aalen-Johansen leaf CIF estimator & simplex property Multi-cause oncology simulation (\(N=800\)) Competing risk probabilities and overall survival must satisfy the simplex identity \(\sum_{c=1}^J F_c(t) + S(t) = 1.0\). Verified across 1,000 grid points: maximum absolute error is \(1.33 \times 10^{-15}\) (machine epsilon). Uno et al. (2011) IPCW Concordance Index (\(C^{\text{Uno}}\)) Mayo Clinic FLCHAIN (\(N=7,874\), 2,172 deaths) Harrell's C is sensitive to study follow-up duration; Uno's IPCW C removes censoring bias via inverse Kaplan-Meier weights. Native Metrics().survival(...) computes Harrell's C (0.784) and Uno's IPCW C (0.781) on raw FLCHAIN data with 1,350 missing creatinine values. Graf et al. (1999) Integrated Brier Score (IBS) with IPCW censoring weights Simulation benchmark (\(N=800\)) IBS evaluates probability calibration across the full timeline \([0, t_{\max}]\) under arbitrary censoring. Benchmark across criteria yields IBS between 0.2136 (tarone_ware) and 0.2297 (peto). Liu & Li (2020), (2021) RMST area divergence splitting Crossing hazards simulation Standard log-rank test loses statistical power when hazards cross. RMST preserves power via integrated area differences. gain="rmst" maintains high split discrimination under crossing hazards where log-rank fails. Schenk et al. (2024) Jackknife pseudo-values for survival trees SurvSet benchmarks Pseudo-values transform right-censored outcomes into continuous pseudo-observations for \(O(N)\) split scanning. gain="pseudo_value" matches full martingale rank ordering with \(O(N)\) linear scans. Haider et al. (2020) D-Calibration for distribution uniformity SurvSet benchmark suite Well-calibrated survival estimators distribute event probabilities uniformly across probability bins: \(\chi^2\) test \(p > 0.05\). d_calibration(durations, events, surv, n_bins=10) outputs \(\chi^2\) statistic and uniformity hypothesis test. Austin et al. (2020) Integrated Calibration Index (ICI) & 1-Calibration GBSG2 Breast Cancer cohort ICI computes IPCW-weighted mean absolute error between predicted survival and observed status at horizon \(t_0\). integrated_calibration_index(durations, events, surv, horizon) outputs ICI, E50, E90, and Emax. Alberge et al. (2026) Multi-cause calibration divergence Mayo Clinic PBC cohort Competing risks calibration must evaluate cause-specific calibration divergences and Brier scores simultaneously. competing_risks_calibration(durations, events, cif_dict, horizon) evaluates per-cause ICI and Brier divergences.

items.title: Time Series Feature Engineering & Additive Forecasting
items.text:
This guide details mltreelib's pure Rust time-feature engine—including entity-grouped calendar day lags, trailing rolling statistics, calendar cycles, and additive trend decomposition—evaluating out-of-time demand forecasting where piecewise linear model trees outperform standard CART step functions.

Script: examples/suites/timeseries_additive_forecasting.py (uv run python examples/suites/timeseries_additive_forecasting.py).

items.title: 1. Domain Context & Out-of-Time Forecasting Pitfalls
items.text:
In enterprise demand planning and energy load forecasting, models face continuous secular trends, intra-week seasonal cycles, and holiday shocks.

Standard flat decision trees fail out-of-sample on trending series: 1. The Step-Function Extrapolation Barrier: A standard decision tree predicts leaf sample means. On future time horizons where target values exceed historical training ranges, step-function trees flatten out completely, predicting the historical maximum rather than extrapolating growth. 2. Calendar Irregularity & Leakage: Simple integer row shifting (df.shift(7)) fails when weekends or maintenance dates are omitted. Real forecasting requires shifting by elapsed calendar days rather than array index offsets. 3. Imputation Overhead: Shifting causes initial observations to be missing (None). Forcing median imputation distorts autoregressive lag relationships.

mltreelib solves this through a pure Rust feature engine coupled with linear-leaf model trees: - calendar_features: Extracts ISO calendar parts (weekday, weekend, month, day_of_year) in zero-allocation Rust. - lag_by_days: Computes entity-grouped calendar day shifts (lag_by_days(keys, dates, values, days=7)), routing unobserved initial history through ModelTree's native missing handler. - windowed_transform: Computes trailing-window rolling statistics (mean, std, min, max, median) over exact calendar day windows. - decomposed_transform: Performs additive seasonal and trend decomposition (statsmodels convention) in pure Rust. - Piecewise Linear Model Trees: Leaves fit regularized linear ridge regressions on autoregressive lags, allowing the tree to extrapolate continuous trends out-of-time.

items.title: 2. Benchmark Study: Multi-Store Retail Demand Panel
items.text:
We evaluate an out-of-time panel of two regional retail locations (store_nyc, store_lon) over 120 days. The model trains on the first 90 days and forecasts the held-out final 30 days.

from datetime import date, timedelta
from mltreelib import (
    Metrics,
    ModelTree,
    calendar_features,
    decomposed_transform,
    lag_by_days,
    windowed_transform,
)

# 1. Feature Engineering in pure Rust
cal = calendar_features(dates, hemisphere="north")
lag1 = lag_by_days(keys, dates, sales, 1)
lag7 = lag_by_days(keys, dates, sales, 7)
win7_mean = windowed_transform(keys, dates, sales, window_days=7, kind="mean")
decomp = decomposed_transform(keys, dates, sales, season_granularity="weekday", trend_window=7)

# Assemble feature matrix
features = ["weekday", "weekend", "lag1", "lag7", "win7_mean"]
X = [[cal["weekday"][i], cal["weekend"][i], lag1[i], lag7[i], win7_mean[i]] for i in range(len(dates))]
y = sales

# Out-of-time split: first 90 days train (180 rows), last 30 days test (60 rows)
split_idx = 180
X_train, y_train = X[:split_idx], y[:split_idx]
X_test, y_test = X[split_idx:], y[split_idx:]

# 2. Fit standard CART decision tree (constant mean leaves)
cart = ModelTree(leaf="mean", max_depth=3, min_rows=15)
cart.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=features)
pred_cart = cart.predict(X_test)

# 3. Fit mltreelib ModelTree (regularized linear leaves)
model_tree = ModelTree(leaf="linear", max_depth=3, min_rows=15, l2=0.05)
model_tree.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=features)
pred_mt = model_tree.predict(X_test)

# 4. Measure holdout performance
metrics = Metrics()
m_cart = metrics.regression(y_test, pred_cart)
m_mt = metrics.regression(y_test, pred_mt)

print(f"CART (Mean)       : Test RMSE = {m_cart['rmse']:.2f}, R2 = {m_cart['r2']:.3f}, MAE = {m_cart['mae']:.2f}")
print(f"ModelTree (Linear): Test RMSE = {m_mt['rmse']:.2f}, R2 = {m_mt['r2']:.3f}, MAE = {m_mt['mae']:.2f}")

items.text:
1. Massive Out-of-Time Accuracy Gain: On the 30-day forecast horizon, ModelTree(leaf="linear") achieves a 66.9% error reduction over standard CART (RMSE drops from 12.87 to 4.26; \(R^2\) rises to 0.977).
  2. Lag Tracking & Autoregressive Continuity (Panel 4): In Panel 4, CART flattens out into horizontal steps that severely underestimate late-period demand growth. ModelTree uses linear leaf coefficients to continuously adjust predictions from lag1 and win7_mean.
  3. Pure Rust Additive Decomposition (Panel 3): decomposed_transform separates the weekly intra-day cycle from secular growth, producing symmetric Gaussian residuals centered at 0 without external dependencies.

items.title: Tobit & Censored Regression Trees
items.text:
Tobit models a latent response censored at a known boundary. A natural lower bound or a real zero alone does not establish censoring. Latent-normal and censoring assumptions must fit the application.

ModelTree provides native Tobit regression leaves (leaf_family="tobit") fitted via iterative reweighted least squares (IRLS / EM) inside tree partitions.

items.title: 1. The Tobit Model Formulation
items.text:
The standard formulation assumes a latent continuous variable \(y^*_i\): $\(y^*_i = x_i' \beta + \epsilon_i, \quad \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\)$

Observed outcomes are left-censored at threshold \(c\) (default \(c = 0\)): $\(y_i = \begin{cases} y^*_i & \text{if } y^*_i > c \\ c & \text{if } y^*_i \le c \end{cases}\)$

The log-likelihood consists of discrete probability mass at \(c\) and continuous Gaussian density for uncensored observations: $\(\ln L = \sum_{y_i = c} \ln \left[ 1 - \Phi\left(\frac{x_i' \beta - c}{\sigma}\right) \right] + \sum_{y_i > c} \left[ -\frac{1}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{(y_i - x_i' \beta)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right]\)$

items.title: 2. ModelTree Tobit Usage
items.text:
from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Fit a piece-wise linear Tobit tree
tree = ModelTree(
    max_depth=2,
    min_rows=30,
    leaf="linear",
    leaf_family="tobit",
    l2=1e-3,
    tobit_threshold=0.0,
)
tree.fit(X, y)

# Predict latent expected response
predictions = tree.predict(X_test)

items.text: On the classic Mroz female labor supply dataset (datasets/external/mroz.csv): - 43.2% of women in the survey reported 0 hours worked. - OLS attenuates the disincentive effect of infant children (kidslt6), giving \(-403.61\) hours. - The fitted Tobit tree leaf coefficient is of \(-436.19\) hours.

items.title: Two-Control Architecture & 0D Leaf Formulations
items.text:
ModelTree decouples tree growth from leaf modeling and provides rich 0D statistical profiles across terminal nodes:

  1. Model configuration:
  2. GrowthControl configures split search, stopping, and pruning.
  3. LeafControl configures the leaf form, family, solver, penalties, and local slope constraints.
  4. Pass each control to ModelTree as an object or a dictionary.
  5. Rich 0D Formulations:
  6. Produce exact 0D statistics across leaves: prob, odds, log_odds, majority_class, var, skew, kurtosis, median, mad, iqr, entropy, gini, zero_fraction, dispersion.
  7. Access directly via leaf["stats"] or tree.leaf_stats().
  8. Predict 0D formulations row-wise on test data: predict(x, kind="prob"|"odds"|"log_odds"|"median"|"stats").
  9. Dual Monotonicity:
  10. tree_monotone: Enforces directional ordering across tree splits: \((\bar{y}_L - \bar{y}_R) \cdot m \le 0\).
  11. leaf_monotone: Enforces directional sign bounds on local linear leaf slopes (\(\beta_j \ge 0\) for +1, \(\le 0\) for -1).
  12. Row & Column Weights:
  13. sample_weight / row_weights / w: Row-level importance weighting.
  14. col_weights: Feature-level split priorities scaling candidate split gains and weighting feature subsampling during col_sample.
  15. Interaction Groups with Column Names:
  16. Restrict root-to-leaf paths using semantic column names (e.g. interaction_groups=[["age", "income"], ["city_tier"]]).

Run the full example.

uv run python examples/two_controls_and_0d_showcase.py

items.title: 1. Configure growth and leaf controls
items.text:
Give the tree a global split constraint on the first feature. Give each local linear model slope constraints on both features.

from mltreelib import GrowthControl, LeafControl, ModelTree

leaves = LeafControl(
    leaf="linear",
    leaf_family="gaussian",
    l1=0.0,
    l2=1e-3,
    leaf_monotone=[1, -1],  # local feature slope constraints
)

growth = GrowthControl(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=10,
    tree_monotone=[1, 0],   # global split ordering
    col_weights=[2.0, 0.5], # feature split priorities
)
model = ModelTree(growth_control=growth, leaf_control=leaves)

Use the constructor examples to pass the same settings through a configuration dictionary or flat keywords.

items.title: 2. 0D Leaf Formulations & Stats Dictionary
items.text:
Train a tree with 0D probability leaves:

clf = ModelTree(leaf="prob", max_depth=2, min_rows=10)
clf.fit(X, y, sample_weight=weights)

# Inspect the full 0D statistics dictionary on every leaf:
for i, leaf in enumerate(clf.leaves()):
    st = leaf["stats"]
    print(f"Leaf {i}: prob={st['prob']:.4f}, odds={st['odds']:.4f}, entropy={st['entropy']:.4f}")
    print(f"         median={st['median']:.4f}, mad={st['mad']:.4f}, iqr={st['iqr']:.4f}")

# Or get the list of leaf stats directly:
all_stats = clf.leaf_stats()

items.title: 3. Flexible Prediction Kinds
items.text:
Predict response values, probabilities, odds ratios, log-odds, medians, or full per-row stats dictionaries:

# Specific 0D formulations:
preds_prob = clf.predict(X_test, kind="prob")
preds_odds = clf.predict(X_test, kind="odds")
preds_lo   = clf.predict(X_test, kind="log_odds")
preds_med  = clf.predict(X_test, kind="median")

# Full 0D stats profile per observation:
preds_stats = clf.predict(X_test, kind="stats")
# Returns a list of dicts: [{"prob": ..., "odds": ..., "entropy": ..., ...}, ...]

items.title: 4. Interaction Groups with Column Names
items.text:
Enforce LightGBM-style interaction constraints using column name lists:

tree = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=5,
    interaction_groups=[["age", "income"], ["city_tier"]],
)

# Column names resolve automatically during fit:
tree.fit(X, y, col_names=["age", "income", "city_tier"])

# Verify split paths respect the groups:
paths = tree.split_paths()
for path in paths:
    print("Path:", path)

items.title: Unsupervised Trees: Predictive Clustering & Anomaly Triage
items.text:
This guide details mltreelib's unsupervised tree architectures—unifying Predictive Clustering Trees (PCT) for interpretable multi-target segmentation with rule extraction and Extended Isolation Forests (EIF) for artifact-free operational anomaly detection.

Script: examples/suites/unsupervised_trees.py (uv run python examples/suites/unsupervised_trees.py).

items.title: 1. Domain Context & Architectural Rationale
items.text:
Unsupervised learning and operational triage traditionally rely on distance-based heuristics (such as \(k\)-means, DBSCAN, or standard Isolation Forests). In regulated and industrial deployments, these methods exhibit two major failure modes:

  1. Uninterpretable Cluster Boundaries: \(k\)-means and GMMs produce soft Voronoi centroids that cannot be translated into auditable decision rules. A domain expert cannot inspect why an applicant or chemical mixture was assigned to a given cluster without evaluating global distance metrics.
  2. Axis-Aligned Ghost Anomalies: Standard Isolation Forests isolate outliers by sampling cuts parallel to feature coordinate axes. In multi-modal or correlated distributions, axis-aligned cuts create artificial rectangular bands of low average path length, producing false-positive "ghost" anomalies in empty regions between inlier clusters.

mltreelib unifies unsupervised learning through specialized tree engines: - Predictive Clustering Trees (ClusterTree(kind="pct")): Partitions feature space by maximizing multi-target variance reduction across all covariates simultaneously, yielding transparent, human-readable rule bounding boxes. - Extended Isolation Forest (AnomalyTree(kind="eif")): Cuts feature space along random oblique hyperplanes with uniformly sampled normal vectors, producing smooth, rotationally invariant anomaly score contours that eliminate ghost artifacts.

flowchart TD
    subgraph Clustering["ClusterTree (kind='pct' | 'cltree')"]
        direction TB
        C1["Unlabeled Data Matrix"] --> C2{"Divisive Variance Reduction\nacross Multi-Targets"}
        C2 --> C3["Terminal Cluster Partitions\n(n_clusters discovered)"]
        C3 --> C4["Interpretable Rule Extraction\n(e.g., alcohol > 10.5 & volatile_acidity <= 0.4)"]
    end

    subgraph Anomaly["AnomalyTree (kind='eif' | 'isolation')"]
        direction TB
        A1["Telemetry Observations"] --> A2{"Oblique Hyperplane Sampling\nw · (x - p) <= 0"}
        A2 --> A3["Path Length Aggregation h(x)"]
        A3 --> A4["Continuous Anomaly Score s(x, n)\n(Rotationally Invariant Contours)"]
    end

    classDef dataBox fill:#1e293b,stroke:#475569,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;
    classDef splitBox fill:#b45309,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;
    classDef nodeBox fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#2b4c7e,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;
    classDef ruleBox fill:#065f46,stroke:#059669,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;

    class C4 ruleBox;

items.title: 2. Benchmark Study: Wine Quality & Multimodal Anomaly Mixture
items.text:
We evaluate clustering on the Wine Quality benchmark (chemical attributes: fixed acidity, volatile acidity, citric acid, residual sugar, chlorides, alcohol) and anomaly scoring on a 2D multimodal mixture with peripheral outliers.

from mltreelib import load_dataset
from mltreelib.anomaly import AnomalyTree
from mltreelib.cluster import ClusterTree

# 1. Predictive Clustering Trees (PCT) on Wine Quality
data = load_dataset("wine_quality")
features = ["fixed_acidity", "volatile_acidity", "citric_acid", "residual_sugar", "chlorides", "alcohol"]
X_wine = [[float(data["columns"][c][i]) for c in features] for i in range(1500)]

pct = ClusterTree(kind="pct", max_depth=3, min_rows=30)
pct.fit(X_wine, col_names=features)

print(f"Discovered clusters: {pct.n_clusters_}")
for idx, rule in enumerate(pct.rules()[:2]):
    print(f"Cluster {idx} rule: {rule['rule']}")

# 2. Extended Isolation Forest (EIF) with oblique hyperplanes
eif = AnomalyTree(kind="eif", max_depth=8, extension_level=1, seed=42)
eif.fit(X_2d, col_names=["x1", "x2"])
scores = eif.predict(X_query, kind="score")

items.title: 3. Empirical Results: Cluster Partitions & Anomaly Contours
items.text:
=== 1. Predictive Clustering Trees (PCT) on Wine Quality ===
Loaded Wine Quality dataset: 1500 samples, features: ['fixed_acidity', 'volatile_acidity', 'citric_acid', 'residual_sugar', 'chlorides', 'alcohol']
Discovered clusters: 8

=== 2. Extended Isolation Forest vs Axis-Aligned Isolation Forest ===
Generated 2D mixture: 600 inliers (2 clusters), 40 peripheral anomalies.
Outlier sample anomaly scores:
  Axis-Aligned IF : [0.590, 0.531, 0.479, 0.590, 0.590]
  Extended IF     : [0.590, 0.709, 0.597, 0.751, 0.590]

items.title: Key Quantitative Findings
items.text:
1. Auditable Cluster Profiles (Panels 1 & 2): ClusterTree(kind="pct") automatically isolates distinct chemical cohorts (such as high-alcohol/low-acidity dessert wines vs dry table wines) with exact bounding rules.
  2. Elimination of Ghost Anomalies (Panels 3 & 4):
  3. In Panel 3, standard axis-aligned Isolation Forest produces artificial cross-shaped grid ridges between the two normal clusters where empty space is falsely flagged as anomalous.
  4. In Panel 4, Extended Isolation Forest's oblique cuts produce smooth circular density contours centered strictly on genuine sample density.
  5. Outlier Discrimination: EIF elevates anomaly scores for true peripheral outliers (up to 0.751) while keeping inliers below the 0.50 contamination boundary.

items.title: Review a fitted tree before handing it off
items.text:
Use this checklist after you run a modeling pathway. The example uses the concrete strength tree to show what to deliver with a fitted regression model.

Download OpenML concrete strength 46917 to datasets/concrete_compressive_strength.parquet. Run this code from the repository root after uv sync.

from pathlib import Path

from examples.real_tree_studies import load, rows
from mltreelib import ModelTree

df = load("concrete_compressive_strength", 46917).sample(frac=1, random_state=2026)
target = "ConcreteCompressiveStrength"
features = df.columns.drop(target).tolist()
train, test = df.iloc[:824], df.iloc[824:]
tree = ModelTree(leaf="linear", max_depth=2, min_rows=40, prune="none")
tree.fit(rows(train, features), train[target].tolist(), col_names=features)
pred = tree.predict(rows(test, features))

review = test[features + [target]].assign(predicted_mpa=pred)
review["error_mpa"] = review["predicted_mpa"] - review[target]
largest_error = review["error_mpa"].abs().nlargest(5).index
print(review.loc[largest_error].to_string(index=False))
print(tree.split_paths())
print([(leaf["id"], leaf["n"]) for leaf in tree.leaves()])
Path("concrete-tree.dot").write_text(tree.to_dot(), encoding="utf-8")

If Graphviz is installed, render that file with dot -Tsvg concrete-tree.dot -o concrete-tree.svg.

Use the diagram to read the structure. Check boundary routing before transcribing the displayed conditions.

items.title: Prepare the handoff
items.text:
1. Inputs. Record feature order, units, allowed categories and the prediction time. Keep a sample with a missing value.
  2. Evaluation. Report errors for the intended decision. Include the baseline, split method and examples of large errors.
  3. Structure. Export the DOT diagram and keep the structured splits and leaves. Check the support behind the smallest leaves.
  4. Deployment. Compare scores on a fixed set of reference rows after moving the model into the serving environment. Include rows near a split and ones with absent fields.

The concrete strength article compares the tree with constant leaves. The serving contract lists the checks needed when you move from an example to a service. For the original churn exercise, see the secondary case on the dataset page.

items.title: How to use the documentation
items.text:
1. Run one pathway. Get its dataset and follow the analysis from split through evaluation.
  2. Change one part. The example library covers missing routing, alternative leaves, calibration diagnostics, retraining and other focused variations.
  3. Review the decision. Use the evaluation guide, visualization catalog and serving contract.

The dataset setup page lists the downloads. Synthetic checks sit after the practical workflows. They make known effects and missing-data behavior easier to test.

items.title: Extend a model tree
items.text:
Start with a regression or classification pathway. Then choose the change that matches the modeling problem. These options are different decisions, not a checklist to enable together.

Need Technique Read next Outcome is censored at a known bound Tobit leaves Tobit example Domain limits on direction or combinations Monotone or interaction constraints Constraint example Preserve segments while updating leaf models Leaf retraining Retraining examples Control fit complexity and flexibility Growth and leaf settings Growth knob tour Different outcome distributions Distributional families Distributional leaves Predict only from approved input columns Feature and interaction controls Parameters

items.title: Censored outcomes: Tobit
items.text:
Tobit is a model for a latent response observed only above a censoring boundary. Structural zeros, truncation and missing outcomes are different problems. Its interpretation depends on the assumed latent model and censoring mechanism.

from random import Random
from mltreelib import ModelTree

rng = Random(12)
x = [[rng.uniform(-2, 2)] for _ in range(160)]
y = [max(0.0, 0.5 + 2 * row[0] + rng.gauss(0, 1)) for row in x]
model = ModelTree(max_depth=0, min_rows=10, leaf="linear",
                  leaf_family="tobit", tobit_threshold=0.0)
model.fit(x[:120], y[:120], col_names=["signal"])
print("Latent predictions:", model.predict(x[120:])[:3])

The response above is the fitted latent expectation, so negative values are possible even though observations are censored at zero. Evaluate the desired observed outcome separately. Correct censoring assumptions do not guarantee an unbiased result on every dataset. See Tobin (1958).

items.title: Constrain shape and interactions
items.text:
from mltreelib import ModelTree

x = [[float(i)] for i in range(40)]
y = [float(i // 10) for i in range(40)]
model = ModelTree(max_depth=2, min_rows=5, leaf="mean", monotone=[1])
model.fit(x, y, col_names=["volume"])
print("Predictions:", model.predict([[0.0], [10.0], [20.0], [30.0]]))

A positive constraint encodes a domain requirement. Check predictions on meaningful grids and held-out data. A check on the healthcare example found two decreases with linear leaves when age increased. The same check found no decreases with mean leaves. This is a tracked behavior gap; a finite grid does not prove monotonicity elsewhere. Do not assume local coefficient signs guarantee global monotonicity. Interaction constraints restrict paths and should also be checked with split_paths().

items.title: Retrain leaves with fixed partitions
items.text:
from mltreelib import LeafControl, ModelTree

x = [[float(i)] for i in range(40)]
y = [float(i // 10) for i in range(40)]
model = ModelTree(max_depth=1, min_rows=5, leaf="mean")
model.fit(x, y, col_names=["volume"])
before = model.splits()
model.retrain(x, [v + 1 for v in y], control=LeafControl(leaf="mean"))
print("Splits preserved:", before == model.splits())
print("Updated prediction:", model.predict([[5.0]]))

This example mutates the model. Use appropriate independent data for evaluation and check that each leaf has sufficient new observations. Fixed partitions can become stale when the population changes. See the hierarchical retraining guide for alternative feature sets and routing.

items.title: Tune deliberately
items.text: Start with max_depth and min_rows to control partition size. Compare mean and linear leaves only when their assumptions and interpretation fit the outcome. Tune on a validation set and keep a final test set untouched. The knob tour is a parameter reference, not a recommended sequence or a substitute for evaluation.

items.title: 1. Domain Context & The Ghost Anomaly Problem
items.text:
Standard Isolation Forests construct trees by sampling orthogonal, axis-aligned cuts. On correlated or multi-modal feature distributions, axis-aligned splits produce artificial rectangular bands of low average path length, creating false-positive "ghost" anomalies in empty spaces between normal clusters.

AnomalyTree(kind="eif") implements Extended Isolation Forest (EIF), sampling random oblique hyperplanes with uniformly distributed normal vectors. This achieves rotationally invariant scoring contours that isolate true anomalies without axis-aligned artifacts.

items.title: 2. Fit the Reference Model and Score New Rows
items.text:
You can evaluate on industrial telemetry using load_dataset("APSFailure") or the UCI Statlog Shuttle benchmark:

from mltreelib import Metrics, load_dataset
from mltreelib.anomaly import AnomalyTree

# 1. Load industrial sensor telemetry
data = load_dataset("APSFailure")
target = "AirPressureSystemFailure"
features = ["aa_000", "ab_000", "ac_000", "ad_000", "ae_000", "af_000"]
n_sample = 10000

y_raw = data["columns"][target][:n_sample]
y = [1 if v in ("pos", "1", 1) else 0 for v in y_raw]
X = [[data["columns"][c][i] for c in features] for i in range(n_sample)]

split = 7000
X_train = [X[i] for i in range(split) if y[i] == 0]  # Fit reference on normal operating states
X_test, y_test = X[split:], y[split:]

# 2. Fit Extended Isolation Forest (oblique cuts, depth=10)
tree = AnomalyTree(kind="eif", max_depth=10, extension_level=1, seed=42)
tree.fit(X_train, col_names=features)

# 3. Score held-out telemetry
scores = tree.predict(X_test, kind="score")

# 4. Allocate fixed 5% operational review budget
budget = round(0.05 * len(scores))
order = sorted(range(len(scores)), key=lambda i: (-scores[i], i))

hits = sum(y_test[i] for i in order[:budget])
total_anomalies = sum(y_test)
print(f"Review Budget Size : {budget} records (Top 5%)")
print(f"Precision at Budget: {hits / budget:.4f}")
print(f"Recall at Budget   : {hits / max(1, total_anomalies):.4f}")

metrics = Metrics()
print(f"ROC-AUC            : {metrics.roc_curve(y_test, scores)['auc']:.4f}")

kind="binary" returns labels from the fitted threshold, and kind="score" returns the same scores as score_samples(). The extended isolation tree and its aliases also expose kind="path_length".

For a fitted EIF, tree.save("anomalies.json") stores the model and fitted threshold. Use AnomalyTree.load("anomalies.json") to restore scoring and labels. The API reference lists the JSON and byte methods.

items.title: 3. Understand the Anomaly Engine Family
items.text:
AnomalyTree provides a unified interface across multiple tree-based anomaly engines:

Engine (kind) Core Mechanism Best Used For "eif" Oblique random hyperplanes with uniform normals Multi-modal, correlated continuous telemetry without ghost artifacts "isolation" Standard axis-aligned recursive bisection Fast baseline on uncorrelated low-dimensional features "det" Density Estimation Trees (piecewise constant density) Estimating exact probability density distributions "hst" Streaming Half-Space Trees with mass-based scoring Online, real-time sliding window data streams "rct" Robust Random Cut Trees (co-displacement scoring) Dynamic time-series streams with concept drift "active" Active learning tree with expert feedback loops Human-in-the-loop analyst triage queues
